The adapted records are self-contained in Grade9V3; no cross-repository runtime/source link is retained. Gravitational-energy and orbital-angular-momentum records remain explicit extensions.

buckets.title: Universal gravitation, free fall and orbital motion
buckets.badge_reason: The Grade-9 slice requires source-receiver force geometry, model-scope checks, inverse-square scaling, local gravitational acceleration and mass-versus-weight; energy/escape and orbital angular momentum remain explicit extensions.

scope.covers: Grade-9 gravitation competency slice: persistent mutual attraction, source-receiver and centre-distance reasoning, universal-law scaling, local g/free-fall test-mass independence, and mass-versus-weight using local g.
excluded: Multi-source gravitational-field superposition unless an explicit later question demands it.
Pressure, buoyancy and Bernoulli-flow content unless a verified Grade-9 source or real question separately demands it.
Escape-speed derivation and orbital angular-momentum reasoning as ordinary Grade-9 Standard syllabus content.
Advanced orbital mechanics, Kepler-law calculation, inside-source field models and relativistic gravity.

capabilities.action: Represent Newtonian gravitation as a persistent mutual attractive interaction between two bodies, with each force assigned to the correct receiver and directed by source-receiver geometry rather than by motion.
capabilities.success_criterion: Draw equal-and-opposite attractive force vectors on distinct bodies along the centre-to-centre line, and preserve the gravity interaction when a body is supported, rising, falling, or the drawing is rotated.

capabilities.action: Distinguish mass from weight by treating weight as the local gravitational force W = m g while keeping the object's mass separate from the local value of g.
capabilities.success_criterion: Keeps mass unchanged for the same object across locations, uses W = m g, distinguishes force units from mass, and predicts weight changes from local g without claiming that mass changes.

capabilities.action: Relate local gravitational acceleration g to gravitational force per unit test mass, derive its test-mass independence from Newton II, and distinguish local g from the universal constant G.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses g = F_grav/m_test and the external-source relation g proportional to M/r^2, cancels the test mass through F_net = m a, predicts equal ideal free-fall acceleration for different test masses at one location, and does not treat 9.8 m/s^2 as universal everywhere.

capabilities.action: Apply the Newtonian universal-law magnitude F = G m1 m2 / r^2 with the correct centre-to-centre separation and stated point-mass/external-spherical model scope.
capabilities.success_criterion: Names the interacting masses and receiver, checks that point-mass or valid external spherical reduction is appropriate, uses centre-to-centre r, applies mass factors linearly and distance through 1/r^2, and keeps force direction tied to the source-receiver line.

capabilities.action: Compare bound and just-escape states using a declared gravitational-energy reference.
capabilities.success_criterion: Explain why the just-escape case requires greater initial kinetic energy at one radius.

capabilities.action: Determine orbital angular-momentum direction for a central-force motion.
capabilities.success_criterion: State the axial direction normal to the orbital plane.

microtopics.title: Gravity is a persistent mutual attraction fixed by source-receiver geometry
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often make gravity one-sided, motion-dependent, or page-down; the rung must keep body ownership and geometric direction explicit.
entry_assumptions: Can identify two interacting bodies and describe the straight line joining their centres.
microtopics.inferential_jump: In the Newtonian model, the two bodies exert equal-and-opposite attractive forces on distinct receivers along the line joining their centres; support or motion state does not switch the interaction on or redirect it.

teaching_path.action: Draw bodies A and B, mark their centres, and identify which body is the receiver for each gravitational force before drawing arrows.
teaching_path.why_valid: A force statement is incomplete without the body on which the force acts; the source-receiver geometry also fixes the line of action.
teaching_path.output: two bodies, one centre-to-centre line, and explicit force-on-body ownership

teaching_path.action: Draw the force on A toward B and the force on B toward A along the same joining line.
teaching_path.why_valid: Newtonian gravity is attractive and mutual; the interaction pair has equal magnitude, opposite directions, and acts on different bodies.
teaching_path.output: paired attractive force vectors on distinct receivers

teaching_path.action: Keep the source positions fixed while changing A from supported to moving upward to falling, and compare the gravitational-force direction in each state.
teaching_path.why_valid: The gravitational-force direction is set by source-receiver geometry, not by velocity or whether the object is currently falling.
teaching_path.output: same gravity interaction retained across support and motion-state changes

teaching_path.action: Rotate the entire diagram or exchange A/B labels and verify that the force pair rotates with the physical joining line and remains attached to the correct bodies.
teaching_path.why_valid: Page orientation and labels are representational choices; the physical source-receiver geometry is invariant.
teaching_path.output: direction follows geometry, not page-down or name labels

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The larger body pulls on the smaller body, but the smaller body does not exert an equal gravitational interaction back.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Earth pulls on an apple. Does the apple exert a gravitational force on Earth too, and if so on which body does that force act?
misconceptions.repair: Draw the two forces as an interaction pair on different receivers: force on apple toward Earth and force on Earth toward apple.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Gravity acts only while an object is falling; support or upward motion turns gravity off.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A book rests on a table and another ball is moving upward. Is a gravitational force present on each object?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the gravity arrow present whenever the mass-source interaction and Newtonian model apply; support or velocity changes other forces/motion, not the existence of gravity.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The gravitational-force direction follows the object's velocity or always points down the page.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If an object moves upward while Earth remains below it, which way does the gravitational-force arrow point?
misconceptions.repair: Use the source-receiver line. The force points toward the attracting source regardless of the object's instantaneous velocity or page orientation.

exit_task.prompt: For a body near a spherical source, draw the gravitational-force direction while the body is (a) supported and (b) moving upward. Then draw the interaction partner force on the source and explain what stays unchanged when the page is rotated.

answer.summary: Gravity remains present in both motion states; the force on the body points toward the source centre, the partner force acts on the source toward the body, and the pair rotates with the physical geometry rather than the page.
reasoning: Support or upward velocity does not switch off the mass-mass interaction.
The source-receiver line fixes the attractive direction.
The two forces act on different bodies as an equal-and-opposite interaction pair.
Rotating the page changes coordinates, not the physical geometry.
answer.check: Reverse the body's velocity while keeping positions fixed; the gravitational-force direction must remain toward the source.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer is directional and relational; it asserts no computed force magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copied and adapted into the local Grade9V3 contract from richer prior internal Physics engineering material, with only Grade-9-relevant force geometry, body ownership and model behavior retained.

predict.prompt: A ball is moving upward after being thrown. Before reading further, does Earth's gravitational force on it point upward with the motion, downward toward Earth, or disappear at the highest point?
predict.defensible_answer: It points toward Earth throughout the motion; the force direction is set by source-receiver geometry.

attempt.produces: A two-body interaction sketch with one arrow owned by each body and both arrows lying on the centre-to-centre line.

rubric.criterion: Each body owns one inward-directed arrow.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner represents gravity as a mutual interaction rather than a one-sided action.

rubric.criterion: Both arrows are collinear with the two centres.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner ties direction to the bodies rather than to page-up or page-down.

accepted: Both bodies have arrows toward the other on the same joining line, with the body labels attached to the correct arrows.
rejected: Only the smaller body has an arrow because the larger body is treated as the sole source; the interaction pair has been lost.

route.ask: What line is fixed by the positions of the two body centres?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the only direction the pair can share before any force is drawn.

route.ask: If A is pulled toward B, what interaction partner must B have?
route.why_this_ask: It makes the second force a consequence of the pair rather than an added rule.

route.ask: Which way must B's force point if it is gravitational attraction?
route.why_this_ask: The learner completes the paired direction from the same joining line.

route.ask: Would swapping the letters make one force disappear?
route.why_this_ask: The relabelling test removes the idea that one named body uniquely 'does the pulling'.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path draws the interaction pair directly; the learner route begins with one familiar force and requires the second force and its direction to be inferred before the completed pair is shown.

boundary_test.prompt: If the same body is held motionless by a table, should its gravitational-force arrow disappear?
boundary_test.answer: No. The gravity interaction remains; the table supplies an additional support force.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner separates gravitational interaction from the body's motion state.

microtopics.title: Universal gravitation: model scope, centre distance and inverse-square scaling
microtopics.badge_reason: The fragile move is not arithmetic: it is deciding whether the point/external-spherical model applies, defining centre-to-centre r, and keeping mass factors separate from the inverse-square distance factor.
entry_assumptions: Can represent gravity as a persistent mutual attractive interaction with body ownership.
Can compare multiplicative and square factors.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Within the Newtonian point-mass model, or outside a spherically symmetric source where the external reduction is valid, F = G m1 m2/r^2 uses centre-to-centre separation; masses enter linearly, distance through the inverse square, and direction remains toward the attracting source.

teaching_path.action: Identify the two interacting masses, name the receiver, mark both centres, and state whether the bodies can be treated as point masses or by an external spherical reduction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The simple inverse-square relation has a model scope; using it before defining the source/receiver and geometric separation can produce a formally neat but physically undefined result.
teaching_path.output: declared receiver, valid simple-source model, and centre-to-centre separation r

teaching_path.action: With both masses fixed, double r and predict the force factor before substituting any numbers.
teaching_path.why_valid: The distance appears squared in the denominator, so r -> 2r gives F -> F/4.
teaching_path.output: inverse-square distance scaling

teaching_path.action: Restore r, double one mass, and compare the force factor with the distance case.
teaching_path.why_valid: Each mass appears to the first power in the numerator, so doubling one mass doubles the magnitude.
teaching_path.output: linear mass scaling distinguished from inverse-square distance scaling

teaching_path.action: Check the result by testing direction, units/model meaning, and the limiting trend as r becomes larger.
teaching_path.why_valid: A correct Newtonian result must remain attractive, use the stated centre distance/model scope, and decrease toward zero as separation becomes very large.
teaching_path.output: model-validity, direction and limiting-case check

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Doubling the separation halves the gravitational force.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two otherwise identical pairs have centre-to-centre separations r and 2r. Is the second force one half, one quarter, or unchanged?
misconceptions.repair: Apply the square to the distance factor: 2r contributes 1/2^2 = 1/4.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: For spherical bodies, r in the simple inverse-square relation is the gap between the surfaces.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two spherical bodies have radii shown and a surface gap labelled. Which distance belongs in the external Newtonian inverse-square model?
misconceptions.repair: Use the centre-to-centre separation. The external spherical reduction treats the source mass as if concentrated at its centre.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The computed gravitational-force direction should be chosen from the object's motion direction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the receiver moves away from the source, does the gravitational-force direction reverse to follow its velocity?
misconceptions.repair: No. Keep the force attractive along the source-receiver line; motion direction is a separate vector.

exit_task.prompt: Two externally spherical bodies are far enough apart for the external Newtonian model. One mass doubles while their centre-to-centre separation triples. State the force factor, identify the distance used, and state the force direction on the receiver.

answer.summary: The force magnitude becomes 2/9 of the original; r is the centre-to-centre separation, and the force on the receiver points toward the other body's centre.
reasoning: One doubled mass contributes a factor of 2.
Tripling centre-to-centre r contributes 1/3^2 = 1/9.
The combined magnitude factor is 2/9.
The attractive direction is set by source-receiver geometry.
answer.check: Undo only the distance change: the remaining doubled-mass case should be twice the original force.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer checks proportional factors only; it does not assert a measured gravitational constant or force value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copied and adapted into Grade9V3 from richer prior internal force-engineering material; retained items are model scope, centre-distance semantics, inverse-square scaling, direction, and limiting-case checks.

predict.prompt: If two masses are unchanged but their centre-to-centre separation doubles, should the gravitational force become one half or one quarter of its original value?
predict.defensible_answer: One quarter, because the distance is squared in the denominator.

attempt.produces: A two-column factor ledger for changing one mass and changing the separation.

rubric.criterion: Mass changes are applied linearly.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the product m1*m2 rather than squaring a mass.

rubric.criterion: Distance changes are squared in the denominator.
rubric.evidence_of: Using inverse-square rather than inverse-linear scaling.

rubric.criterion: r is identified as centre-to-centre separation.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the intended geometric quantity before scaling.

accepted: mass ×2; separation ×3; force factor 2/9.
rejected: Force factor 2/3, which treats the distance dependence as inverse-linear.

route.ask: What geometric distance does the gravitation model use between two bodies in this representation?
route.why_this_ask: The scaling cannot be trusted until r is identified correctly.

route.ask: If only r changes by a factor k, where does that factor appear in the relation?
route.why_this_ask: It elicits the inverse-square structure before arithmetic.

route.ask: If one mass changes by a factor q, is that factor squared too?
route.why_this_ask: It separates the linear mass dependence from the squared distance dependence.

route.ask: How do independent mass and distance factors combine?
route.why_this_ask: The learner assembles the reusable scaling rule rather than memorising one example.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path demonstrates isolated factor changes; the learner route reconstructs which factor belongs to which part of the proportionality before combining them.

boundary_test.prompt: If the field point/receiver were inside an extended non-point source, is the same external point-mass reduction automatically justified?
boundary_test.answer: No. The simple external-spherical reduction has a scope; an inside-source or otherwise extended distribution needs a different source model.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner treats the inverse-square relation as a model with conditions, not an everywhere-unqualified formula.

microtopics.title: Local gravitational acceleration: force per unit mass and free-fall mass independence
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners can conflate force with field/acceleration, treat 9.8 m/s^2 as universal, or assume a heavier object must accelerate more because it feels a larger gravitational force.
entry_assumptions: Can apply the Newtonian inverse-square force model with its centre-distance scope.
Can use F_net = m a for one chosen body.
microtopics.inferential_jump: At one field point in the Newtonian test-mass model, local g is gravitational force per unit test mass. Combining F_grav = G M m/r^2 with F_net = m a cancels the test mass, giving local acceleration proportional to M/r^2 rather than to the falling object's mass.

teaching_path.action: Choose a source mass M and one spatial point at centre-distance r; distinguish the local gravitational acceleration g at that point from the gravitational force on a particular test mass placed there.
teaching_path.why_valid: Local g characterizes the source/location in the test-mass model; force additionally depends on which test mass is present.
teaching_path.output: one source/location with local g separated from object-specific force

teaching_path.action: For a test mass m at that point, write gravitational force as proportional to M m/r^2 and also as m a under ideal free fall.
teaching_path.why_valid: Both expressions describe the same net gravitational force on the chosen falling body.
teaching_path.output: same test-mass factor m visible in both force descriptions

teaching_path.action: Cancel the common nonzero test-mass factor and interpret the result as local g proportional to M/r^2.
teaching_path.why_valid: The source mass and location remain after the test-mass factor cancels, so the ideal free-fall acceleration is independent of the falling object's mass at that point.
teaching_path.output: a = g at that location; g depends on source/location, not test-mass choice

teaching_path.action: Test two changes separately: double the test mass at fixed location, then move the field point farther from the same source.
teaching_path.why_valid: The first change doubles force but not g; the second changes local g through the source-distance dependence.
teaching_path.output: test-mass independence separated from spatial variation of local g

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A heavier object has a larger gravitational force, so it must have a larger ideal free-fall acceleration.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At one location, a 10 kg object feels twice the gravitational force of a 5 kg object. Must it accelerate twice as fast in ideal free fall?
misconceptions.repair: Use the same mass in both gravity and F = m a. Force and inertia both scale with test mass, so the mass factor cancels from acceleration.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Gravitational force and local g are the same physical quantity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two different masses are placed at the same location. Must the gravitational force and the local g be numerically identical for both?
misconceptions.repair: Local g is force per unit mass. Different masses can feel different forces at the same location while sharing the same local g.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: g is universally 9.8 m/s^2 everywhere.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the same source mass is observed at a much larger centre-distance, must local g stay equal to the near-surface value?
misconceptions.repair: No. The familiar near-Earth value is a local approximation; outside the source, the Newtonian model gives local g proportional to M/r^2.

exit_task.prompt: At one location near the same source, compare a 2 kg and a 6 kg test mass: how do their gravitational forces and ideal free-fall accelerations compare? Then state what happens to the local g if the observation point is moved farther from the source.

answer.summary: The 6 kg mass feels three times the gravitational force, but both test masses have the same ideal free-fall acceleration at that location; moving farther from the same external source decreases local g according to the inverse-square distance dependence.
reasoning: Gravitational force is proportional to test mass.
Newton's second law contains the same test mass as inertia, so the test mass cancels from acceleration.
Local g therefore characterizes the source/location in the test-mass model.
For an external point/spherical source, increasing r decreases g through the 1/r^2 dependence.
answer.check: Double only the test mass: force doubles but g/a does not. Increase only r: local g must decrease.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer compares proportionalities and asserts no numerical value for g.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copied and adapted into Grade9V3 from richer prior internal gravitational-field engineering; multi-source superposition and higher-depth field work were deliberately excluded from this Grade-9 slice.

predict.prompt: A 10 kg object feels twice the gravitational force of a 5 kg object at the same location. Must its ideal free-fall acceleration also be twice as large?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Its inertia is also twice as large, so the acceleration is the same in the ideal free-fall model.

attempt.produces: A two-line derivation showing the falling mass in both gravitational force and F = m a, followed by a same-location comparison of two test masses.

rubric.criterion: The same test mass appears in both force descriptions before cancellation.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner is not hiding the reason mass independence occurs.

rubric.criterion: Force and acceleration are distinguished.
rubric.evidence_of: A heavier object may have larger force while retaining the same acceleration.

accepted: F_grav proportional to M m/r^2 and F_net = m a; cancel m, so a depends on M and r, not the falling mass.
rejected: The heavier object accelerates more because its gravitational force is larger, with no inertial mass comparison.

route.ask: Which body's mass appears in the gravitational force as the test-mass factor?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies the factor whose effect is being questioned.

route.ask: Where does that same body's mass appear in Newton's second law?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must connect force magnitude to inertial response.

route.ask: What happens to that common nonzero factor when the two expressions describe the same force?
route.why_this_ask: The cancellation is the conceptual reason for mass-independent g.

route.ask: What should two different masses do at the same location if air resistance is ignored?
route.why_this_ask: The learner transfers the derivation back to observable motion.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path writes both force descriptions explicitly; the learner route begins from the apparent contradiction of larger force but equal acceleration and reconstructs the shared mass factor.

boundary_test.prompt: Does test-mass independence mean local g must have the same value at every distance from the source?
boundary_test.answer: No. It means g at one location is independent of the chosen test mass; g can still vary with source mass and distance.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner separates test-mass independence from spatial constancy.

microtopics.title: Mass stays with the object; weight is its local gravitational force
microtopics.badge_reason: Everyday language and scale readings encourage mass/weight conflation; the learner must keep object mass, local g, and gravitational force as different quantities.
entry_assumptions: Can explain local gravitational acceleration g.
Can distinguish a force from a mass.
microtopics.inferential_jump: For the same object, mass is kept distinct from local gravitational acceleration, while weight is the gravitational force W = m g and therefore changes if local g changes.

teaching_path.action: Place the same unchanged object at locations A and B and keep its mass m explicitly the same in both records.
teaching_path.why_valid: The comparison changes environment/location, not which object is being considered.
teaching_path.output: same object, same mass m, possibly different local g

teaching_path.action: At each location identify weight as the local gravitational force and write W = m g.
teaching_path.why_valid: Weight is a force on the object, whereas mass is the object's inertial/gravitational mass parameter in this model.
teaching_path.output: W_A = m g_A and W_B = m g_B

teaching_path.action: Halve local g without changing the object and compare mass, weight, and units.
teaching_path.why_valid: For fixed m, weight scales with g; mass remains in kilograms while weight is a force.
teaching_path.output: same mass; half g gives half weight

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Mass and weight are the same quantity, so a smaller weight reading means the object's mass decreased.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: The same object is moved to a location where local g is smaller. Which changes: the object's mass, its weight, or both?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the object's mass fixed. Weight is the local gravitational force W = m g, so changing g changes weight without changing mass.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Because local g is often written near 9.8, weight is effectively a fixed property of the object everywhere.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Would the same object necessarily have the same weight at a location with a different local gravitational acceleration?
misconceptions.repair: No. Weight follows the local g through W = m g; the same object's mass is the quantity held fixed.

exit_task.prompt: The same object is moved from location A to B, where local g is half as large. Compare its mass and weight, identify which quantity is a force, and state the relation used.

answer.summary: The mass is unchanged; the weight at B is half the weight at A. Weight is the force and obeys W = m g.
reasoning: The object is unchanged, so its mass stays m.
Weight is the local gravitational force.
With the same m and half the local g, W is halved.
answer.check: Return the object to location A: its weight returns to the original value without any mass change.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer uses a relative factor only; it asserts no numerical value of g or weight.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copied and adapted into the local Grade9V3 contract from prior internal gravitation engineering, keeping only the mass/weight distinction needed by the current Grade-9 competency.

predict.prompt: If an unchanged object is taken somewhere that local g is smaller, which can change: its mass, its weight, or both?
predict.defensible_answer: Its weight can change; its mass stays the same for the unchanged object in this model.

attempt.produces: A two-location table with columns for mass, local g and weight.

rubric.criterion: The mass entry is unchanged between locations.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating the object property from local gravitational force.

rubric.criterion: Weight changes in the same factor as g for fixed mass.
rubric.evidence_of: Using W = m g as a local force relation.

accepted: same m; if g halves, W halves.
rejected: Mass halves because the scale reading/weight halves.

route.ask: Did the object itself change when it moved between locations?
route.why_this_ask: It fixes the mass comparison before introducing the local force.

route.ask: What physical force does 'weight' represent here?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents weight from being treated as a synonym for mass.

route.ask: For fixed m, how should W respond if g changes by a factor?
route.why_this_ask: The learner derives the scaling instead of memorising two labels.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path states W = m g after fixing the object; the learner route begins with the physical identity of the object and reconstructs why only weight follows local g.

boundary_test.prompt: If two locations have the same local g and the same unchanged object is used, can W = m g alone produce different weights?
boundary_test.answer: No. Same m and same g give the same weight.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner ties weight changes to mass and local gravitational acceleration rather than to location labels.

microtopics.title: Gravitational binding uses a chosen zero of potential energy
microtopics.badge_reason: The rung must keep potential, kinetic, and total energy distinct while comparing bound motion with just-escape motion.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish kinetic energy from force and can use conservation of mechanical energy qualitatively.
Can describe a reference choice for an energy zero.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Gravitational potential energy is negative when zero is chosen at infinite separation, and changes in that energy trade with kinetic energy in orbital and escape problems.

teaching_path.action: Choose infinite separation as the zero reference, then mark a finite separation as a bound configuration below that reference.
teaching_path.why_valid: Potential energy values require a reference choice; with zero at infinite separation, attraction makes finite-separation gravitational potential energy negative.
teaching_path.output: infinite separation: potential reference = 0 | finite bound separation: potential energy < 0

teaching_path.action: At one fixed radius, increase the object's speed while keeping the source mass and energy reference unchanged.
teaching_path.why_valid: At fixed separation the gravitational potential term is unchanged, so the energy change enters through kinetic energy.
teaching_path.output: same radius + faster motion -> same gravitational potential term + greater kinetic term

teaching_path.action: Compare circular bound motion with the limiting case that just reaches infinite separation with no speed left.
teaching_path.why_valid: The just-escape case must reach the chosen zero-potential reference without residual kinetic energy, so it requires more initial kinetic energy than a bound circular case at the same radius.
teaching_path.output: same launch radius | bound circular case: remains finite | just-escape case: reaches infinity with final speed = 0

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Negative gravitational potential energy means the object has negative total energy in every gravitational motion.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can a moving satellite have negative potential energy but positive kinetic energy at the same instant?
misconceptions.repair: Keep potential, kinetic, and total energy separate; the sign of one term does not determine the sign of each other term.

exit_task.prompt: At one radius from a central mass, compare a bound circular case with a just-escape case. Explain why the escape case needs the greater initial speed without deriving a speed formula.

answer.summary: The escape case needs greater initial kinetic energy because it must climb from negative gravitational potential energy to the zero reference at infinite separation while arriving with no kinetic energy left.
reasoning: Both cases begin at the same radius, so they share the same gravitational potential energy initially.
The chosen zero lies at infinite separation, above the finite-radius potential value.
Just escape must supply enough kinetic energy to reach that zero-energy boundary, so it requires more initial kinetic energy than the bound circular case.
answer.check: Change the chosen numerical zero of potential energy while preserving all energy differences; the physical comparison between bound and just-escape cases must remain unchanged.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer compares energy signs and relative requirements without asserting a calculated speed or energy value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created conceptual energy rung. It avoids introducing the blocked potential-energy and escape-speed equations as library relations while preserving the matrix's qualitative distinction.

predict.prompt: A satellite at one radius has negative gravitational potential energy. Does that force its kinetic energy to be negative too?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Kinetic energy can be positive at the same instant; the terms must be tracked separately.

attempt.produces: A qualitative energy ledger for a bound case and a just-escape case at the same starting radius.

rubric.criterion: Both cases use the same potential-energy zero.
rubric.evidence_of: The sign comparison is made against one declared reference.

rubric.criterion: The escape case is assigned the larger initial kinetic contribution.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner connects escape to reaching the zero-energy boundary rather than to a memorized speed formula.

accepted: The ledger marks finite-radius potential energy below zero, positive kinetic energy, and a larger initial kinetic contribution for the just-escape case.
rejected: The response says 'potential is negative, therefore all energy is negative' and never separates the kinetic contribution.

route.ask: Where has the potential-energy zero been chosen?
route.why_this_ask: A sign has no meaning until its reference is fixed.

route.ask: At the same radius, which energy contribution changes when only speed changes?
route.why_this_ask: It separates the state set by position from the motion term.

route.ask: What must be true at infinity in the just-escape boundary case?
route.why_this_ask: The learner constructs the target state used to compare required starting energy.

route.ask: Why does that boundary require more initial kinetic energy than remaining bound?
route.why_this_ask: It elicits the qualitative energy trade rather than an equation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative construction fixes the zero and walks through a speed change before naming the escape boundary; the elicitation begins by challenging the sign misconception and makes the learner build the reference-state comparison themselves.

boundary_test.prompt: If the potential-energy zero were shifted to a different reference, would the required physical escape speed change?
boundary_test.answer: No. Shifting the zero changes assigned potential values but not the energy differences that govern the motion.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner distinguishes a chosen potential-energy reference from the physical energy change needed for escape.

microtopics.title: Central gravity conserves orbital angular momentum about the centre
microtopics.badge_reason: The rung is both an origin condition and an axial-direction distinction, so the orbital plane and viewing side must remain explicit.
entry_assumptions: Can identify the line from a chosen centre to a moving body and the direction of its motion.
Can use an out-of-plane convention for an axial quantity.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A central gravitational force has zero torque about the source centre, so orbital angular momentum is conserved; its axial-vector direction is perpendicular to the orbital plane.

teaching_path.action: Mark the source centre O, a satellite position, and its motion direction in one orbital plane.
teaching_path.why_valid: The angular-momentum statement needs a specified origin and the plane defined by position and motion.
teaching_path.output: origin O | position arrow: in orbital plane | motion arrow: in orbital plane

teaching_path.action: Draw the gravitational force back toward O at several satellite positions and compare its line with the position arrow each time.
teaching_path.why_valid: A central force is collinear with the position line from O, so it has no lever arm about O and cannot change total orbital angular momentum there.
teaching_path.output: position 1: force line through O -> zero turning effect | position 2: force line through O -> zero turning effect

teaching_path.action: View the same physical orbit from the opposite face and reapply the axial direction convention instead of relying on clockwise words alone.
teaching_path.why_valid: The physical angular-momentum direction is fixed by the cross-product orientation, while the viewer's page symbol changes when the viewing side reverses.
teaching_path.output: same physical orbit | front view: axial symbol one way | back view: page symbol reversed, physical axial direction unchanged

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Angular momentum points along the direction the satellite is moving around the orbit.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A satellite moves in the page. Is its angular momentum vector in the page or perpendicular to it?
misconceptions.repair: Use the cross-product orientation: position and momentum lie in the orbital plane; angular momentum is axial and normal to that plane.

exit_task.prompt: A satellite's position and motion are drawn in an orbital plane around centre O. State the angular-momentum direction and explain why the central gravitational force does not change total angular momentum about O.

answer.summary: Orbital angular momentum is perpendicular to the orbital plane, with its axial direction set by the position-to-motion orientation; central gravity acts along the position line through O, so it supplies no turning effect about O.
reasoning: Position and motion lie in the orbital plane and define an oriented pair.
The associated angular-momentum direction is normal to that plane rather than tangent to the path.
Gravity points through O, leaving no lever arm about O, so total angular momentum about that centre remains unchanged.
answer.check: Reverse the viewing side but not the physical orbit; the page symbol may reverse, yet the physical axial direction and conservation statement must remain the same.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The response identifies an axial direction and a conservation condition without computing angular momentum, torque, or orbital speed.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created central-force and axial-direction rung. It deliberately avoids adding a quantitative orbital relation and uses the out-of-plane convention as the key representation check.

predict.prompt: A satellite moves counter-clockwise as seen from one side of its orbital plane. Does its angular momentum point along the tangent direction of motion?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Its angular momentum is axial and perpendicular to the orbital plane, with direction determined from the position and motion orientation.

attempt.produces: An orbital-plane sketch with in-plane position and motion arrows plus one normal axial-direction marker tied to a named viewing side.

rubric.criterion: The angular-momentum marker is normal to the orbital plane.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner distinguishes an axial quantity from the in-plane polar vectors.

rubric.criterion: The central force is drawn through the source centre.
rubric.evidence_of: The conservation claim is justified from zero turning effect about the same origin.

accepted: The diagram keeps position and motion in the plane, places angular momentum normal to it, and shows each gravitational-force line passing through O.
rejected: Angular momentum is drawn tangent to the orbit because it is confused with the satellite's motion direction.

route.ask: Which two directions lie in the orbital plane at the satellite's current position?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies the pair whose orientation determines the axial quantity.

route.ask: Where does the gravitational-force line pass relative to O?
route.why_this_ask: It exposes the central-force geometry before conservation is named.

route.ask: What direction is left for an axial quantity built from two in-plane directions?
route.why_this_ask: The learner supplies the out-of-plane distinction rather than copying an arrow.

route.ask: What changes in the page symbol when you look from the opposite side?
route.why_this_ask: It tests the convention against viewpoint reversal.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path establishes the plane, demonstrates the central-force geometry, then checks viewpoint reversal; the learner route withholds the axial direction until the in-plane pair and origin geometry have been identified.

boundary_test.prompt: If a small non-central thrust acts on the satellite, may the same angular-momentum conservation claim about O be assumed?
boundary_test.answer: No. A force not directed through O can provide a turning effect about O, so the conservation condition must be checked again.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner ties conservation to central-force geometry about the named origin rather than to orbital motion in general.

question_families.title: Gravitational interaction, model-scope, local-g and weight practice
solution_structure: Identify the interacting bodies and the receiver; separate force vectors from velocity/motion vectors.
Check whether the point-mass or external-spherical Newtonian model is valid and define centre-to-centre r.
For force scaling, separate linear mass factors from the inverse-square distance factor.
For local g/free fall, separate source/location from the chosen test mass and use the test-mass cancellation through F = m a.
For mass-versus-weight, keep mass, local g and force in distinct roles with W = m g.
Use energy/escape or orbital-angular-momentum reasoning only when the question explicitly demands that extension.
Verify direction, units/model meaning, and a limiting or counterfactual case.

demand_dimensions.model_choice: Decide whether the bucket's authored construction applies before using it.
demand_dimensions.representation_translation: Translate the task into already-authored quantities or directions without changing the physical claim.
demand_dimensions.reasoning_steps: Carry the authored reasoning sequence through its independent check rather than stopping at a label.
demand_dimensions.novelty: Map unfamiliar roles onto already-taught quantities; no new scientific relation is introduced by practice.

safe_variations: Change surface labels, orientation, or context while preserving the same authored decision structure.
transfer_boundaries: The learner must test the conservation condition after an additional non-central force is introduced rather than applying central-force conservation automatically.
common_wrong_routes: A massive body pulls on a smaller body, but the smaller body does not pull back with an equal interaction.

questions.stem: Two separated bodies are shown with their centres marked. Draw the gravitational-force direction on each body and explain what changes if the body labels are exchanged.

answer.summary: Each body has a gravitational-force arrow directed toward the other along the same centre-to-centre line; exchanging labels only exchanges ownership of the arrows.
reasoning: The two centres determine the common line of action.
The force on A points from A toward B.
The force on B points from B toward A, so the interaction remains paired when labels swap.
answer.check: Rotate the entire drawing without changing the bodies or their separation; both force arrows should rotate with the joining line rather than stay tied to the page.

hints.text: Start by asking yourself: What line is fixed by the positions of the two body centres?
Treat gravity as an interaction pair: each body experiences a force directed toward the other along the same line.

teaching_routes.title: Declarative Grade-9 gravitation route: force geometry → inverse-square model → local g → weight
entry_needs: Start from mutual gravitation; use Newton II only where free-fall acceleration is derived. Energy/escape and orbital angular momentum are extension records, not ordinary Grade-9 Standard scope.
learner_actions: Assign each gravitational force to the correct receiver and use source-receiver geometry for direction.
Check the point/external-spherical model and use centre-to-centre r before applying inverse-square scaling.
Separate object-specific gravitational force from local g and derive test-mass independence with Newton II.
Distinguish mass from weight using W = m g.
Enter binding/escape or orbital-angular-momentum reasoning only under explicit extension demand.
help_plan: Ask which body owns the force arrow before discussing magnitude.
Mark the source centre and receiver/field point before giving the inverse-square factor.
Keep the same test mass visible in both gravity and F = m a before cancellation.
Use separate columns for mass, local g and weight.
Do not expose field superposition or orbital formulas as Grade-9 core support.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: Completed Grade-9 core reasoning is visible; retained R4/R5 extension reasoning remains explicitly separable from the core competency slice.

source_preferences.reason: The imported candidate has no authority and is not used as a normative source.

when_not_suitable: Do not use this route to imply that multi-source field superposition, pressure/buoyancy, escape speed or orbital angular momentum belongs to the ordinary Grade-9 core slice.
Do not treat the near-Earth value of g as universal or the external spherical model as valid inside arbitrary mass distributions.

teaching_routes.title: Elicited Grade-9 gravitation route: reconstruct force, model scope, local g and weight
entry_needs: Same Grade-9 core as Core1A, with learner commitments before each model response; extension rungs are entered only when separately demanded.
learner_actions: Predict whether gravity persists when motion/support state changes.
Predict mass and distance scaling only after naming the receiver and centre distance.
Resolve why larger gravitational force on a heavier body does not mean larger free-fall acceleration.
Predict what changes between mass and weight when local g changes.
Enter energy/orbit reconstruction only for separately justified extension demand.
help_plan: Use a supported/upward-moving counterexample before explaining persistent gravity.
Ask which distance the model requires before correcting inverse-square arithmetic.
Ask where the test mass appears in both equations before cancelling it.
Ask whether the object itself changed before correcting mass/weight confusion.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: Prediction and attempt precede reconstruction for the Grade-9 core; extension records retain their existing elicitation closures.

source_preferences.reason: The authored source supplies the complete closure needed for independent study.

when_not_suitable: Do not turn local-g reconstruction into multi-source field superposition.
Do not present extension rungs as default Grade-9 teaching.

subject: Physics
scope_summary: Grade-9 Work, Energy and Power spine adapted from the repository owner's richer prior Physics engineering corpus and localized to Grade9V3. It preserves system-boundary energy accounting, signed work, kinetic/potential energy, conditional mechanical-energy conservation and power without inheriting donor readiness or curriculum authority.

resources.title: Adapted local Work, Energy and Power teaching source
resources.section: Signed work, energy accounting, conservation conditions and power
resources.rights_status: Author-created project draft; no external curriculum or scientific-review authority claimed.
resources.selection_reason: Copies and adapts durable Work/Energy semantics into the local Grade9V3 teaching contract; no cross-repository dependency or donor release authority remains.

buckets.title: Work, energy and power
buckets.badge_reason: The main difficulty is choosing the analysed object/system, preserving work sign and reference choices, and distinguishing total-energy accounting from the conditional K+U mechanical-energy shortcut.

conventions.statement: Name the object or collection whose energy account is being discussed before classifying transfers.
For work, compare the force direction with the actual displacement direction before assigning a sign.

scope.covers: Grade-9 work, kinetic and near-Earth gravitational potential energy, work-energy reasoning, explicit system-boundary energy accounting, conditional mechanical-energy conservation, quantitative relation choice, derivations and average-power reasoning.
excluded: Variable-force integration and calculus-based work.
Elastic potential-energy formulae and other higher-grade stores unless separately demanded.
Treating K + U = constant as unconditional in dissipative or externally driven cases.

capabilities.action: Classify work as positive, zero, or negative from force and displacement directions.
capabilities.success_criterion: Chooses one body/event and displacement, classifies positive/zero/negative work from the force component along that displacement, and rejects perpendicular force as a work contribution.

capabilities.action: Relate the sign of net work to the direction of kinetic-energy change.
capabilities.success_criterion: Builds net work from all force contributions on the same chosen body/interval and maps its sign to increase, no change or decrease in kinetic energy.

capabilities.action: Decide whether an interaction may be represented by a potential-energy change.
capabilities.success_criterion: Reject kinetic friction as an endpoint-only potential-energy account.

capabilities.action: Declare the physical system and decide whether K + U may be treated as constant or whether non-conservative/external transfer must remain explicit.
capabilities.success_criterion: States the system/boundary, distinguishes total-energy conservation from mechanical-energy conservation, and rejects unchanged K + U when frictional or external transfer changes the mechanical account.

capabilities.action: Distinguish total work from average power and decide when instantaneous power can be determined.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses W/Delta t for an interval average and requires same-instant force/velocity information for instantaneous power.

capabilities.action: Calculate Grade 9 work, kinetic energy and near-Earth gravitational potential-energy changes and connect them with work-energy and conservation conditions.
capabilities.success_criterion: Selects W, K, ΔU, work-energy or K+U relations only after declaring body/system, frame/reference and model conditions, and checks whether non-conservative transfer is zero before using mechanical-energy conservation.

capabilities.action: Derive K = 0.5 m v^2 and the near-Earth raised-body potential-energy expression from already-authored work, force and motion relations.
capabilities.success_criterion: Shows the relation chain and model assumptions for both derivations rather than presenting either expression as a memorized formula.

microtopics.title: Only the along-path part of a force contributes to work
microtopics.badge_reason: Force size alone feels decisive until a strong perpendicular force is contrasted with the actual displacement.
entry_assumptions: Can identify one chosen body, its displacement over the stated interval, and the direction of a force acting on that same body.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Work depends on how a force points relative to the actual displacement: along the motion gives positive work, opposite gives negative work, and a perpendicular force gives zero work.

teaching_path.action: Draw one displacement direction and compare three force arrows: along it, perpendicular to it, and opposite it.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding the path fixed isolates orientation as the only thing changing.
teaching_path.output: case A: force along path.  case B: force perpendicular to path.  case C: force opposite path.

teaching_path.action: For each case, ask whether the force has a part that carries the object along the path direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: Work records transfer through displacement, so only the force contribution along that displacement can change the work sign.
teaching_path.output: along -> positive.  perpendicular -> zero.  opposite -> negative.

teaching_path.action: Increase the size of the perpendicular force while keeping it exactly perpendicular to the same path.
teaching_path.why_valid: If orientation, not force size alone, controls the zero-work case, enlarging a perpendicular force must leave the work classification unchanged.
teaching_path.output: larger perpendicular force -> work still zero.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any force acting on a moving object does positive work because the object moves.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A mass moves in a circle while a force points toward the centre. Does that inward force do work along the instantaneous tangential displacement?
misconceptions.repair: Compare the force direction with the actual displacement direction; only the along-path contribution can produce work.

exit_task.prompt: Three forces act separately during the same rightward displacement: one rightward, one upward, and one leftward. Classify the work sign in each case without calculating a magnitude.

answer.summary: Rightward force: positive work. Upward force: zero work. Leftward force: negative work.
reasoning: The rightward force points with the displacement.
The upward force is perpendicular to the displacement.
The leftward force points against the displacement.
answer.check: Rotate the path instead of the force arrows; the classifications must follow the relative orientation, not page directions by themselves.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer classifies work sign only; it contains no computed work value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Local Grade9V3 work-sign construction enriched from prior internal engineering with same-object/event and constant-force model discipline; no donor runtime link remains.

predict.prompt: A strong force points exactly upward while an object moves exactly right. Before using any formula, should that force do positive work on the rightward displacement?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Because the force is perpendicular to the displacement, its work on that displacement is zero.

attempt.produces: A positive/zero/negative classification for three force directions relative to one fixed displacement, plus a short reason for each.

rubric.criterion: The perpendicular case is classified as zero even when the force is large.
rubric.evidence_of: Using orientation rather than force size alone.

rubric.criterion: Along and opposite cases receive opposite work signs.
rubric.evidence_of: Tracking whether the force contribution aids or opposes the displacement.

accepted: 'Along: positive; perpendicular: zero; opposite: negative, because only the along-path contribution sets the sign.'
rejected: 'All three are positive because a force acts while the object moves.' This ignores the force/path orientation.

route.ask: Which way does the object actually move during the interval?
route.why_this_ask: The path direction must be fixed before the force can be compared with it.

route.ask: For the upward force, does any part of that arrow point along the rightward path?
route.why_this_ask: The learner reaches the zero case geometrically before receiving a sign rule.

route.ask: What changes when the force is flipped to point left while the path stays rightward?
route.why_this_ask: The opposite case makes the sign distinction visible.

route.ask: If the upward arrow gets longer but stays perpendicular, should the classification change?
route.why_this_ask: The variation checks whether force size has been incorrectly substituted for orientation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path states all three orientation cases. The learner route begins from the perpendicular counterexample, then reconstructs the sign pattern and tests it by changing force size.

boundary_test.prompt: The object has no displacement during the interval. Can a force do work through that interval in this displacement-based account?
boundary_test.answer: No. With no displacement, there is no along-path transfer to count as work in this account.
boundary_test.confirms: Work here requires displacement as well as force orientation.

microtopics.title: Net work sign tracks kinetic-energy change
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners may attach energy change to one named force rather than to the combined work of all forces.
entry_assumptions: Can classify the sign of each force's work from its direction relative to displacement.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The combined work of all acting forces determines the direction of kinetic-energy change: positive net work increases it, zero net work leaves it unchanged, and negative net work decreases it.

teaching_path.action: Keep the same initial motion and compare three cases whose combined work is positive, zero, or negative.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding the initial state fixed isolates net-work sign as the changed condition.
teaching_path.output: case A: net work positive.  case B: net work zero.  case C: net work negative.

teaching_path.action: Match each net-work sign to whether the motion ends with greater, unchanged, or smaller kinetic energy.
teaching_path.why_valid: Net work is the energy transfer associated with the change in kinetic energy; the sign fixes the direction of that change.
teaching_path.output: positive -> kinetic energy increases.  zero -> unchanged.  negative -> decreases.

teaching_path.action: Use a braking situation as a check: the braking contribution points opposite the motion and the object slows.
teaching_path.why_valid: A familiar negative-work case should agree with a decrease in kinetic energy if the sign mapping is correct.
teaching_path.output: braking case: net work negative -> final kinetic energy lower than initial.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Only a positive force magnitude can increase kinetic energy; negative work cannot be represented physically.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A braking force acts opposite the motion. What sign is its work, and what should happen to kinetic energy?
misconceptions.repair: Combine the work of all acting forces to obtain net work, then match its sign to whether kinetic energy increases, stays unchanged, or decreases.

exit_task.prompt: For three otherwise comparable motions, the net work is described as positive, zero, and negative. State the corresponding direction of kinetic-energy change without calculating any energy value.

answer.summary: Positive net work means kinetic energy increases; zero means no change; negative means kinetic energy decreases.
reasoning: The comparison holds the starting motion fixed.
The sign of the combined work indicates the sign of the kinetic-energy change.
No individual force alone decides the result unless it is the only contributor.
answer.check: Use braking as the negative case: slowing must correspond to a decrease in kinetic energy.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer states only increase/no-change/decrease and contains no computed energy value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created sign mapping with no numerical work-energy equation.

predict.prompt: A moving object is braking. Before calculating anything, should the combined work over the braking interval correspond to increasing or decreasing kinetic energy?
predict.defensible_answer: Decreasing kinetic energy, so the net work over the interval is negative.

attempt.produces: A three-row mapping from net-work sign to kinetic-energy change, with the braking case used as one check.

rubric.criterion: Positive, zero, and negative net work map to increase, no change, and decrease respectively.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating sign from magnitude while preserving the energy-change direction.

rubric.criterion: The braking example is placed in the negative/decrease row.
rubric.evidence_of: Connecting the abstract sign mapping to a physical check.

accepted: 'Positive -> increase; zero -> unchanged; negative -> decrease. Braking belongs in negative -> decrease.'
rejected: 'Negative work means negative kinetic energy.' This confuses a change with the nonnegative energy quantity itself.

route.ask: During braking, is the force contribution along the motion or opposite it?
route.why_this_ask: The prior rung supplies the sign without introducing a new equation.

route.ask: Does the object end the interval moving with more or less kinetic energy than it began?
route.why_this_ask: The observable motion gives the direction of energy change.

route.ask: Which net-work sign belongs with that decrease?
route.why_this_ask: The learner links sign to change rather than memorizing the three-row table.

route.ask: What should zero net work imply in the same comparison?
route.why_this_ask: The zero case closes the mapping and tests that zero means no change rather than no energy.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path presents the sign mapping then checks braking. The learner route starts from braking, infers the negative/decrease connection, then generalizes to the complete mapping.

boundary_test.prompt: An object has nonzero kinetic energy throughout an interval but the net work over that interval is zero. Must the kinetic energy itself be zero?
boundary_test.answer: No. Zero net work means the kinetic energy does not change; it may remain nonzero.
boundary_test.confirms: The rule concerns change in kinetic energy, not the existence of kinetic energy.

microtopics.title: Potential energy belongs only to endpoint-determined interactions
microtopics.badge_reason: It is tempting to hide every force inside an energy label, especially once gravitational potential energy is familiar.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish work contributions by sign and can reason about the net work over a path.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Potential energy can replace the work bookkeeping for an interaction only when the relevant energy change is fixed by the endpoints; path-dependent friction must remain an explicit transfer.

teaching_path.action: Choose two routes between the same starting and ending heights and compare the gravitational energy change.
teaching_path.why_valid: If the endpoint change is the same for both routes, the account does not need the detailed path to determine that interaction's energy change.
teaching_path.output: route A: same start/end heights.  route B: same start/end heights.  gravitational potential-energy change: same.

teaching_path.action: Now add kinetic friction and compare a short route with a longer route between comparable endpoints.
teaching_path.why_valid: Friction acts along the travelled path, so changing path length changes its energy transfer even when endpoints are comparable.
teaching_path.output: short path -> smaller friction transfer.  longer path -> larger friction transfer.

teaching_path.action: Ask whether one endpoint-only energy label could predict both friction cases without knowing which path was taken.
teaching_path.why_valid: If two paths with comparable endpoints give different friction transfers, endpoint information alone cannot represent that interaction.
teaching_path.output: friction: path identity required; endpoint-only potential-energy replacement rejected.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every force can be assigned a potential energy so that its work can be hidden inside U.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can kinetic friction be represented by a single potential-energy difference that depends only on the start and finish positions?
misconceptions.repair: Use potential energy only for interactions whose energy change is fixed by endpoints; keep path-dependent friction as an explicit transfer.

exit_task.prompt: Two routes share the same start and finish heights. Gravity gives the same potential-energy change on both, while friction removes more energy on the longer route. Which interaction is eligible for endpoint-only potential-energy bookkeeping?

answer.summary: Gravity is eligible in this comparison; kinetic friction is not, because its transfer changes with the path.
reasoning: The gravitational potential-energy change is fixed by the shared endpoints.
The frictional transfer changes when the route length changes.
An endpoint-only account cannot represent a path-dependent interaction.
answer.check: Change the route while keeping the endpoints fixed; an eligible endpoint-only contribution stays the same while the frictional transfer need not.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer classifies interactions by endpoint versus path dependence and computes no energy value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created path-dependence discrimination; no potential-energy formula is asserted.

predict.prompt: Two paths start and end at the same heights, but one is much longer and rough. Before calculating, can one endpoint-only energy label represent the frictional transfer on both paths?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Friction depends on the travelled path, so comparable endpoints do not fix its transfer.

attempt.produces: A two-column classification of gravity and kinetic friction as endpoint-determined or path-dependent, supported by the two-route comparison.

rubric.criterion: Gravity is classified as endpoint-determined for the stated height comparison.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the unchanged start/end heights across routes.

rubric.criterion: Kinetic friction is classified as path-dependent.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing that route length changes the frictional transfer.

accepted: 'Gravity: endpoint-determined here. Friction: path-dependent, so keep its transfer explicit.'
rejected: 'Both get potential energy because both are forces.' This ignores the path test.

route.ask: If the start and finish heights are unchanged, what happens to the gravitational potential-energy change when the route bends?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the endpoint-only comparison using a familiar interaction.

route.ask: What changes for friction when the travelled route becomes longer?
route.why_this_ask: The contrasting interaction exposes path dependence.

route.ask: Could one endpoint-only label distinguish the short and long friction routes?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must test the proposed bookkeeping against two cases it would have to separate.

route.ask: Which interaction can therefore be replaced by an endpoint energy change in this comparison?
route.why_this_ask: The classification is produced from the path test rather than memorized as a list.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path gives the two-route comparisons. The learner route first establishes one endpoint-determined case, then breaks the same idea with friction and derives the eligibility rule.

boundary_test.prompt: Two different routes have the same start and finish but, by coincidence, friction removes the same amount of energy on both. Does that coincidence prove friction is endpoint-determined?
boundary_test.answer: No. A single matching pair does not remove the path dependence; changing the path can still change the frictional transfer.
boundary_test.confirms: Eligibility is about dependence on endpoints in general, not accidental equality in one example.

microtopics.title: Mechanical energy is constant only after the system and transfer account close
microtopics.badge_reason: The familiar K+U equality is easy to apply before declaring the system or checking friction/external transfer, which confuses total-energy conservation with the narrower mechanical-energy shortcut.
entry_assumptions: Can decide which interactions belong in potential energy and which transfers must remain explicit.
Can identify a chosen physical system and its initial/final states.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Energy conservation is broader than K+U conservation: after the system boundary and energy stores/transfers are declared, K+U may be treated as constant only when no non-conservative or unaccounted dissipative/external transfer changes that mechanical account.

teaching_path.action: Choose the physical system and initial/final states, then list which energy stores are inside the account and which transfers cross its boundary.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same physical interaction can appear as an internal store change or an external transfer depending on the declared system; declaring the boundary prevents omission and double counting.
teaching_path.output: explicit system boundary, K/U stores and crossing transfers

teaching_path.action: Compare a smooth descent with a rough descent between the same endpoints using the same declared system and reference.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding the states and account fixed isolates frictional/non-conservative transfer as the changed condition.
teaching_path.output: smooth case: no dissipative transfer in the mechanical account; rough case: dissipative transfer present

teaching_path.action: Track K and U in both cases and mark an explicit transfer/non-mechanical channel in the rough case instead of forcing K+U to stay constant.
teaching_path.why_valid: Total energy can remain conserved while the selected mechanical stores decrease because energy is transferred to other stores or the environment.
teaching_path.output: smooth -> K+U can remain constant when conditions close; rough -> Δ(K+U) follows the non-conservative transfer

teaching_path.action: Before writing K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f, ask whether non-conservative work or dissipative/external transfer is zero for the chosen interval and account.
teaching_path.why_valid: The mechanical-energy conservation equation is a conditional simplification, not the general conservation law.
teaching_path.output: conservation shortcut used only after the zero-extra-transfer condition is established

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Because energy is conserved, K + U must be constant in every mechanical situation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A block slides down a rough ramp. Does the law of conservation of energy by itself justify K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f?
misconceptions.repair: No. Declare the system and account for frictional/non-conservative transfer. Total energy conservation is broader than constancy of the selected mechanical stores.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: When friction reduces K + U, energy has been destroyed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A sliding block stops on a rough horizontal surface. If K decreases to zero, where can the energy go?
misconceptions.repair: Expand the account or mark the transfer to thermal/internal/environmental stores. Mechanical energy can decrease without violating total-energy conservation.

exit_task.prompt: A block descends from the same height on a smooth track and a rough track. State the system/account you are using, decide whether K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f is justified in each case, and explain where the 'missing' mechanical energy goes in the rough case.

answer.summary: For the smooth case, K+U may be constant if no other transfer changes the chosen mechanical account. For the rough case, friction/non-conservative transfer must be represented; the decrease in mechanical energy is transferred to other stores rather than destroyed.
reasoning: Declare one physical system and use the same reference across the compared states.
Mechanical-energy conservation is the special case with zero non-conservative/unaccounted transfer.
Friction opens the K+U-only account, so an explicit transfer or expanded store inventory is needed.
Total energy conservation does not require the selected mechanical stores to remain constant.
answer.check: Remove friction while keeping the same system/states: the extra transfer channel should vanish and the mechanical K+U account may close.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer decides whether a conservation form is applicable and computes no energy or speed.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copied and adapted into the local Grade9V3 contract from richer prior internal Work/Energy engineering, especially the system-boundary and conditional-mechanical-conservation distinction.

predict.prompt: A block reaches the bottom of a rough track from the same starting height as on a smooth track. Before writing K plus U, should you expect the same final kinetic energy?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Friction transfers energy out of the mechanical K-plus-U account, so the rough case can end with less kinetic energy.

attempt.produces: A smooth-versus-rough energy account that marks whether an extra transfer is present before deciding if K plus U stays constant.

rubric.criterion: The smooth case is allowed an unchanged K-plus-U account only after checking that no extra transfer is present.
rubric.evidence_of: Making conservation conditional rather than automatic.

rubric.criterion: The rough case carries friction explicitly outside the K-plus-U-only account.
rubric.evidence_of: Not hiding a path-dependent transfer inside the conservation statement.

accepted: 'Smooth: no extra transfer, so K + U can remain constant. Rough: friction transfers energy, so include that transfer explicitly.'
rejected: 'K + U is conserved in both because energy is always conserved.' This confuses total energy conservation with the narrower mechanical account.

route.ask: What is held the same between the smooth and rough descents?
route.why_this_ask: It fixes the endpoint energy change so roughness is the meaningful difference.

route.ask: What extra transfer exists only on the rough track?
route.why_this_ask: The conservation decision depends on identifying what crosses the mechanical account.

route.ask: If that transfer removes part of the mechanical energy, can the same K-plus-U total stay unchanged by itself?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must connect the transfer inventory to the conservation condition.

route.ask: What question should you ask before writing an unchanged K-plus-U statement in any new problem?
route.why_this_ask: It turns the comparison into a reusable model-choice check.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path compares smooth and rough accounts directly. The learner route first identifies the one changed transfer, then uses it to decide whether the mechanical account can close.

boundary_test.prompt: A rough surface is present but no relative displacement occurs during the interval. Does the label 'rough' alone prove mechanical energy was dissipated?
boundary_test.answer: No. The actual transfer/work over the stated interval must be established; a named interaction alone is not enough.
boundary_test.confirms: The conservation decision is based on the actual account and transfer, not a keyword.

microtopics.title: Power is an energy-transfer rate, not the work itself
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often keep the same units and reasoning for work and power or treat an interval average as an instantaneous value.
entry_assumptions: Can identify work as an energy transfer and can keep an energy account over a stated interval.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Average power uses total work over a positive interval, while instantaneous power needs force and velocity information at the same instant; equal total work does not imply equal power.

teaching_path.action: Compare two machines that perform the same work over different elapsed times.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding work fixed isolates time as the factor that changes average power.
teaching_path.output: same W; shorter Delta t -> larger W / Delta t.

teaching_path.action: Calculate average power from total work divided by the positive elapsed interval.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-AVERAGE-POWER is the gate-owned interval-rate relation.
teaching_path.output: P_avg = W / Delta t.

teaching_path.action: At one instant, resolve the force onto the velocity direction and pair that component with the instantaneous speed.
teaching_path.why_valid: Instantaneous power depends on the force-velocity alignment at that same instant, not on the whole interval total.
teaching_path.output: same instant: F_parallel and v.

teaching_path.action: Use a perpendicular-force case as a boundary check.
teaching_path.why_valid: F_parallel becomes zero although a nonzero force and nonzero speed are both present.
teaching_path.output: force perpendicular to velocity -> F_parallel = 0 -> instantaneous power = 0.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If two machines do the same work, they have the same power.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two machines each transfer the same energy, but one finishes in half the time. Must their average powers be equal?
misconceptions.repair: Keep work fixed and divide by each machine's own elapsed time; power is a rate, not the transfer total.

exit_task.prompt: A machine transfers 120 J of work in 4 s. Find its average power. Then state whether that average alone is enough to know the instantaneous power halfway through the interval.

answer.summary: Average power is 30 W. The average alone is not enough to determine the instantaneous power halfway through the interval.
reasoning: Use P_avg = 120 J / 4 s = 30 W.
An interval average does not specify how the rate varied within the four seconds.
Instantaneous power would require same-instant force and velocity information, such as F_parallel and v.
answer.check: A second machine could transfer the same 120 J in the same 4 s with a varying rate and still have the same 30 W average.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created power-rate distinction bound to gate-owned average and instantaneous relations and Physics validators.

predict.prompt: Two machines do the same work, but one takes twice as long. Before calculating, must their powers be equal?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The machine taking longer has the smaller average power because the same transfer is spread over more time.

attempt.produces: An average-power calculation plus a statement of what extra information would be needed for instantaneous power.

rubric.criterion: Computes average power as work divided by elapsed time.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating power as a rate rather than another name for work.

rubric.criterion: Does not infer instantaneous power from the average alone.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating interval and same-instant information.

accepted: 120 J / 4 s = 30 W; instantaneous power still needs same-instant force and velocity information.
rejected: 120 J or 120 W, or saying the instantaneous power must also be 30 W solely because the average is 30 W.

route.ask: What total energy transfer is fixed over the whole interval?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies the numerator without yet supplying the rate relation.

route.ask: What positive time interval belongs to that transfer?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the averaging window.

route.ask: What would you need to know at one instant instead of over the whole interval?
