route.why_this_ask: It forces the distinction between average and instantaneous information.

route.ask: What happens if force is perpendicular to velocity?
route.why_this_ask: The boundary checks the force-direction dependence of instantaneous power.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path contrasts the two rate definitions directly; the learner route begins from equal-work machines and reconstructs why interval totals cannot determine a same-instant rate.

boundary_test.prompt: A nonzero force is exactly perpendicular to a nonzero velocity. What is the instantaneous mechanical power from that force?
boundary_test.answer: Zero, because the signed force component along the velocity direction is zero.
boundary_test.confirms: Instantaneous power depends on force-velocity alignment, not force magnitude alone.

microtopics.title: Grade 9 work and mechanical-energy equations are one ledger
microtopics.badge_reason: The arithmetic is direct; the difficult part is deciding which account and relation the situation permits.
entry_assumptions: Can classify work sign and decide whether extra frictional/outside transfer closes or opens the mechanical-energy account.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Work, kinetic energy, near-Earth gravitational potential-energy change, work-energy and mechanical-energy conservation are linked bookkeeping statements with explicit body/system, frame/reference and model conditions; K+U conservation is only the zero-nonconservative-transfer special case.

teaching_path.action: Choose the body/system, displacement direction, reference frame and height reference before calculating.
teaching_path.why_valid: Work sign and energy values depend on these declarations.
teaching_path.output: chosen body/account; path direction; frame; height reference.

teaching_path.action: Use W = F_parallel s, K = 0.5 m v^2 and Delta U_g = m g Delta h for the matching quantities.
teaching_path.why_valid: Each gate-owned relation defines one distinct part of the energy ledger.
teaching_path.output: W = F_parallel s; K = 0.5 m v^2; Delta U_g = m g Delta h, all in joules under their stated conditions.

teaching_path.action: Relate net work to Delta K, or equate endpoint K + U only when no extra transfer crosses the chosen account.
teaching_path.why_valid: The work-energy theorem and mechanical-energy conservation answer different bookkeeping questions.
teaching_path.output: W_net = Delta K; closed account -> K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f.

teaching_path.action: Use a rough-track counterexample to test whether a claimed K + U conservation statement is allowed.
teaching_path.why_valid: Frictional transfer opens the mechanical account and invalidates unchanged K + U by itself.
teaching_path.output: rough path -> include transfer; do not force K + U constant.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Once kinetic and potential energy appear, K + U must always be conserved.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A block descends the same height on a rough track and a smooth track. Must the final kinetic energies match?
misconceptions.repair: Inventory transfers first. Friction can move energy out of the mechanical account, so identical endpoints do not guarantee the same K + U ledger.

exit_task.prompt: A 2 kg object moves at 3 m/s. Find its translational kinetic energy. Then state what additional condition is required before using K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f for a later motion.

answer.summary: K = 9 J. Mechanical-energy conservation additionally requires that no frictional or outside transfer change the chosen K + U account.
reasoning: The conservation equation is conditional, not automatic.
If friction or an outside agent transfers energy, that transfer must be included.
answer.check: Doubling the speed to 6 m/s would quadruple K to 36 J.

microtopics.research_contribution: Local quantitative Grade-9 Work/Energy closure enriched from prior internal engineering with system-boundary, reference-consistency and model-validity checks.

predict.prompt: Two 2 kg objects move at 3 m/s and 6 m/s. Does the faster one have twice the kinetic energy?
predict.defensible_answer: No. K depends on speed squared, so doubling speed gives four times the kinetic energy.

attempt.produces: A kinetic-energy calculation plus a conservation-condition statement.

rubric.criterion: Computes kinetic energy with speed squared.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the gate-owned Grade 9 relation.

rubric.criterion: States the no-extra-transfer condition before using mechanical-energy conservation.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating conservation as a conditional ledger.

accepted: 2 kg at 3 m/s -> 9 J; conserve K+U only when no extra transfer changes the account.
rejected: K = m v or automatic K+U conservation on a rough path.

route.ask: Which energy depends on motion in the declared frame?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies K.

route.ask: How does speed enter that relation?
route.why_this_ask: It protects the square dependence.

route.ask: What transfer inventory must be checked before conserving K + U?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs the model condition.

route.ask: What does a rough path do to the account?
route.why_this_ask: It provides the boundary falsifier.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path builds the ledger from declarations; the learner route starts from a kinetic-energy scaling question and then tests the conservation boundary.

boundary_test.prompt: If a body is instantaneously at rest in the declared frame, what is its translational kinetic energy?
boundary_test.answer: Zero.
boundary_test.confirms: K is nonnegative and vanishes at zero speed.

microtopics.title: Derive kinetic and raised-body potential energy from the work ledger
microtopics.badge_reason: The endpoint formulae are simple; the harder work is maintaining one physical model through the force, motion and work substitutions.
entry_assumptions: Can use F_net = m a for one chosen body in an inertial frame.
Can use v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s on a constant-acceleration interval.
Can calculate constant-force work from the signed force component along displacement.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The Grade 9 energy expressions follow from previously owned mechanics: constant-force work plus Newton/kinematics yields the change in kinetic energy, while a controlled lift against near-Earth weight yields the increase m g h in gravitational potential energy.

teaching_path.action: For the kinetic-energy derivation, choose a body accelerated by a constant net force along its displacement from initial speed u to final speed v.
teaching_path.why_valid: This controlled case makes F_net = m a, W_net = F_net s and the constant-acceleration no-time relation valid on the same interval.
teaching_path.output: W_net = F_net s = m a s; v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s.

teaching_path.action: Eliminate a s using the no-time kinematic relation and identify the net-work change as the kinetic-energy change.
teaching_path.why_valid: The two equations describe the same body and interval, and the work-energy theorem identifies net work with Delta K.
teaching_path.output: a s = (v^2-u^2)/2 -> W_net = 0.5 m(v^2-u^2) = Delta K; choosing K=0 at v=0 gives K = 0.5 m v^2.

teaching_path.action: For the potential-energy derivation, raise the body slowly through vertical height h so acceleration is zero and the applied upward force balances the near-Earth weight.
teaching_path.why_valid: Zero acceleration makes the applied force magnitude equal the weight magnitude m g, while the displacement is along the applied force.
teaching_path.output: a = 0 -> F_applied = F_weight = m g; upward displacement = h.

teaching_path.action: Calculate the external lifting work and identify it with the increase of gravitational potential energy in the controlled lift.
teaching_path.why_valid: With negligible kinetic-energy change in the slow lift, the work transferred into the object-gravity account appears as gravitational potential-energy increase.
teaching_path.output: W_applied = F_applied h = m g h -> Delta U_g = m g h.

teaching_path.action: Check both derivations at their zero boundaries.
teaching_path.why_valid: At v=0 the chosen kinetic-energy expression must vanish, and at h=0 the gravitational potential-energy change must vanish.
teaching_path.output: v = 0 -> K = 0; h = 0 -> Delta U_g = 0.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: K = 0.5 m v^2 and m g h are definitions that cannot be connected to earlier mechanics.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can you reach each expression using work plus previously learned force/motion relations without assuming the final formula?
misconceptions.repair: For K, combine W_net = F_net s, F_net = m a and v^2-u^2 = 2as. For raised-body U_g, use a slow lift where F_applied = m g and W_applied = F_applied h.

exit_task.prompt: Derive the Grade 9 kinetic-energy expression for a body accelerated from rest by a constant net force, then derive the increase in gravitational potential energy when the same mass is raised slowly through height h near Earth's surface.

answer.summary: From W_net = m a s and v^2 = 2 a s for motion from rest, W_net = 0.5 m v^2, so K = 0.5 m v^2 with K=0 at rest. For a slow lift, F_applied = m g and W_applied = m g h, so Delta U_g = m g h.
reasoning: Constant-force work and Newton's second law give W_net = F_net s = m a s.
For constant acceleration from rest, v^2 = 2 a s, hence a s = v^2/2 and W_net = 0.5 m v^2.
By the work-energy theorem and the chosen zero at rest, K = 0.5 m v^2.
For a slow vertical lift, zero acceleration requires F_applied = F_weight = m g.
Work by that applied force through height h is m g h, which is stored as the increase in gravitational potential energy.
answer.check: The derived expressions satisfy the zero boundaries v=0 -> K=0 and h=0 -> Delta U_g=0.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit is a symbolic derivation using gate-owned relations; it makes no independent numerical claim.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created Grade 9 derivation route for the two energy expressions explicitly required by the verified CBSE learning outcomes.

predict.prompt: If an object's speed doubles at fixed mass, should the kinetic-energy expression that emerges from the work derivation double or quadruple?
predict.defensible_answer: It should quadruple because the derivation produces a speed-squared dependence.

attempt.produces: A symbolic relation chain for K and a second relation chain for the raised-body potential-energy change.

rubric.criterion: Derives K by combining work, Newton's second law and constant-acceleration kinematics before invoking the work-energy theorem.
rubric.evidence_of: Showing W_net = m a s = 0.5 m(v^2-u^2) rather than quoting K.

rubric.criterion: Derives the raised-body potential-energy change from a controlled slow lift against weight.
rubric.evidence_of: Showing F_applied = m g and W_applied = m g h before identifying Delta U_g.

accepted: From rest: W_net = mas and v^2=2as -> W_net=0.5mv^2 -> K=0.5mv^2.
Slow lift: F_applied=mg and W=Fh -> Delta U_g=mgh.
rejected: Writing K=0.5mv^2 and U=mgh with no derivation or model conditions.

route.ask: Which three already-owned relations can all describe the same constant-force acceleration interval?
route.why_this_ask: This reconstructs the kinetic-energy derivation from prior mechanics.

route.ask: How can you replace a s using v^2-u^2 = 2as?
route.why_this_ask: This creates the speed-squared dependence.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path presents two controlled derivations in order; the learner route starts from the previously owned mechanics and reconstructs why the familiar energy expressions have their particular forms.

boundary_test.prompt: What do the two derived expressions predict at v = 0 and at zero height change?
boundary_test.answer: K = 0 at v = 0, and Delta U_g = 0 when the height change is zero.
boundary_test.confirms: Both derivations respect their natural zero boundaries.

conditions: For the kinetic derivation the net force is constant and collinear with the displacement.
For the potential-energy derivation the lift is slow enough that acceleration is zero and local g is approximately uniform.

answer.summary: The two required chains are W_net = mas = 0.5mv^2 -> K = 0.5mv^2 from rest, and slow lift F_applied = mg -> W_applied = mgh -> Delta U_g = mgh.
reasoning: Use W_net = F_net s and F_net = ma.
Use v^2 = 2as from rest to replace as by v^2/2.
Use the work-energy theorem to identify the result as K when the initial kinetic energy is zero.
For the slow lift, zero acceleration makes the applied force balance the weight magnitude mg.
Applied work through vertical height h is therefore mgh and becomes the gravitational potential-energy increase.
answer.check: At v=0 the derived K is zero; at h=0 the derived potential-energy change is zero.

hints.text: For kinetic energy, first write work as net force times displacement and replace net force with m a.
Then use the no-time constant-acceleration relation to replace the product a s.
For potential energy, make the lift slow enough that the applied force balances weight.

questions.stem: Design a simple-pendulum investigation of mechanical-energy conservation. State what quantities you would compare between release and the lowest point, what ideal relation you expect, and how real losses would appear in the data.
conditions: Use a small enough swing and a fixed pivot so the bob follows the same arc.
Choose one gravitational-potential reference consistently.

answer.summary: Measure release height relative to the lowest point and the bob’s speed at the lowest point, compare m g Delta h with 0.5 m v^2, repeat trials, and interpret a systematic shortfall in kinetic energy as evidence of friction/air losses rather than forcing exact equality.
reasoning: At release from rest, the chosen mechanical account is mainly gravitational potential energy relative to the bottom.
At the lowest point, potential energy is minimum and kinetic energy is maximum.
Under the ideal no-loss model, m g Delta h should match 0.5 m v^2 within experimental uncertainty.
Use repeated trials and the same reference height and mass throughout.
If measured kinetic energy is consistently smaller, include pivot friction, air resistance or measurement error rather than claiming exact mechanical-energy conservation.
answer.check: The experiment tests a conditional conservation model; it should not erase observed losses to make K+U exactly constant.

hints.text: Choose the bottom as a convenient height reference and compare release energy with energy at the lowest point.
The ideal equality is m g Delta h = 0.5 m v^2; real data should be compared with it, not forced to match it.

conventions.statement: Choose the body before listing forces; each listed force must name an external agent acting on that body.
State whether the observer is accelerating before deciding whether a pseudo-force is part of the chosen description.

capabilities.action: Relate zero net force to unchanged velocity.
capabilities.success_criterion: Accept steady motion as compatible with zero net force.

capabilities.action: Distinguish zero net force from the absence of individual forces.
capabilities.success_criterion: Recognize that nonzero forces can cancel in the net force.

capabilities.action: Assign each force arrow to the body on which that force acts.
capabilities.success_criterion: Place a partner force on the other body's diagram rather than the chosen body's diagram.

capabilities.action: Decide whether an observer description requires a pseudo-force.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify accelerating-observer cases that need the added pseudo-force convention.

capabilities.action: Relate signed net external force to acceleration with F_net = m a.
capabilities.success_criterion: Builds the force sum for one chosen body before solving for signed acceleration or net force.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns qualitative contact-level friction existence and direction from relative sliding or slip tendency. It does not own coefficient-based magnitude/state selection; that belongs to CAP-NLM-FRICTION-QUANT.

capabilities.action: Identify friction as a contact force that opposes relative sliding or the tendency to slide.
capabilities.success_criterion: Draws friction along the contact surface in the direction that opposes relative sliding/tendency, not automatically opposite the object's velocity.

capabilities.action: Identify Newton-third-law force pairs as equal and opposite forces of the same interaction acting on different bodies.
capabilities.success_criterion: Names both bodies and keeps the two partner forces on separate free-body diagrams.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns static-feasibility and kinetic-friction model selection after the body/contact model is declared: determine N, solve the no-slip friction demand, compare with the static bound, and switch models only when the contact state justifies it. It does not create separate capabilities for every incline, block-stack, or force-angle context.

capabilities.action: Decide whether static friction can supply the tangential force required by the chosen-body dynamics; if relative sliding is established, use the declared kinetic-friction model.
capabilities.success_criterion: Obtains the actual normal force from the free-body dynamics, computes the friction required for no slip, accepts static friction only when |f_required| <= mu_s N, uses equality only at impending slip, and switches to |f_k| = mu_k N only after relative sliding is established.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns the kinematic consequence of an active fixed-separation constraint and the body-versus-system boundary used with Newton II. It does not license common acceleration after the constraint is lost, and it does not own equal-string-tension or pulley-length geometry.

capabilities.action: Identify which bodies are constrained to share one acceleration component and write consistent body-specific or whole-system Newton-II equations.
capabilities.success_criterion: States the physical constraint that fixes relative separation, uses one compatible sign convention, gives constrained bodies the same acceleration component only when justified, and cancels internal partner forces only in a whole-system force sum rather than on an individual-body FBD.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns force transmission in one declared ideal string/redirection model: body-specific tension forces, one common tension magnitude when justified, and tension obtained from Newton II rather than identified automatically with weight. It does not own the string-length kinematic constraint.

capabilities.action: Use one declared ideal-string model to assign tension forces and, where justified, one common tension magnitude throughout that same string.
capabilities.success_criterion: States the ideal massless-taut-string and frictionless/massless redirection assumptions, puts each tension arrow on the body it acts on, uses one tension magnitude only under those assumptions, and refuses that equality for a nonideal rope or pulley model.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns conversion of one fixed-pulley inextensible-string geometry into signed displacement, velocity and acceleration constraints. The length relation is a kinematic claim and does not by itself prove equal tension.

capabilities.action: Convert constant length of one taut inextensible string over one fixed ideal pulley into the corresponding displacement, velocity, or acceleration relation.
capabilities.success_criterion: Declares coordinates along the two string segments, writes the fixed-length relation y_A + y_B = constant, derives a_A + a_B = 0 in those coordinates, and does not generalize that result to movable/compound pulley geometry.

microtopics.title: Zero net force allows steady motion
microtopics.badge_reason: Everyday friction makes continued motion look as if it needs a continuing push.
entry_assumptions: Can tell whether an object's velocity is changing.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Zero net force does not mean zero motion; it means velocity does not change, so rest and steady motion are both compatible with the same condition.

teaching_path.action: Separate the statement 'is moving' from the statement 'is changing its velocity.'
teaching_path.why_valid: Motion and change of motion are different observations, and only the second identifies acceleration.
teaching_path.output: state A: moving steadily.  state B: speeding up, slowing down, or turning.

teaching_path.action: Imagine a low-friction cart after the hand has stopped touching it and compare successive equal-time snapshots.
teaching_path.why_valid: Once the hand is gone, a continuing steady velocity can be observed without a continuing forward push.
teaching_path.output: successive equal-time snapshots -> equal forward position advances; velocity unchanged.

teaching_path.action: Compare the released moving cart with a cart that starts at rest under the same zero-net-force condition.
teaching_path.why_valid: If both keep their initial velocities, the rule is about unchanged velocity rather than about rest.
teaching_path.output: moving cart: stays steady.  resting cart: stays at rest.  both show no velocity change.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A force must keep acting in the direction of motion or the object must stop.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A low-friction cart is pushed and then released. After the hand loses contact, what horizontal force is required merely to keep it moving steadily?
misconceptions.repair: Separate velocity from change of velocity: a net force is required for acceleration, not for the existence of motion.

exit_task.prompt: One cart is at rest and another moves steadily in a straight line. For each, decide whether zero net force is compatible with the motion and explain the common rule.

answer.summary: Zero net force is compatible with both. Each cart can keep its current velocity unchanged.
reasoning: Rest is a zero velocity that stays zero.
Steady straight motion is a nonzero velocity that stays unchanged.
The shared condition is no change of velocity, not no motion.
answer.check: Ask whether the motion description contains speeding up, slowing down, or turning. If none occurs, zero net force remains compatible.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer classifies motion qualitatively and asserts no computed force or acceleration.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created first-law contrast. It states no force equation and promotes no candidate-packet formula.

predict.prompt: A low-friction cart is already moving when the push ends. Must a new forward force keep acting just to preserve that motion?
predict.defensible_answer: No. If the net force is zero, the cart can keep the velocity it already has.

attempt.produces: A two-case prediction for a released moving cart and an initially resting cart under the same zero-net-force condition.

rubric.criterion: The moving cart is allowed to continue steadily.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating motion from acceleration.

rubric.criterion: The resting cart is allowed to remain at rest under the same rule.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing unchanged velocity as the common condition.

accepted: 'The moving cart keeps moving steadily; the resting cart stays at rest. Neither has to change velocity.'
rejected: 'Zero net force makes both carts stop.' This turns zero net force into a command for zero velocity rather than unchanged velocity.

route.ask: After the hand leaves the cart, is the hand still exerting the forward push?
route.why_this_ask: It removes the continuing-contact explanation before discussing what the cart does.

route.ask: What would count as a change of velocity in the next few moments?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must name acceleration-like changes rather than equate movement itself with force.

route.ask: If none of those changes occurs, what part of the cart's motion is staying the same?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies unchanged velocity as the invariant.

route.ask: Does that same rule also allow a cart whose starting velocity is zero?
route.why_this_ask: The rest case checks that the learner has not replaced one special state with another.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path presents the moving and resting cases as a finished comparison. The learner route first removes the push, defines what change would look like, then discovers that both cases share unchanged velocity.

boundary_test.prompt: A cart moving east begins to slow down. Can zero net force still describe that interval?
boundary_test.answer: No. Slowing down is a change of velocity, so the zero-net-force condition no longer fits the stated interval.
boundary_test.confirms: The rule is about unchanged velocity, not simply about whether the object is moving.

microtopics.title: Nonzero forces can cancel
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often read a zero total as evidence that nothing is present instead of as cancellation among directed contributions.
entry_assumptions: Can interpret zero net force as unchanged velocity.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Several nonzero forces can act on one body while their directed sum is zero; the motion responds to the net result rather than to the mere presence of forces.

teaching_path.action: List two opposite pushes on the same object as separate contributions before combining them.
teaching_path.why_valid: Keeping the contributions visible prevents a zero total from being mistaken for no forces.
teaching_path.output: leftward push: present.  rightward push: present.

teaching_path.action: Make the two opposite pushes equal in size and combine their directional effects.
teaching_path.why_valid: Equal opposite contributions cancel in the net result while each contribution still exists.
teaching_path.output: two nonzero opposite pushes -> net force: zero.

teaching_path.action: Increase both opposite pushes together while keeping them equal.
teaching_path.why_valid: The individual forces change while the zero net result persists, directly separating the parts from their sum.
teaching_path.output: larger opposite pushes: still net force zero; individual forces remain nonzero.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If the net force is zero, no forces are acting.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A book rests on a table. Are there no forces on the book, or can nonzero forces add to zero?
misconceptions.repair: List every interaction force on the body, then combine their directions; cancellation belongs to the net result, not to the individual forces.

exit_task.prompt: An object has two equal opposite forces acting on it. Explain what is zero and what is not, then state what motion change the net result predicts.

answer.summary: The net force is zero, but both individual forces are nonzero. The zero net result predicts no change of velocity.
reasoning: Each force remains an actual interaction on the body.
Opposite equal directional effects cancel only when combined.
A zero net force is consistent with unchanged velocity.
answer.check: Increase both forces equally; the net remains zero even though neither individual force disappears.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The response uses only equality, opposition, and zero/nonzero classification; it asserts no computed force magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created cancellation contrast, deliberately separate from any force-acceleration equation.

predict.prompt: Two people push the same box equally hard in opposite directions. If the box has zero net force, does that mean neither person is exerting a force?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Both forces are present; their opposite directional effects cancel in the net result.

attempt.produces: A force inventory that keeps both opposite contributions visible plus a separate statement of the net result.

rubric.criterion: Both nonzero contributions remain listed.
rubric.evidence_of: Not confusing cancellation with absence.

rubric.criterion: Only the combined result is labelled zero.
rubric.evidence_of: Locating the zero at the level of the sum.

accepted: 'Left push present; right push present; equal and opposite, so the net force is zero.'
rejected: 'No forces act because the net is zero.' This deletes the interactions instead of combining them.

route.ask: Before adding anything, how many pushes are physically acting on the box?
route.why_this_ask: It fixes the inventory before a zero total can erase it.

route.ask: Which directions do those pushes point?
route.why_this_ask: Cancellation requires direction, so the learner has to preserve it.

route.ask: If the two sizes match, what happens to the combined directional effect?
route.why_this_ask: The zero is derived from the pair rather than assumed from the motion.

route.ask: If both people push harder by the same amount, which statements change and which stay true?
route.why_this_ask: The variation separates individual magnitudes from the net result.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path lists and combines the forces. The learner route commits to the inventory first, then derives cancellation and tests it by changing both contributions together.

boundary_test.prompt: One of the two equal opposite pushes is removed. Is the net force still zero?
boundary_test.answer: No. One nonzero force remains without an equal opposite contribution to cancel it.
boundary_test.confirms: Zero net force came from cancellation between present forces, not from a property of the object.

microtopics.title: A free-body diagram belongs to one chosen body
microtopics.badge_reason: Equal-and-opposite partner forces look like natural cancellations until the learner asks which body each arrow actually acts on.
entry_assumptions: Can keep several forces visible even when their net effect is zero.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A free-body diagram contains forces acting on one chosen body only; the equal-and-opposite partner of an interaction acts on the other body and belongs on that other body's diagram.

teaching_path.action: Choose the cart as the body to describe and require every arrow to answer 'who acts on the cart?'
teaching_path.why_valid: The ownership question gives one mechanical test for whether a force belongs on the chosen body's diagram.
teaching_path.output: chosen body: cart.  every listed arrow must be an agent -> cart force.

teaching_path.action: For the horse-cart contact, place the horse-on-cart force on the cart diagram and place the cart-on-horse partner on a separate horse diagram.
teaching_path.why_valid: The two forces belong to one interaction but act on different bodies, so combining them on one body's diagram changes the question being asked.
teaching_path.output: cart diagram: horse -> cart.  horse diagram: cart -> horse.

teaching_path.action: Switch the chosen body from cart to horse and rebuild the inventory from the ownership question.
teaching_path.why_valid: A correct diagram changes when the chosen body changes even though the physical interaction is the same.
teaching_path.output: switch body -> switch which contact-force arrow belongs in the diagram; partner arrows never cancel on one diagram.

teaching_path.action: When a physical force is resolved into components for chosen axes, keep the body-force inventory unchanged: use the components as a representation of that one force in the equations, not as additional interaction forces alongside the original vector.
teaching_path.why_valid: Resolving a vector changes its coordinate representation, not the number of physical interactions acting on the body. Counting both the original force and its components double-counts the same interaction.
teaching_path.output: one physical force -> either original vector representation or its signed components in the chosen equations, never both as separate forces

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Equal and opposite partner forces cancel each other on one body's free-body diagram.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A horse pulls a cart and the cart pulls back equally. Which of those two forces acts on the cart, and which acts on the horse?
misconceptions.repair: Choose one body first. Put only forces acting on that body on its diagram; draw the partner force only when the other body is chosen.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: After resolving weight on an incline, mg, mg sin(theta) and mg cos(theta) are three separate forces on the block.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If gravity is one Earth-on-block interaction, did choosing tilted axes create two new physical agents?
misconceptions.repair: No. Weight remains one physical force. Its parallel/perpendicular components are the coordinate representation used in the chosen equations; do not add the original mg again to those component sums.

exit_task.prompt: A person pushes a box. Describe the two contact-force partner arrows and state which one belongs on the box's free-body diagram.

answer.summary: The person's force on the box belongs on the box diagram. The box's equal-and-opposite force on the person belongs on the person's diagram.
reasoning: Choose the box first.
Ask which member of the contact pair acts on the box.
The partner acts on the person, so it cannot cancel the first force on the box diagram.
answer.check: Switch the chosen body to the person; the membership of the two partner arrows must switch with it.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer assigns force ownership qualitatively and contains no computed force value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created body-ownership construction. A drawable FREE_BODY_DIAGRAM representation is intentionally not authored in this track.

predict.prompt: A horse pulls a cart while the cart pulls back on the horse. If you draw only the cart, should both of those horizontal forces appear on the cart's free-body diagram?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Only the horse-on-cart force acts on the cart; the cart-on-horse partner belongs on the horse's diagram.

attempt.produces: Two separate body inventories, one for the cart and one for the horse, with the contact partner arrows assigned to the body each arrow acts on.

rubric.criterion: Each diagram contains only the member of the contact pair acting on its chosen body.
rubric.evidence_of: Using force ownership rather than visual cancellation.

rubric.criterion: The partner arrows are placed on different body diagrams.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing that equal-and-opposite partners do not cancel within one body's inventory.

accepted: 'Cart: horse pushes cart forward. Horse: cart pushes horse backward.' The two arrows are on different diagrams.
rejected: Both equal-and-opposite arrows drawn on the cart and crossed out. This puts a force acting on the horse into the cart's inventory.

route.ask: Which single body are you describing first?
route.why_this_ask: The diagram has no ownership until a body is chosen.

route.ask: For the horse-on-cart force, which object receives the push?
route.why_this_ask: The receiver test decides membership without requiring a named law.

route.ask: For the cart-on-horse partner, which object receives that push?
route.why_this_ask: The same test places the partner on the other diagram.

route.ask: When you switch the chosen body, which contact arrow moves into the new inventory?
route.why_this_ask: Rebuilding the diagram tests whether body ownership, rather than arrow pairing, controls placement.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path demonstrates two correct diagrams. The learner route begins from one chosen body and repeatedly applies the receiver test until the separation of partner arrows is forced.

boundary_test.prompt: Two hands push the same box equally in opposite directions. Can those two forces both appear on the box's free-body diagram?
boundary_test.answer: Yes. Both hands act on the same chosen box, so both forces belong there and may cancel in the net force.
boundary_test.confirms: The rule is body ownership, not a ban on opposite arrows appearing together.

microtopics.title: An accelerating observer needs a declared pseudo-force convention
microtopics.badge_reason: The same physical interactions can be described by observers with different accelerations, and the extra convention is easy to omit when the observer is inside the accelerating vehicle.
entry_assumptions: Can build a force inventory for one chosen body.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A force-based account depends on the observer: a non-accelerating observer uses the physical interaction forces, while an accelerating observer must add the corresponding pseudo-force convention to describe the same observed motion consistently.

teaching_path.action: Describe the same loose object first from the roadside and then from inside a bus, stating whether each observer is accelerating.
teaching_path.why_valid: The observer choice is part of the model; leaving it implicit makes two different descriptions look contradictory.
teaching_path.output: roadside: observer acceleration zero.  bus during start: observer acceleration forward.

teaching_path.action: Keep the physical interactions unchanged and compare what the accelerating bus observer sees the loose object do relative to the bus.
teaching_path.why_valid: The apparent backward motion comes from the observer's changing motion, not from a newly discovered physical contact on the object.
teaching_path.output: bus accelerates forward -> loose object appears to shift backward relative to the bus.

teaching_path.action: Add a backward pseudo-force only in the accelerating-observer description and compare it with the roadside account.
teaching_path.why_valid: The added convention compensates for the observer's acceleration without inventing a new physical interaction.
teaching_path.output: roadside account: physical forces only.  accelerating-bus account: same physical forces plus backward pseudo-force.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The same ordinary-force diagram can be used unchanged in any accelerating observer's frame.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A loose mass appears to accelerate backward inside a bus that starts forward. Can the bus observer use only the same physical-force inventory as the roadside observer?
misconceptions.repair: State the observer first. Use physical interactions alone for a non-accelerating observer; for an accelerating observer include the corresponding pseudo-force consistently.

exit_task.prompt: A bus accelerates forward and a loose object appears to move backward relative to the bus. Compare the roadside and bus-observer force descriptions without calculating any magnitude.

answer.summary: The roadside description uses the physical interactions only. The accelerating bus description adds a backward pseudo-force convention to account for the observer's acceleration.
reasoning: The physical interactions on the object do not change merely because the observer changes.
The bus observer is accelerating relative to the roadside observer.
The pseudo-force belongs to that accelerating-observer description rather than to a new physical agent.
answer.check: Repeat the comparison once the bus moves at steady speed; the extra pseudo-force should no longer be needed for the observer change alone.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer classifies observer descriptions and contains no computed pseudo-force or acceleration magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created observer-choice boundary. No pseudo-force equation is asserted; a quantitative treatment would require upstream gate ownership.

predict.prompt: A bus starts forward and a loose object seems to shift backward to a passenger. Before adding any new force, did a new physical agent suddenly begin pulling the object backward?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The physical interactions need not change; the passenger's observer description changes because the bus is accelerating.

attempt.produces: Two labelled observer descriptions of the same object: roadside and accelerating bus, with a statement of where the pseudo-force convention appears.

rubric.criterion: The roadside description keeps only physical interactions.
rubric.evidence_of: Not inventing a new physical agent when the observer changes.

rubric.criterion: The bus description adds the pseudo-force specifically because that observer accelerates.
rubric.evidence_of: Attaching the convention to observer acceleration rather than to the object.

accepted: 'Roadside: physical forces only. Accelerating bus: same physical forces plus a backward pseudo-force for the bus description.'
rejected: 'A new backward physical force appears when the bus starts.' This confuses an observer convention with an interaction.

route.ask: Did the set of physical objects touching or attracting the loose object change when the bus started?
route.why_this_ask: It tests whether a new physical agent exists before any observer convention is introduced.

route.ask: Which observer is accelerating during the bus start?
route.why_this_ask: The extra convention is tied to observer acceleration, so this must be explicit.

route.ask: What does the passenger see the loose object do relative to the bus?
route.why_this_ask: The observed relative motion is the phenomenon the bus description has to account for.

route.ask: Where should the pseudo-force be added so the two descriptions remain consistent about the same physical situation?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must attach the added term to the accelerating observer rather than to a new physical interaction.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path compares two observer accounts directly. The learner route first rules out a new physical agent, identifies which observer accelerates, then introduces the pseudo-force as a modelling convention.

boundary_test.prompt: The bus now travels at constant velocity. Does changing from the roadside observer to the bus observer by itself require the added pseudo-force?
boundary_test.answer: No. With no observer acceleration in this comparison, the extra pseudo-force convention is not required merely because the observers move relative to each other.
boundary_test.confirms: The trigger is observer acceleration, not observer motion in general.

microtopics.title: Net force, not any one force, sets acceleration
microtopics.badge_reason: The difficult step is completing a one-body force inventory before using the simple equation.
entry_assumptions: Can choose one body, draw its external forces, and distinguish zero from nonzero net force.
microtopics.inferential_jump: For a chosen body of positive mass in the Grade 9 inertial-frame model, acceleration points with the signed net external force and satisfies F_net = m a.

teaching_path.action: Choose one body, declare a positive direction, and list only external forces acting on that body.
teaching_path.why_valid: The net-force relation applies to one body's external force sum.
teaching_path.output: one body; one signed axis; signed external-force list.

teaching_path.action: Add the signed forces to obtain F_net, then use F_net = m a.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-NEWTON-SECOND-LAW is the gate-owned relation for the chosen body.
teaching_path.output: F_net = signed sum; a = F_net / m.

teaching_path.action: Return to an equal-opposite force case.
teaching_path.why_valid: The relation must recover zero acceleration when the signed force sum is zero.
teaching_path.output: F_net = 0 -> a = 0 for m > 0.

teaching_path.action: Choose axes that make the active constraint easy to express; for a fixed inclined contact, use parallel/perpendicular axes when helpful, resolve the physical forces into those axes, and write separate signed Newton-II equations.
teaching_path.why_valid: Newton II is coordinate-independent. Aligning one axis with the contact makes maintained contact explicit as a_perp=0 while leaving the tangential acceleration free to be nonzero.
teaching_path.output: contact-aligned model: Sigma F_parallel = m a_parallel; Sigma F_perp = m a_perp, with maintained fixed contact -> a_perp = 0

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Acceleration points with whichever individual force looks largest in the diagram.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two 10 N forces act opposite each other on a body. Does either force make the body accelerate in its direction?
misconceptions.repair: Add all signed external forces first; acceleration follows the net force, not an isolated arrow.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If a block on a fixed incline has zero acceleration perpendicular to the plane, its total acceleration must be zero.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can a block remain in contact with a fixed plane while speeding up down the plane?
misconceptions.repair: Yes. Maintained contact sets only a_perp=0. The parallel component a_parallel is determined independently by the net force along the plane.

exit_task.prompt: A 4 kg body has a net external force of +12 N along a declared axis. Find its acceleration.

answer.summary: The acceleration is +3 m/s^2.
reasoning: Use F_net = m a for the chosen body.
The positive sign matches the net-force direction.
answer.check: Multiplying 4 kg by +3 m/s^2 recovers +12 N.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created Grade 9 net-force calculation bound to the Newton-second-law gate and validator.

predict.prompt: A body moves right while its net external force points left. Which way is its acceleration?
predict.defensible_answer: Left, with the net force; velocity direction does not set acceleration direction.

attempt.produces: A one-body signed force sum and a signed acceleration.

rubric.criterion: Sums forces before using F = ma.
rubric.evidence_of: Using net external force rather than a selected force.

rubric.criterion: Keeps the acceleration sign consistent with the chosen axis.
rubric.evidence_of: Maintaining direction through the scalar component equation.

rejected: Using the direction of velocity to choose acceleration sign.

route.ask: Which body are we solving for?
route.why_this_ask: It fixes force ownership.

route.ask: What is the signed sum of forces on that body?
route.why_this_ask: It constructs the quantity the law uses.

route.ask: What positive mass belongs to that same body?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents cross-body substitution.

route.ask: Does the zero-net-force boundary give zero acceleration?
route.why_this_ask: It independently checks the result.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path builds the force sum directly; the learner route starts from the body choice and uses the zero-force boundary as a final falsifier.

boundary_test.prompt: If the net external force is zero on a positive-mass body, what acceleration does F_net = ma give?
boundary_test.answer: Zero acceleration.
boundary_test.confirms: The second-law relation is consistent with the earlier first-law constant-velocity case.

microtopics.title: Friction opposes relative sliding at a contact
microtopics.badge_reason: Friction is often memorized as 'opposite motion', which fails for driven or rolling contacts.
entry_assumptions: Can choose one body and identify external contact interactions acting on it.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Friction is a contact force along the surface that opposes relative sliding, or the tendency for relative sliding, between the contacting surfaces; it is not defined by the object's overall velocity alone.

teaching_path.action: Choose the body and mark the contact surface before deciding a friction direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: Friction belongs to a specific contact interaction, so its direction must be read from relative motion at that contact.
teaching_path.output: chosen body; named contact; tangent direction available.

teaching_path.action: Imagine the relative sliding or tendency to slide if friction were absent, then point friction opposite that relative tendency.
teaching_path.why_valid: Contact friction resists relative sliding between the surfaces.
teaching_path.output: friction tangent to contact and opposite relative sliding/tendency.

teaching_path.action: Check a conveyor-belt case where the belt can frictionally accelerate an object in the same direction as the object's motion.
teaching_path.why_valid: The counterexample falsifies the shortcut 'friction always points opposite velocity'.
teaching_path.output: friction direction follows contact slip tendency, not a universal page-direction rule.

teaching_path.action: Decide whether any tangential friction is required at all; allow friction to be zero when the contact has neither relative sliding nor a tendency to slide.
teaching_path.why_valid: Friction is a responsive tangential contact force, not an automatic nonzero force merely because two rough surfaces touch.
teaching_path.output: contact-state check -> friction may be zero when no tangential force is required.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Friction always points opposite the object's velocity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A moving conveyor belt speeds up a box resting on it. Can the friction on the box point in the same direction as the box's motion?
misconceptions.repair: Decide the relative sliding tendency at the contact first; friction opposes that tendency.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Two rough surfaces in contact must always exert a nonzero friction force.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A crate and rough platform already move together at constant velocity. If no horizontal force is otherwise required, must the friction force be nonzero merely because the surfaces are rough?
misconceptions.repair: No. Ask what relative sliding or slip tendency would occur without friction. If none exists and no tangential force is required, friction can be zero.

exit_task.prompt: A box is placed on a conveyor belt moving to the right faster than the box. Before the box matches the belt speed, what direction is the friction force on the box?

answer.summary: The friction force on the box points to the right.
reasoning: Relative to the belt, the box tends to slip left at the contact.
Friction opposes that relative slip tendency.
Therefore the belt's friction on the box points right and accelerates it.
answer.check: The answer is allowed to point with the box's motion because friction is defined by the contact slip tendency, not by the box's velocity alone.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit asserts only the contact-force direction in a qualitative conveyor-belt case.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created Grade 9 friction counterexample.

predict.prompt: Must friction on a moving object always point opposite the object's motion?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Its direction opposes relative sliding or the tendency to slide at the contact.

attempt.produces: A contact-level slip-tendency statement and a friction arrow.

rubric.criterion: Names the relative slip tendency at the contact.
rubric.evidence_of: Reasoning from the contact rather than object velocity alone.

rubric.criterion: Points friction opposite that relative slip tendency.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the physical definition consistently.

accepted: Belt outruns box -> box slips left relative to belt -> friction on box points right.
rejected: Friction must point left because the box moves right.

route.ask: Which two surfaces are in contact?
route.why_this_ask: It locates the interaction.

route.ask: Which way would those surfaces slide relative to each other without friction?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies the relevant tendency.

route.ask: Which way must friction oppose that relative motion?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs the force direction.

route.ask: Does that direction have to oppose the box's ground-frame velocity?
route.why_this_ask: It tests the common shortcut.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path begins from the contact; the learner route begins from the misleading object-velocity shortcut and repairs it through relative slip.

boundary_test.prompt: If there is no relative sliding and no tendency to slide at a contact, must friction be nonzero?
boundary_test.answer: No. Friction can be zero when no tangential contact force is needed.
boundary_test.confirms: Friction responds to the contact constraint rather than existing automatically whenever surfaces touch.

microtopics.title: Third-law partner forces act on different bodies
microtopics.badge_reason: Equal-and-opposite wording invites learners to cancel a pair that belongs to two different bodies.
entry_assumptions: Can assign force arrows to the body on which they act.
microtopics.inferential_jump: One interaction produces two partner forces of equal magnitude and opposite direction, but they act on different bodies and therefore do not cancel in a single body's net-force sum.

teaching_path.action: Name the interaction as 'A on B' and 'B on A' before drawing arrows.
teaching_path.why_valid: The agent-target wording records which body owns each partner force.
teaching_path.output: force of A on B belongs to B; force of B on A belongs to A.

teaching_path.action: Draw equal-length opposite arrows on the two different body diagrams.
teaching_path.why_valid: Newton's third-law partners are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction for the same interaction.
teaching_path.output: partner arrows: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different bodies.

teaching_path.action: Ask whether either single body's force sum contains both partner arrows.
teaching_path.why_valid: A force diagram for one body includes only forces acting on that body.
teaching_path.output: third-law partners do not cancel inside one body's F_net unless another separate force happens to balance one.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Action and reaction cancel each other, so interacting bodies cannot accelerate.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: When a person pushes a cart, do the person's force on the cart and the cart's force on the person both appear on the cart's free-body diagram?
misconceptions.repair: No. Put each partner on the body it acts on; only then sum forces for one body.

exit_task.prompt: A swimmer pushes water backward. Identify the third-law partner force and state which body each force acts on.

answer.summary: The swimmer pushes the water backward, and the water pushes the swimmer forward with an equal-magnitude opposite force. The two forces act on different bodies.
reasoning: The interaction is swimmer-water contact.
Swimmer on water acts on the water.
Water on swimmer acts on the swimmer in the opposite direction.
answer.check: Only the water-on-swimmer force belongs on the swimmer's free-body diagram.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit identifies interaction partners, directions and body ownership without a computed magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created Grade 9 third-law body-ownership construction.

predict.prompt: If action and reaction are equal and opposite, why do they not automatically make the net force on one object zero?
predict.defensible_answer: They act on different objects, so they are not both terms in the same object's force sum.

attempt.produces: Two agent-target force statements and one arrow on each body.

rubric.criterion: Names both partner forces with agent and target.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping force ownership explicit.

rubric.criterion: Places the partners on different body diagrams.
rubric.evidence_of: Avoiding false cancellation in one net-force sum.

accepted: swimmer on water backward; water on swimmer forward; different bodies.
rejected: Both arrows cancel on the swimmer.

route.ask: What is the interaction?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies the partner pair.

route.ask: Which body receives the first force?
route.why_this_ask: It assigns ownership.

route.ask: Which body receives the partner?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents both arrows landing on one diagram.

route.ask: Can both partners appear in one body's force sum?
route.why_this_ask: It tests the cancellation misconception.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path names agent-target pairs before drawing; the learner route starts from the cancellation paradox and resolves it by body ownership.

boundary_test.prompt: Can a third-law partner force ever be the force that balances another force on the same body?
boundary_test.answer: A separate force may happen to balance it, but its own third-law partner acts on the other body and is not the balancing term on the same diagram.
boundary_test.confirms: Equal-and-opposite third-law pairing is different from same-body force balance.

microtopics.title: Quantitative static and kinetic friction conditions
microtopics.badge_reason: The difficult decision is not substituting mu N; it is determining the required tangential force, the actual normal reaction, and whether the contact can remain static.
entry_assumptions: Can determine friction direction from relative slip tendency.
Can write Newton-II equations for a chosen body.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Static friction is a responsive contact force: solve for the friction required to prevent relative slip and compare it with the limiting value mu_s N. Equality is a threshold condition, while the kinetic model is used only after sliding is established.

teaching_path.action: Build the chosen-body FBD and determine the normal reaction N from the force balance or acceleration perpendicular to the contact; do not assume N = mg.
teaching_path.why_valid: The normal reaction is the contact force needed by the actual perpendicular dynamics and can differ from mg when the surface is inclined or other forces have perpendicular components.
teaching_path.output: perpendicular force equation -> actual N >= 0

teaching_path.action: Assume no relative sliding provisionally and solve the tangential Newton-II equation for the static friction value f_required that would make that motion possible.
teaching_path.why_valid: Static friction takes the value required by the no-slip state, provided the contact can supply it.
teaching_path.output: no-slip dynamics -> f_s = f_required

teaching_path.action: Compare |f_required| with mu_s N.
teaching_path.why_valid: The static-contact model permits any required value only up to the limiting magnitude.
teaching_path.output: |f_required| <= mu_s N -> static state feasible; |f_required| > mu_s N -> static state impossible

teaching_path.action: Use |f_s| = mu_s N only at impending slip; if relative sliding is already established, use |f_k| = mu_k N with direction opposing the relative sliding.
teaching_path.why_valid: The limiting equality and the sliding model describe different contact states and are not unconditional identities.
teaching_path.output: impending slip -> |f_s| = mu_s N; sliding -> |f_k| = mu_k N

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Friction always equals mu N.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A small horizontal force is applied to a block that remains at rest. Must static friction already equal mu_s N?
misconceptions.repair: No. First solve the force required for no slip. Static friction matches that requirement up to its limit; equality occurs only at impending slip.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The normal force is always mg.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If an extra force presses a block into a horizontal surface, can the normal reaction still be assumed equal to mg?
misconceptions.repair: Determine N from the perpendicular free-body equation. N = mg is only a special case.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If both mu_s and mu_k are given, the coefficients themselves tell you which friction model to use.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A problem gives both mu_s and mu_k but does not say whether the contact slips. Can you choose kinetic friction just because mu_k is supplied?
misconceptions.repair: No. Determine the contact state first: test whether the no-slip friction demand fits within mu_s N. Use the kinetic model only after sliding is established.

exit_task.prompt: A contact has known normal reaction N and coefficient mu_s. The no-slip force equation requires tangential friction f_required. State the test for whether static contact is possible, when equality with mu_s N is justified, and what changes once sliding is established.

answer.summary: Static contact is possible when |f_required| <= mu_s N. Equality |f_s| = mu_s N is justified only at impending slip. After relative sliding is established, use the kinetic model |f_k| = mu_k N with direction opposite the relative sliding.
reasoning: Static friction supplies the required no-slip value rather than an automatic maximum.
The limiting value mu_s N is a bound and becomes an equality only at the threshold of slipping.
The kinetic model belongs to a different contact state: established relative sliding.
answer.check: If f_required = 0, the rule must allow f_s = 0 even when mu_s N is nonzero; that falsifies the unconditional f = mu N shortcut.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit compares a symbolic friction demand with a symbolic static bound and distinguishes contact states; no numerical force is computed.

microtopics.research_contribution: ExamSIDE friction-threshold demand justifies a separate quantitative contact-state decision while preserving the qualitative friction-direction capability as its prerequisite.

predict.prompt: A block remains at rest while the applied tangential force is gradually increased. Before impending slip, must static friction already equal mu_s N?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Static friction adjusts to the value required to prevent relative slip, up to the limit mu_s N.

attempt.produces: A contact-state decision that computes the no-slip friction requirement, compares it with the static limit, and selects the correct model.
attempt.model_response: Find N from the FBD, solve for f_required under no slip, compare |f_required| with mu_s N, and use the kinetic model only after sliding is established.

route.ask: What normal reaction does the actual perpendicular force equation require?
route.why_this_ask: The friction limit depends on the real N, not a memorized mg shortcut.

route.ask: If the contact did not slip, what friction value would the tangential equation require?
route.why_this_ask: Static friction is determined by the demand of the no-slip state before the limit is tested.

route.ask: Is that required magnitude within mu_s N?
route.why_this_ask: The inequality decides whether the assumed static state is physically available.

route.ask: Which contact state, if any, justifies an equality with a coefficient times N?
route.why_this_ask: It separates impending slip from established sliding.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner begins by testing an assumed no-slip state and lets the inequality accept or reject it; the completed teaching path states the contact-state rules explicitly.

boundary_test.prompt: If the no-slip equation requires zero friction while mu_s N is positive, what is the static-friction magnitude?
boundary_test.answer: Zero. Static friction need not sit at its maximum.
boundary_test.confirms: The static relation is an inequality/response rule, not an unconditional equality.

microtopics.title: Connected bodies and a justified common acceleration
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners must distinguish a kinematic constraint from a force interaction and must not cancel internal forces inside individual-body equations.
entry_assumptions: Can draw one FBD per chosen body.
Can apply signed Newton II to one chosen body.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Bodies share an acceleration component only when a physical constraint keeps their relative separation fixed along that coordinate; the shared acceleration can link separate Newton-II equations, while internal partner forces cancel only if the bodies are deliberately treated as one system.

teaching_path.action: Identify the connection/contact condition and state exactly which relative separation is fixed.
teaching_path.why_valid: A common acceleration is a kinematic consequence of a constraint, not a default property of nearby bodies.
teaching_path.output: fixed relative separation along chosen coordinate -> common constrained acceleration component

teaching_path.action: Choose one compatible sign convention for every body equation and assign the constrained acceleration component consistently.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same physical acceleration cannot change sign merely because the equation changed bodies.
teaching_path.output: same-sense coordinates -> a_A = a_B = a

teaching_path.action: Write one Newton-II force sum for each body, keeping every inter-body force on the body it acts on.
teaching_path.why_valid: The interaction forces are external to each individual body and therefore belong in its own equation.
teaching_path.output: body A: Sigma F_A = m_A a; body B: Sigma F_B = m_B a

teaching_path.action: If treating A+B as one system, add the two body equations and cancel only the internal A-on-B/B-on-A pair in that system sum.
teaching_path.why_valid: Internal partner forces cancel in the combined system equation because both members are included, not because either force is absent from a body FBD.
teaching_path.output: system: Sigma F_external = (m_A + m_B) a; internal pair absent only after equations are combined

teaching_path.action: Match the chosen system boundary to the requested quantity: use the combined constrained system when internal forces are irrelevant to the shared acceleration, then isolate the body or subsystem that makes a requested interaction force external.
teaching_path.why_valid: An internal interaction disappears from a whole-system force sum, so that boundary is efficient for acceleration but cannot by itself determine the internal force that was cancelled.
teaching_path.output: target shared acceleration -> whole constrained system; target internal/contact force -> isolate a body or subsystem while carrying the same justified acceleration.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any two touching or connected bodies automatically have the same acceleration.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If two blocks are touching but one loses contact, what keeps their accelerations equal after separation?
misconceptions.repair: Name the active constraint first. Equal acceleration is justified only while the relative-separation condition remains enforced.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The contact force between two bodies can be cancelled from each individual FBD because it is an internal force of the pair.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: On body A alone, is the force from body B external to A?
misconceptions.repair: Yes. Keep it in A's equation. It cancels only after A and B are deliberately combined into one system equation.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Bodies with the same acceleration must have the same net force.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two connected bodies of different masses share acceleration a. Must their individual net forces be equal?
misconceptions.repair: No. The constraint can make their accelerations equal while Newton II gives different net forces m_A a and m_B a when the masses differ.

exit_task.prompt: Two bodies are constrained to keep a fixed separation along one straight coordinate. State the acceleration relation, write the form of the two body equations, and explain when their interaction force can disappear from an equation.

answer.summary: With same-sense coordinates the constraint gives a_A = a_B = a. Each body keeps the interaction force in its own Newton-II equation; the equal-and-opposite pair cancels only in a combined A+B system equation.
reasoning: Fixed relative separation implies equal velocity and acceleration components along the constrained coordinate.
Each individual body experiences the partner force as an external force.
When both bodies are included in one system, the internal partner pair cancels in the summed equation.
answer.check: If the connection breaks, the acceleration equality must no longer be asserted automatically.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit states symbolic acceleration and force-sum structure for constrained bodies; no numerical acceleration or force is computed.

microtopics.research_contribution: ExamSIDE contact and connected-body demand justifies a story-neutral fixed-separation/common-acceleration decision while preserving body-versus-system force ownership.

predict.prompt: Two blocks move together without separating. Can you assign different accelerations along their common line while their separation stays fixed?
predict.defensible_answer: No. While the fixed-separation constraint holds, their acceleration components along that coordinate are equal.

attempt.produces: A declared connection constraint plus one signed Newton-II equation per body and an optional combined-system equation.
attempt.model_response: State the fixed-separation constraint first, use one sign convention, set the constrained acceleration components equal, and cancel internal partner forces only after combining both body equations.

route.ask: What physical condition keeps the two bodies' relative separation fixed?
route.why_this_ask: It makes the common acceleration a consequence rather than an assumption.

route.ask: With one coordinate direction chosen, what must be true of their constrained acceleration components?
route.why_this_ask: It converts the physical constraint into the shared kinematic variable.

route.ask: Which interaction force belongs in each body's own equation?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents system-level cancellation from contaminating body-specific FBDs.

route.ask: Only after adding the two body equations, which force pair cancels?
route.why_this_ask: It locates internal-force cancellation at the correct system boundary.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner first proves the acceleration relation from the connection and only then decides whether to keep separate body equations or add them into a system equation.

boundary_test.prompt: The contact between the bodies is lost. May a_A = a_B still be imposed from the old connection?
boundary_test.answer: No. Once the constraint no longer keeps their separation fixed, their accelerations must be determined from their new individual dynamics.
boundary_test.confirms: Common acceleration is conditional on an active kinematic constraint.

microtopics.title: Ideal-string tension belongs to each body-specific FBD
microtopics.badge_reason: Equal tension is a model consequence, not a property of every rope/pulley setup, and the two tension arrows act on different bodies.
entry_assumptions: Can assign forces to the body they act on.
Can apply Newton II to a chosen body.
microtopics.inferential_jump: For one taut massless ideal string, with any redirection treated as frictionless and massless, the tension magnitude can be represented by one T throughout that same string; each body still receives its own tension force along the local string direction.

teaching_path.action: State the idealization before using one tension symbol: taut inextensible massless string, with any pulley/redirection frictionless and massless for this bounded model.
teaching_path.why_valid: Uniform tension is a consequence of the ideal model and must not be silently transferred to a nonideal rope or pulley.
teaching_path.output: ideal single string model declared -> one tension magnitude T is admissible throughout that string

teaching_path.action: For each attached body, draw the string's pull along the local string direction away from the body.
teaching_path.why_valid: Tension is a force exerted by the string on that body and belongs on that body's FBD.
teaching_path.output: body A FBD contains string-on-A force of magnitude T; body B FBD contains string-on-B force of magnitude T

teaching_path.action: Use the same symbol T for those magnitudes only while the declared ideal assumptions hold.
teaching_path.why_valid: A massless string segment cannot sustain a nonzero net force in this idealized model, and a frictionless massless redirection does not create a tension-magnitude jump.
teaching_path.output: T_A = T_B = T under the declared ideal-string/redirection conditions

teaching_path.action: Check whether the problem introduces rope mass, elasticity, pulley friction, or rotational inertia; if it does, stop using equal tension unless a different model justifies it.
teaching_path.why_valid: Those changes alter the force transmission assumptions that supported one common T.
teaching_path.output: nonideal feature present -> equal-tension relation not licensed by this capability

teaching_path.action: Determine the tension magnitude from a chosen body's signed Newton-II equation; do not replace T by mg or by an applied force merely because those forces appear in the same setup.
teaching_path.why_valid: Uniform tension says the ideal string transmits one magnitude throughout itself; it does not say that magnitude equals some different force. For a hanging body, T=mg only in the special zero-acceleration case.
teaching_path.output: for +y upward on a hanging mass: T - mg = ma_y; therefore a_y=0 -> T=mg, a_y>0 -> T>mg, and a_y<0 -> T<mg.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Tension forces at the two ends of a string cancel because they are equal and opposite.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Do the two end tensions act on the same chosen body?
misconceptions.repair: No. Put the tension force acting on each body in that body's own FBD. Equal magnitudes across the ideal string do not make them a cancelling pair on one body.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every rope over every pulley has the same tension on both sides.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What model assumptions justify using one symbol T throughout the rope?
misconceptions.repair: State the ideal massless string and frictionless/massless redirection assumptions first. Without them, equal tension is not automatic.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The tension in a string holding a hanging mass is always equal to the mass's weight.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A hanging mass accelerates upward. Can T still equal mg while Newton II gives a nonzero upward net force?
misconceptions.repair: Write the signed body equation. With upward positive, T-mg=ma, so upward acceleration requires T>mg; equality belongs only to zero vertical acceleration.

exit_task.prompt: Two bodies are attached to the same taut ideal string, redirected only by a frictionless massless fixed pulley. State the tension relation and explain where the two tension forces appear.

answer.summary: Under the declared ideal model, both string segments have the same tension magnitude T. Each body has its own string-on-body tension force on its own FBD; the forces are not cancelled across separate body diagrams.
reasoning: The ideal assumptions license one common tension magnitude throughout the same string.
Each tension force acts on a different body and points along that body's local string segment.
Equal magnitude does not mean the forces cancel in an individual-body equation.
answer.check: If the pulley is explicitly frictional or the rope has significant mass, this capability must refuse to assume equal tension.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit states the model-conditional symbolic equality of tension magnitudes and assigns the forces to their bodies; no numerical tension is computed.

microtopics.research_contribution: ExamSIDE string and tension demand justifies an explicit ideal-string model decision with body-specific force ownership; no general rope or pulley equality is claimed.

predict.prompt: Two masses hang from the ends of one ideal string over a fixed ideal pulley. May the same symbol T be used for the tension magnitude on both sides?
predict.defensible_answer: Yes, but only because the string/pulley model has been declared ideal; each mass still has its own tension force on its own FBD.

attempt.produces: An explicit model declaration plus separate body FBD tension assignments using one common magnitude only when justified.
attempt.model_response: Declare the ideal string/pulley assumptions, put a tension arrow on each affected body along the local string, and use T_A = T_B = T only under those assumptions.

route.ask: What assumptions about the string and pulley have actually been declared?
route.why_this_ask: Equal tension must be tied to a model rather than memorized as universal.

route.ask: Which body does each string force act on?
route.why_this_ask: It keeps equal magnitudes from becoming an invalid cancellation on one FBD.

route.ask: Under those assumptions, can the two tension magnitudes be represented by one T?
route.why_this_ask: It derives the compact relation only after model and ownership are fixed.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner has to earn the single tension symbol by first stating the model and assigning the two forces to their bodies.

boundary_test.prompt: The pulley axle has significant friction. Does this capability still guarantee equal tension on the two sides?
boundary_test.answer: No. The ideal redirection assumption has been broken, so equal tension is no longer guaranteed by this model.
boundary_test.confirms: Uniform tension is model-conditional, not universal.

microtopics.title: One fixed-pulley string gives one length constraint
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must translate geometry into one fixed-length equation rather than memorize a pulley-count rule.
entry_assumptions: Can identify a common-acceleration connection when separation is fixed.
Can use an ideal single-string tension model when forces are also being solved.
microtopics.inferential_jump: For one taut inextensible string over one fixed ideal pulley, the two changing straight segment lengths add to a constant; with coordinates measured away from the pulley this gives y_A + y_B = constant and therefore a_A + a_B = 0.

teaching_path.action: Restrict the model to one taut inextensible string over one fixed ideal pulley and choose y_A and y_B positive away from the pulley along the two straight segments.
teaching_path.why_valid: The coordinate declaration determines the signs in the length relation and blocks accidental import of movable-pulley rules.
teaching_path.output: single fixed pulley; coordinates y_A,y_B measured away from pulley

teaching_path.action: Write the variable part of the string length as y_A + y_B and set its total equal to a constant.
teaching_path.why_valid: An inextensible string has fixed total length; the wrapped portion around a fixed pulley is constant in this bounded geometry.
teaching_path.output: y_A + y_B = L_free = constant

teaching_path.action: Differentiate the fixed-length relation at the kinematic level needed by the problem.
teaching_path.why_valid: A constant length has zero time derivative at each order.
teaching_path.output: v_A + v_B = 0 and a_A + a_B = 0

teaching_path.action: Translate the signed result back into motion: if A accelerates farther from the pulley, B accelerates toward it with equal magnitude.
teaching_path.why_valid: The two segment changes must cancel to preserve total string length.
teaching_path.output: |a_A| = |a_B| with opposite signs in the declared away-from-pulley coordinates

teaching_path.action: Keep the kinematic string-length claim separate from the force-transmission claim: derive the acceleration relation from inextensibility and fixed geometry, and use equal tension only when the independent ideal-string/redirection assumptions license it.
teaching_path.why_valid: The acceleration relation comes from constant string length, whereas tension equality comes from the force model. One statement is not the proof of the other.
teaching_path.output: fixed-length geometry -> a_A + a_B = 0 in the declared coordinates; ideal force-transmission model -> T_A = T_B. Treat these as separate justified statements.
