questions.stem: A rough horizontal platform and a crate on it are already moving together at constant velocity. At the instant considered there is no other horizontal force on the crate. Must a nonzero friction force act on the crate merely because the surfaces are rough?
conditions: The crate has no horizontal acceleration.
The crate and platform have no relative sliding or tendency to separate in speed at the instant considered.

answer.summary: No. The friction force can be zero.
reasoning: If friction vanished at this instant, the crate would continue with its current velocity because no other horizontal force changes it.
The platform is also moving at that same constant velocity, so no relative slip tendency is created.
Therefore no tangential contact force is required and static friction may be zero.
answer.check: Roughness sets the range of friction the contact can provide; it does not force the contact to use a nonzero value.

rubric.criterion: Tests the contact state by imagining friction removed.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizes that friction is responsive rather than automatic.

rubric.criterion: Concludes that no relative slip tendency appears in the stated constant-velocity state.
rubric.evidence_of: Uses the correct contact-level criterion.

rubric.criterion: Allows f=0 despite a rough contact.
rubric.evidence_of: Rejects the 'rough means nonzero friction' shortcut.

adaptation.reason: Changes a stationary zero-friction case into a moving rough-contact case where the learner must decide whether friction is needed rather than equating motion with friction.

hints.text: If the friction force vanished for an instant, would the crate begin sliding relative to the platform under the stated conditions?

transfer.statement: The learner must decide not to invoke a friction force despite rough moving contact; the contact model is selected from slip tendency, not from the presence of motion or a coefficient.

questions.stem: A block of mass m is pushed on a rough horizontal floor by a force P directed at an angle theta below the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction is mu_s. Derive the largest P for which the block can remain at rest.
conditions: 0 < theta < 90 degrees.
The block remains in contact with the floor.
Assume cos(theta)-mu_s sin(theta) > 0.

answer.summary: At impending slip, N=mg+P sin(theta) and P cos(theta)=mu_s N, so P_max = mu_s m g / (cos(theta)-mu_s sin(theta)).
reasoning: The downward component of P increases the normal reaction, so the vertical balance gives N=mg+P sin(theta).
For a static state, friction must oppose the horizontal push; the maximum available value is reached only at impending slip.
At the threshold, P cos(theta)=mu_s[mg+P sin(theta)].
Rearranging gives P[cos(theta)-mu_s sin(theta)]=mu_s mg and hence the stated P_max.
answer.check: Setting theta=0 reduces the result to P_max=mu_s mg, the ordinary horizontal-push threshold.

rubric.criterion: Computes N from the vertical force balance including the downward component of P.
rubric.evidence_of: Does not assume N=mg.

rubric.criterion: Uses static-friction equality only at impending slip.
rubric.evidence_of: Distinguishes a threshold condition from an unconditional friction law.

rubric.criterion: Derives the threshold expression with the force-angle term retained in both horizontal and vertical components.
rubric.evidence_of: Carries the coupled normal-force/friction effect through the algebra.

adaptation.reason: Changes a known sub-threshold horizontal pull into an angled-force threshold derivation where the applied force itself changes the normal reaction and therefore the friction limit.

hints.text: Before using any friction limit, how does the downward component of the applied force change the normal reaction?
At the largest no-slip force, the static inequality is exactly at its boundary; combine that threshold with the vertical force balance.

transfer.statement: The learner must carry a force that changes both the tangential demand and the normal reaction through the static-friction threshold instead of treating mu_s mg as a fixed limit.

questions.stem: A block of mass m rests on a block of mass M on a smooth floor. A horizontal force F is applied to the upper block m. The coefficient of static friction between the blocks is mu_s. Derive the largest F for which the blocks move together without slipping.
conditions: The lower block has no other horizontal contact force from the floor.
The contact between the two blocks remains horizontal.

answer.summary: If the blocks move together, a=F/(m+M). The lower block needs friction f_required=Ma. With N=mg at the interface, no slip requires MF/(m+M) <= mu_s m g, so F_max = mu_s m g (m+M)/M.
reasoning: Under the no-slip assumption, treat both blocks as one system to obtain the common acceleration a=F/(m+M).
Now isolate the lower block M. Its only horizontal force is the friction from the upper block, so f_required=Ma=MF/(m+M).
The interface normal is N=mg because the upper block has no vertical acceleration or other vertical force.
Static contact is feasible only while f_required <= mu_s N; equality gives the threshold F_max.
answer.check: The friction needed to accelerate the lower block is the quantity tested against the static limit; using f=mu_s N for every smaller F would erase the dependence on F.

rubric.criterion: Uses one common acceleration only under the provisional no-slip constraint.
rubric.evidence_of: Treats shared acceleration as a contact-state consequence rather than an automatic fact.

rubric.criterion: Isolates the lower block to identify the required friction as Ma.
rubric.evidence_of: Assigns friction to the correct body and does not cancel the internal force on an individual-body FBD.

rubric.criterion: Compares the required friction with mu_s mg and solves the resulting threshold.
rubric.evidence_of: Tests static feasibility rather than assuming limiting friction from the start.

adaptation.reason: Changes an already-sliding single-body friction calculation into a no-slip two-body contact where the required friction must be derived first and only then tested against the static limit.

hints.text: Assume no slip provisionally. Which acceleration would the two-block system then have?
After finding the common acceleration, isolate the lower block: what horizontal force must give that block its acceleration?

transfer.statement: The learner must rebuild the no-slip force account after the applied force moves to the other body, rather than copying the friction equation from the earlier stacked-block threshold item.

questions.stem: Blocks A and B are side by side on a smooth horizontal floor, with A to the left of B and no adhesive connection. Compare two cases. In case 1 a horizontal force pushes A to the right into B and contact is maintained. In case 2 the same force pulls A to the left, away from B. In which case may one common horizontal acceleration be imposed, and why?
conditions: The contact force is an ordinary normal force and cannot pull the blocks together.
The floor is frictionless.

answer.summary: A common acceleration is justified in case 1 while maintained contact fixes the separation. It is not justified in case 2: the normal contact cannot pull B after A is pulled away, so the contact constraint is lost.
reasoning: Common acceleration must be earned from an active constraint that fixes relative separation.
When A is pushed into B and contact is maintained, the normal interaction can enforce the shared motion.
When A is pulled away from B, an ordinary normal force cannot act as a tensile connector to keep them together.
After separation, each block's acceleration must be obtained from its own remaining forces.
answer.check: If a proposed case-2 solution assigns a nonzero pulling normal force on B to preserve contact, it has given an ordinary contact force a capability it does not have.

hints.text: What physical condition must stay active before equal acceleration can be imposed?
Ask whether an ordinary contact normal can keep acting when A tries to move away from B.

questions.stem: Masses m_A and m_B, with m_B > m_A, hang from the two ends of one taut massless inextensible string over one fixed frictionless massless pulley. Derive the acceleration magnitude a and the common string tension T. State explicitly why T is not equal to either hanging weight during the acceleration.
conditions: Mass A accelerates upward and mass B accelerates downward.
Use the same acceleration magnitude a for the two ends, as required by the fixed string-length constraint.
Neglect air resistance.

answer.summary: The acceleration magnitude is a=(m_B-m_A)g/(m_A+m_B), and the common tension is T=2m_A m_B g/(m_A+m_B). During the motion T>m_A g and T<m_B g, so it is not equal to either weight unless the corresponding acceleration is zero.
reasoning: The fixed inextensible string gives equal acceleration magnitudes for the two ends while the ideal string/pulley model licenses one common tension T.
For A, upward positive gives T-m_A g=m_A a.
For B, downward positive gives m_B g-T=m_B a.
Adding the equations gives a=(m_B-m_A)g/(m_A+m_B).
Substitution into either body equation gives T=2m_A m_B g/(m_A+m_B).
Because A accelerates upward, its tension exceeds m_A g; because B accelerates downward, its tension is below m_B g.
answer.check: If m_A=m_B, the formula reduces to a=0 and T=mg, recovering the equilibrium special case.

hints.text: Separate the two claims you need: what fixes the acceleration relationship, and what licenses one common tension magnitude?
Write one signed Newton-II equation for each mass, then add the equations to eliminate T.

questions.stem: Two blocks A and B are initially touching on a smooth horizontal floor, with A to the left of B. A horizontal force F is suddenly applied to A toward the left, away from B. A proposed solution treats A+B as one connected system and writes a=F/(m_A+m_B). Decide whether that model is valid immediately after the force is applied. If it is not, state the two accelerations.
conditions: There is no glue, string, or other connector.
The contact is an ordinary normal interaction that cannot pull.
Take rightward as positive.

answer.summary: The common-acceleration model is invalid because the force makes A separate from B and an ordinary normal contact cannot pull them together. Immediately after contact is lost, a_A=-F/m_A and a_B=0.
reasoning: The earlier common-acceleration rule applies only while an active condition fixes the blocks' separation.
Here F drives A away from B, so maintaining contact would require a tensile contact force on B, which an ordinary normal interaction cannot supply.
Once the contact force becomes zero, B has no horizontal force and therefore zero horizontal acceleration.
A has the applied leftward force F, so with rightward positive its acceleration is -F/m_A.
answer.check: The rejected value F/(m_A+m_B) would require B to accelerate left even though no horizontal interaction remains on B.

rubric.criterion: Rejects common acceleration because the stated contact cannot enforce fixed separation under the applied force.
rubric.evidence_of: Treats the constraint as conditional rather than automatic.

rubric.criterion: Sets the post-separation contact force to zero.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizes that an ordinary normal interaction cannot pull.

rubric.criterion: Obtains a_A=-F/m_A and a_B=0 in the declared sign convention.
rubric.evidence_of: Rebuilds the individual-body dynamics after the constraint is lost.

adaptation.reason: Turns the qualitative maintained-versus-lost-contact contrast into a dynamics task where the learner must reject a familiar whole-system equation and rebuild the two body accelerations.

hints.text: Before using one acceleration, ask what interaction would have to keep the separation fixed after A is pulled away from B.

transfer.statement: The learner must decide that the common-acceleration connected-system model has ceased to apply, rather than being told that contact is maintained.

questions.stem: Two masses remain attached to one taut inextensible string that does not slip on a fixed pulley. The pulley is now stated to have appreciable rotational inertia, and no rotational-dynamics relation is supplied. A student claims that both T_A=T_B and a_A+a_B=0 must either survive together or fail together. Decide which statement can still be obtained from the bounded material, and which statement is no longer licensed.
conditions: Coordinates y_A and y_B are measured positive away from the fixed pulley along the two straight string segments.
The string remains taut and inextensible and does not slip.
Do not invent a torque or rotational-inertia equation.

answer.summary: The kinematic relation a_A+a_B=0 still follows from the fixed total string length. Equal tension T_A=T_B is no longer guaranteed by the taught ideal redirection model once appreciable pulley rotational inertia is introduced. A quantitative tension difference is outside this packet.
reasoning: The signed acceleration relation is derived from the inextensible string's fixed length and the two changing straight segments.
That geometric argument does not use equality of tension magnitudes.
The one-common-T rule was licensed by the ideal massless/frictionless redirection model.
Introducing appreciable pulley rotational inertia breaks that force-transmission idealization, so the packet must refuse equal tension without supplying a replacement dynamics model.
answer.check: If the pulley is restored to the massless ideal model, both claims are licensed again, but for different reasons: geometry for the acceleration relation and force transmission for equal tension.

rubric.criterion: Retains a_A+a_B=0 from the fixed-length geometry.
rubric.evidence_of: Can identify the kinematic origin of the string constraint independently of force transmission.

rubric.criterion: Refuses to assert T_A=T_B after the ideal redirection assumption is broken.
rubric.evidence_of: Treats equal tension as model-conditional.

rubric.criterion: Does not manufacture a numerical or symbolic nonideal-pulley tension relation.
rubric.evidence_of: Respects the stated boundary of the available model.

adaptation.reason: Breaks only the ideal force-transmission assumption from an ideal Atwood setup while preserving fixed inextensible-string geometry, forcing the learner to separate the two model claims.

hints.text: Which statement is derived from total string length, and which statement depends on the pulley/string force idealization?

transfer.statement: The learner must preserve the kinematic length constraint while rejecting the equal-tension model after only the force-transmission assumption changes.

questions.stem: A block of mass m is released from rest on a smooth fixed plane inclined at angle theta above the horizontal. Choose axes that make the contact constraint simple, determine the normal reaction, and find the block's acceleration along the plane.
conditions: 0 < theta < 90 degrees.
The plane is fixed and smooth.
The block remains in contact with the plane.

answer.summary: Using axes parallel/perpendicular to the plane, weight has components mg sin(theta) down the plane and mg cos(theta) into the plane. Maintained contact gives N=mg cos(theta), and the tangential equation gives acceleration g sin(theta) down the plane.
reasoning: Choose the block and use +parallel down the plane and +perpendicular outward from the plane.
The physical forces are weight mg and the normal reaction N.
Resolve weight into mg sin(theta) parallel down the plane and mg cos(theta) perpendicular into the plane.
Maintained contact gives a_perp=0, so N-mg cos(theta)=0.
Along the plane, mg sin(theta)=m a_parallel, so a_parallel=g sin(theta) down the plane.
answer.check: At theta=0 the tangential acceleration tends to zero and N tends to mg; as theta approaches 90 degrees, N tends to zero and the tangential acceleration tends to g.

hints.text: Which axis choice turns maintained contact into one simple acceleration statement?
With axes parallel/perpendicular to the plane, resolve weight before writing the two signed Newton-II equations.

questions.stem: A block rests on a rough fixed plane inclined at angle theta. The coefficient of static friction is mu_s. Determine the friction required for rest and derive the condition under which the static state is possible.
conditions: No other force acts on the block.
The block is tested for rest; do not assume limiting friction at the start.

answer.summary: For rest, N=mg cos(theta) and static friction must act up the plane with required magnitude mg sin(theta). Rest is feasible when mg sin(theta) <= mu_s mg cos(theta), equivalently tan(theta) <= mu_s.
reasoning: Without friction the block tends to slide down the plane, so static friction required for rest points up the plane.
The perpendicular equation gives N=mg cos(theta).
The no-slip tangential equation requires f_required=mg sin(theta).
Static contact is possible only if f_required <= mu_s N.
Cancelling mg cos(theta)>0 gives tan(theta)<=mu_s.
answer.check: The calculation uses equality f_s=mu_s N only at the limiting angle; for a smaller angle the actual static friction is below its maximum.

hints.text: First ask which way the block would tend to slip if friction vanished.
Find N from the perpendicular equation, solve the friction required for rest, then compare that requirement with mu_s N.

questions.stem: A block is already sliding down a rough fixed plane inclined at angle theta. The coefficient of kinetic friction is mu_k. Derive its acceleration along the plane.
conditions: The sliding direction is down the plane.
No other force acts on the block.
The plane is fixed.

answer.summary: N=mg cos(theta). Kinetic friction has magnitude mu_k mg cos(theta) and points up the plane, so the down-plane acceleration is a=g[sin(theta)-mu_k cos(theta)].
reasoning: Maintained contact gives N=mg cos(theta).
Because the block is sliding down relative to the plane, kinetic friction points up the plane.
With down-plane positive, m a=mg sin(theta)-mu_k mg cos(theta).
Divide by m to obtain a=g[sin(theta)-mu_k cos(theta)].
answer.check: Setting mu_k=0 recovers the smooth-plane result a=g sin(theta).

hints.text: The block is already sliding down the plane; which way must the kinetic friction act at the contact?
Use the perpendicular equation for N, then write the tangential net force with down the plane positive.

questions.stem: A block of mass m is on a smooth fixed plane that rises to the right at angle theta above the horizontal. A horizontal force P pushes the block to the right. Determine the normal reaction and the acceleration along the plane.
conditions: 0 < theta < 90 degrees.
The block remains in contact with the smooth plane.
The applied force P is horizontal and rightward.

answer.summary: Relative to plane-aligned axes, P has P cos(theta) up the plane and P sin(theta) into the plane. Thus N=mg cos(theta)+P sin(theta), and a_parallel=[P cos(theta)-mg sin(theta)]/m with uphill positive.
reasoning: Choose +parallel uphill and +perpendicular outward from the plane.
Resolve the horizontal force into P cos(theta) uphill and P sin(theta) into the plane.
Resolve weight into mg sin(theta) downhill and mg cos(theta) into the plane.
Maintained contact gives N-mg cos(theta)-P sin(theta)=0.
The parallel equation is P cos(theta)-mg sin(theta)=m a_parallel.
answer.check: At P=0 the result reduces to the ordinary smooth-incline equations, with negative uphill acceleration -g sin(theta).

hints.text: The horizontal applied force is not parallel to the plane. Which component presses into the plane and which acts along it?
Resolve P and mg in the same plane-aligned axes, use a_perp=0 for N, then use the parallel equation for acceleration.

questions.stem: A block rests on a smooth fixed incline. A student draws three downward-related force arrows on the same free-body diagram: mg vertically downward, mg sin(theta) down the plane, and mg cos(theta) into the plane. Diagnose the diagram and state how the weight should be represented when writing plane-aligned equations.
conditions: The only physical interactions are Earth-on-block gravity and plane-on-block normal contact.
The question is about force ownership and representation, not numerical calculation.

answer.summary: The diagram double-counts gravity. Weight mg is one physical force. For plane-aligned equations it may be represented by the components mg sin(theta) down the plane and mg cos(theta) into the plane, but the original mg must not also be added as a separate force in those component sums.
reasoning: A free-body inventory is a list of physical interactions acting on the chosen body.
Gravity is one Earth-on-block interaction, represented by the vector mg.
Resolving that vector into parallel/perpendicular components changes its coordinate description only.
The component equations may use the two components instead of the unresolved weight vector; they are not two new agents.
answer.check: The physical-force count remains two in this smooth-contact case: weight and normal reaction.

hints.text: Did choosing new axes create any new physical object acting on the block?
Keep one gravity interaction; use either its original vector or its resolved components in a given equation representation, not both.

questions.stem: The same smooth fixed-incline problem is solved by two students. Student A uses axes parallel/perpendicular to the plane. Student B keeps horizontal/vertical laboratory axes. Decide whether both coordinate choices are physically valid, and explain why Student A's choice usually makes the contact constraint and acceleration easier to express.
conditions: Both students use one consistent inertial frame.
The plane is fixed and smooth.
No numerical angle is required.

answer.summary: Both coordinate systems are valid if used consistently. Plane-aligned axes are usually simpler because maintained contact becomes a_perp=0 and the unknown acceleration has only a parallel component; horizontal/vertical axes require projecting both the normal force and the constrained acceleration.
reasoning: Changing axes does not change the physical forces or motion.
In plane-aligned axes, the normal reaction lies on the perpendicular axis and the tangential motion lies on the parallel axis.
The contact condition is therefore stated directly as a_perp=0.
In horizontal/vertical axes the same normal and acceleration must be represented by components, which is valid but algebraically less direct.
answer.check: A correct solution in either coordinate system must predict the same physical acceleration vector and normal reaction.

rubric.criterion: Accepts both coordinate systems as valid representations.
rubric.evidence_of: Treats axis choice as modelling convenience rather than a physical law.

rubric.criterion: Identifies a_perp=0 as the simple contact statement in plane-aligned axes.
rubric.evidence_of: Connects representation choice to the active constraint.

rubric.criterion: States that horizontal/vertical axes require extra projection rather than different physics.
rubric.evidence_of: Preserves coordinate invariance of Newton II.

adaptation.reason: Changes a direct plane-aligned calculation into a comparison of two coordinate representations, requiring the learner to distinguish physical validity from modelling convenience.

hints.text: Does rotating the coordinate axes change which objects exert forces on the block?
Compare how the maintained-contact condition is written in each axis choice.

transfer.statement: The learner must translate the same fixed-incline dynamics between contact-aligned and laboratory axes without treating one representation as different physics.

questions.stem: A block is at rest on a rough incline. A controllable force P acts up the plane. In one trial P is slightly smaller than mg sin(theta); in another it is slightly larger than mg sin(theta), and in both trials the available static friction is sufficient to prevent motion. Determine the static-friction direction in each trial without assuming that friction always points uphill.
conditions: The plane is fixed.
The block remains at rest in both stated trials.
P acts exactly parallel to the plane.

answer.summary: When P<mg sin(theta), the no-friction tendency is down the plane, so static friction acts up the plane. When P>mg sin(theta), the no-friction tendency is up the plane, so static friction acts down the plane. At P=mg sin(theta), the required static friction is zero.
reasoning: Friction direction follows the relative slip tendency that would exist without friction.
Compare the applied uphill force P with the downhill gravity component mg sin(theta).
If gravity's component is larger, friction must act uphill to maintain rest.
If P is larger, friction must act downhill.
If the two non-friction tangential forces balance exactly, no tangential friction is required.
answer.check: The physical direction changes continuously through a zero-friction case rather than remaining permanently uphill.

rubric.criterion: Uses the no-friction slip tendency rather than the object's current zero velocity.
rubric.evidence_of: Applies the contact-level friction-direction rule.

rubric.criterion: Assigns uphill friction for P<mg sin(theta) and downhill friction for P>mg sin(theta).
rubric.evidence_of: Responds correctly to the reversed tangential tendency.

rubric.criterion: Allows zero friction at P=mg sin(theta).
rubric.evidence_of: Does not force a nonzero friction value merely because the surface is rough.

adaptation.reason: Adds a variable tangential applied force so the friction direction can reverse while the block remains static, testing slip-tendency reasoning rather than a memorized uphill direction.

hints.text: Temporarily remove friction from the model. Which way would the block tend to move in each trial?

transfer.statement: The learner must choose the static-friction direction from the changed slip tendency, including a zero-friction boundary, instead of carrying over the familiar downhill-gravity case.

questions.stem: A block of mass m is held at rest on a rough fixed plane that rises to the right at angle theta. A horizontal force P pushes to the right. The coefficient of static friction is mu_s. Derive the condition on P and theta for the block to be able to remain at rest.
conditions: 0 < theta < 90 degrees.
The applied force is horizontal.
Do not assume the static-friction direction in advance; use a signed required value.

answer.summary: With uphill positive, N=mg cos(theta)+P sin(theta). The static friction required by rest is f_required=mg sin(theta)-P cos(theta). Static equilibrium is feasible exactly when |mg sin(theta)-P cos(theta)| <= mu_s[mg cos(theta)+P sin(theta)].
reasoning: Resolve P into P cos(theta) uphill and P sin(theta) into the plane.
The perpendicular rest condition gives N=mg cos(theta)+P sin(theta).
The tangential rest equation P cos(theta)+f_s-mg sin(theta)=0 gives the signed required friction f_required=mg sin(theta)-P cos(theta).
Do not choose a friction direction separately; the sign of f_required supplies it.
The static model is feasible when the magnitude of that required value does not exceed mu_s N.
answer.check: At P=0 the condition reduces to tan(theta)<=mu_s; if P cos(theta)=mg sin(theta), the required friction is zero.

rubric.criterion: Includes the inward perpendicular component P sin(theta) when finding N.
rubric.evidence_of: Does not assume N=mg cos(theta) after another force is applied.

rubric.criterion: Solves a signed f_required from the tangential equilibrium equation.
rubric.evidence_of: Lets the equation determine the required friction direction.

rubric.criterion: Tests |f_required| against mu_s N instead of setting friction equal to its limit immediately.
rubric.evidence_of: Uses the static-feasibility model correctly.

adaptation.reason: Adds rough contact and an unknown friction direction to the same horizontal-force geometry, requiring a signed friction demand and static-feasibility test after the altered normal reaction is found.

hints.text: Which part of the horizontal force changes the contact normal, and which part changes the tangential force demand?
Find N first, then solve the signed friction needed for rest before comparing its magnitude with the static limit.

transfer.statement: The learner must integrate force decomposition, altered normal reaction, signed friction demand and static feasibility in dependency order rather than copying N=mg cos(theta) or f=mu_s N.

questions.stem: A proposed plane-aligned solution writes the tangential force sum as mg + mg sin(theta) and the perpendicular force sum as N - mg - mg cos(theta). The solver says the component terms were added because the weight was resolved. Identify the modelling error and write the correct role of the weight in the two component equations.
conditions: The block is on a smooth fixed incline.
Only gravity and the normal reaction act.

answer.summary: The solution double-counts the same weight vector. In plane-aligned equations, gravity contributes mg sin(theta) down the plane and mg cos(theta) into the plane; the unresolved mg is not added again. Thus the tangential gravity term is mg sin(theta), and the perpendicular equation uses N-mg cos(theta)=0 for maintained contact.
reasoning: Weight mg is one physical force, not three.
Resolving it replaces its representation in the chosen component equations.
The original vector magnitude mg is not itself a signed scalar component along either tilted axis.
Use the two appropriate components in the two equations and keep the normal as the separate contact force.
answer.check: The corrected equations account for exactly two physical interactions: Earth-on-block gravity and plane-on-block normal contact.

rubric.criterion: Identifies double-counting of gravity as the error.
rubric.evidence_of: Distinguishes physical-force inventory from vector components.

rubric.criterion: Uses mg sin(theta) only in the tangential gravity contribution.
rubric.evidence_of: Assigns the correct component to the along-plane equation.

rubric.criterion: Uses mg cos(theta) only in the perpendicular gravity contribution and N separately.
rubric.evidence_of: Builds the maintained-contact equation without re-adding mg.

adaptation.reason: Changes a diagram diagnosis into a faulty pair of component equations, requiring the learner to preserve force ownership through a different representation.

hints.text: How many physical interactions act on the smooth-contact block, and did the axis rotation create another agent?
A resolved vector contributes one scalar component to each axis equation; the original vector is not added again as a third scalar term.

transfer.statement: The learner must recognize the same force/component double-counting error after it moves from a drawn FBD into algebraic component equations.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and travels the same distance s down the same incline of angle theta in two trials. On a smooth surface the time is t_0. On a rough surface the block slides throughout and the time is t > t_0. Assuming kinetic friction coefficient mu_k is constant, derive mu_k in terms of theta, t_0 and t.
conditions: Both trials start from rest at the same point.
The incline angle and travel distance are unchanged.
The rough-surface trial has established downward sliding with constant mu_k.

answer.summary: Smooth acceleration is a_0=g sin(theta), rough acceleration is a=g[sin(theta)-mu_k cos(theta)]. Since s=(1/2)at^2 from rest, a/a_0=t_0^2/t^2. Therefore mu_k=tan(theta)[1-t_0^2/t^2].
reasoning: The smooth trial gives a_0=g sin(theta).
The rough sliding trial gives a=g[sin(theta)-mu_k cos(theta)].
Equal distance from rest gives s=(1/2)a_0 t_0^2=(1/2)a t^2, hence a/a_0=t_0^2/t^2.
Substitute the two incline accelerations and solve for mu_k.
This yields mu_k=tan(theta)[1-t_0^2/t^2].
answer.check: Because t>t_0, the bracket is positive. If t approaches t_0, the inferred mu_k approaches zero.

rubric.criterion: Builds the smooth and rough incline accelerations from the corresponding force models.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeps the contact-state physics distinct between trials.

rubric.criterion: Uses equal-distance constant-acceleration kinematics to relate a/a_0 to t_0^2/t^2.
rubric.evidence_of: Connects the NLM result to the measured timing representation.

rubric.criterion: Solves to mu_k=tan(theta)[1-t_0^2/t^2] and checks its limiting sign.
rubric.evidence_of: Completes the cross-topic reasoning and verifies plausibility.

adaptation.reason: Changes a direct rough-incline acceleration derivation into an inference from smooth-versus-rough travel times over the same distance, requiring the NLM result to be connected to constant-acceleration kinematics.

hints.text: The two trials cover the same distance from rest. What relation connects distance, constant acceleration and travel time in each trial?
Express the rough acceleration from the friction model and the smooth acceleration from the no-friction model, then eliminate the common distance.

transfer.statement: The learner must combine the established rough-incline dynamics with an independent timing representation to infer the friction coefficient, rather than being asked directly for acceleration.

teaching_routes.title: Reveal Grade-9 Newton-law spine with bounded friction/connection preparation and frame extension
entry_needs: Can tell whether an object's velocity is changing; the specific turning-point diagnostic from Motion is not a prerequisite.
learner_actions: Separate motion from change of motion.
Keep individual forces distinct from their net result.
Assign each force to the body on which it acts.
Determine friction direction from relative slip tendency.
Use signed net external force with F_net = m a.
Test static friction against its limit before using a limiting or kinetic formula.
Apply a common acceleration only when an active connection keeps the relevant separation fixed.
Use one common tension magnitude only under explicit ideal-string/redirection assumptions.
Derive the one-fixed-pulley acceleration relation from constant string length rather than a pulley-count rule.
Keep Newton-third-law partner forces on different bodies.
Use observer-frame/pseudo-force reasoning only when an explicit extension question demands it.
help_plan: Use a released low-friction cart for the first-law contrast.
Use two separate body inventories before any force equations.
For friction, ask for N and f_required before revealing any coefficient formula.
For connected bodies, ask what physical condition keeps the relative separation fixed.
For a string/pulley task, require the ideal assumptions and actual length equation before any tension or acceleration shortcut.
Use roadside versus accelerating-bus descriptions for the observer boundary.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: Completed constructions are visible only after body ownership, contact state, connection model and any string geometry are declared; coefficient and constraint relations are never presented as unconditional apparatus formulas.

source_preferences.reason: The four rungs are authored here without promoting candidate-packet authority.

when_not_suitable: Do not treat accelerating-frame/pseudo-force reasoning as ordinary Grade-9 Standard syllabus content.
Do not infer momentum-conservation or collision content from the presence of Newton's laws.
Do not use the single-fixed-pulley relation for movable/compound pulley geometry.
Do not assume equal tension after an ideal-string or ideal-redirection assumption is broken.

teaching_routes.title: Elicit Grade-9 Newton-law spine with bounded friction/connection preparation and frame extension
entry_needs: Same intrinsic Grade-9 force-law coverage as Core1A; no inferred learner mastery and no turning-point prerequisite.
learner_actions: Predict whether zero net force can coexist with steady motion.
Build body-specific force inventories before combining forces.
Predict friction direction from contact slip tendency.
Use the net force to predict acceleration.
Decide whether a static contact can supply the required friction before selecting a coefficient equality.
Name the connection that justifies a common acceleration.
Earn one tension symbol by stating the ideal-string model.
Reconstruct the one-fixed-pulley acceleration relation from constant string length.
Separate Newton-third-law partners by body.
Enter observer-frame reconstruction only for explicit extension demand.
help_plan: Ask which body receives each force before naming any pairing rule.
Ask what friction value the no-slip equations require before asking about a coefficient limit.
Ask which relative separation is fixed before offering a common acceleration.
Ask which string segments actually change length before offering a pulley relation.
Ask whether a physical agent changed before introducing a pseudo-force.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: Prediction, reconstruction, misconception diagnosis and boundary tests precede the closed reveal.

source_preferences.reason: Each elicitation cycle is authored specifically for the corresponding rung.

when_not_suitable: Do not substitute a declarative diagram for the learner's body-ownership decision.
Do not present pseudo-force/frame-choice content as ordinary Grade-9 Standard syllabus material.
Do not hand over mu N as the friction value before the learner decides the contact state.
Do not hand over equal tension or an acceleration ratio without the model/geometry that justifies it.

data.meaning: Illustrative steady speed available to compiled study obligations; none of the authored exits depends on its numerical value.

data.meaning: Mass in the authored Newton-second-law exit task.
Signed acceleration in the authored Newton-second-law exit task.

application_contexts.title: Block on a fixed inclined plane
application_contexts.description: A rigid plane at angle theta to the horizontal used as an application context for body-specific FBDs, contact-aligned axes, force decomposition, Newton II, normal reaction and friction-state reasoning.
invariants: The plane is fixed unless a question explicitly states otherwise.
One may choose axes parallel and perpendicular to the plane without changing the physical forces.
For maintained contact with a fixed plane, the body's acceleration perpendicular to the plane is zero.
The normal reaction is determined by the perpendicular dynamics; it is not automatically mg.
If friction is present, its direction and model are determined from relative sliding or slip tendency at the contact.

variation_dimensions.name: plane_angle
variation_dimensions.description: Vary theta while keeping the same fixed-plane geometry.

variation_dimensions.name: surface_state
variation_dimensions.description: Vary smooth, static-rough, impending-slip and established-sliding contact.

variation_dimensions.name: applied_force_direction
variation_dimensions.description: Vary forces parallel to the plane, horizontal, or otherwise angled so the normal reaction may change.

variation_dimensions.name: representation
variation_dimensions.description: Vary contact-aligned versus laboratory horizontal/vertical axes while preserving the same physical situation.

task_objectives: Build a correct chosen-body force account without inventing component forces as extra interactions.
Resolve the required force components relative to the declared axes.
Use perpendicular dynamics to determine N and tangential dynamics to determine acceleration or required friction.
Check friction feasibility or sliding state only after the contact-normal dynamics are established.
scope_limits: No moving wedge or accelerating-plane constraint.

buckets.title: Thermodynamics and heat engines
buckets.badge_reason: The conceptual ladder turns on system boundaries, state/path distinctions, cycle plots, and reservoir limits rather than vector reasoning.

capabilities.action: Classify internal energy as stored state and heat or work as boundary transfers.
capabilities.success_criterion: Distinguish internal energy from heat and work using a chosen system boundary.

capabilities.action: Compare state-function change across different process paths with common endpoints.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify internal-energy change as common to paths sharing both endpoint states.

capabilities.action: Interpret a directed pressure-volume cycle from state return and loop direction.
capabilities.success_criterion: State the net internal-energy change for a complete cycle.

capabilities.action: Distinguish the thermodynamic efficiency ceiling from mechanical friction losses.
capabilities.success_criterion: Reject complete heat-to-work conversion for a cyclic engine between finite reservoirs.

microtopics.title: Internal energy is stored; heat and work are transfers
microtopics.badge_reason: The entry distinction must be made with a system boundary before any energy-balance law is introduced.
entry_assumptions: Can identify a physical system and its surroundings and can distinguish stored energy from an energy-transfer event.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A system contains internal energy, while heat and work name energy transferred across its boundary; a body does not contain 'heat'.

teaching_path.action: Draw a boundary around one chosen system and label internal energy inside the boundary.
teaching_path.why_valid: Stored energy belongs to the state of the chosen system, so it must be located with the system before transfers are discussed.
teaching_path.output: inside boundary: internal energy | outside boundary: surroundings

teaching_path.action: Add one arrow crossing the boundary because of a temperature difference and a second arrow crossing because the surroundings mechanically compress the system.
teaching_path.why_valid: Both arrows represent energy crossing the system boundary, but they are classified by the transfer mechanism rather than stored as substances inside.
teaching_path.output: temperature-driven transfer -> heat crossing boundary | mechanical compression -> work crossing boundary

teaching_path.action: Stop both transfers and isolate the system after its state has changed, then ask which labels still describe something contained in the system.
teaching_path.why_valid: Once crossing stops, the stored internal energy remains a state property, whereas heat and work no longer name things sitting inside the isolated body.
teaching_path.output: isolated final system: internal energy remains a state label | current heat transfer = none | current work transfer = none

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A hot object contains heat, and cooling means some of that heat remains stored inside it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: When a hot block is isolated after heating stops, is 'heat' still a substance stored in the block?
misconceptions.repair: Name the stored quantity internal energy; reserve heat for energy crossing the boundary because of temperature difference.

exit_task.prompt: A block has finished being heated and is now isolated. Classify 'internal energy', 'heat', and 'work' as stored in the system or as names for energy transfer, and justify the classification using the boundary.

answer.summary: Internal energy is a state quantity stored in the system; heat and work describe energy transfers across the boundary and are not substances contained after the transfers stop.
reasoning: The system boundary separates what belongs to the state from what crosses between system and surroundings.
Internal energy describes the system's stored microscopic energy.
Heat and work classify transfer mechanisms, so when no transfer is occurring they are not contents of the isolated system.
answer.check: Redraw the same physical object as part of a larger chosen system; the bookkeeping boundary changes, so every claimed transfer must be reconsidered relative to that boundary.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The response is a classification of energy roles and includes no computed energy quantity.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created thermodynamic entry rung based on the matrix distinction; it intentionally stops before the blocked quantitative energy-balance equation at R2.

predict.prompt: A hot block has been disconnected from its heater and isolated. Does it still 'contain heat'?
predict.defensible_answer: No. It contains internal energy; heat names energy transfer across a boundary due to temperature difference.

attempt.produces: A boundary diagram classifying one stored-energy label inside and two possible transfer arrows across the boundary.

rubric.criterion: Internal energy is placed with the system state.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner distinguishes stored energy from a transfer process.

rubric.criterion: Heat and work are shown crossing the boundary rather than sitting inside.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner uses the system boundary to classify transfer mechanisms.

accepted: The diagram places internal energy inside the system and labels heat or work only on boundary-crossing arrows.
rejected: The diagram draws a quantity called 'heat stored inside' after the transfer has ended, preserving the misconception the rung must remove.

route.ask: What is the system whose energy you are talking about?
route.why_this_ask: The classification cannot be made until the bookkeeping boundary is chosen.

route.ask: Which events actually cross that boundary?
route.why_this_ask: It turns vague energy language into observable transfers.

route.ask: When every crossing stops, which energy label still describes the system's state?
route.why_this_ask: The isolation test separates stored state from transfer names.

route.ask: What wording should replace 'the block contains heat'?
route.why_this_ask: The learner performs the conceptual repair in ordinary language.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path labels the boundary and transfer mechanisms explicitly; the elicitation starts from the everyday phrase 'contains heat' and makes the learner use the boundary to decide which words can remain after isolation.

boundary_test.prompt: If two systems at the same temperature are placed in contact and no energy crosses because of temperature difference, is there a heat transfer between them at that moment?
boundary_test.answer: No. Without temperature-driven energy crossing the boundary, heat transfer is not occurring even though both systems possess internal energy.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner treats heat as a transfer process rather than as a stock determined simply by temperature.

microtopics.title: Internal-energy change is fixed by endpoint states, not process path
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must read a Cartesian pressure-volume diagram as multiple paths between the same endpoints without turning path area into a state property.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish an initial state, a final state, and a process connecting them.
Can use a pressure-volume plot to trace alternative paths qualitatively.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Internal energy is a state function: its change depends only on endpoint states, while heat and work can differ between paths connecting the same endpoints.

teaching_path.action: Mark one initial point A and one final point B on a pressure-volume plot, then draw two visibly different paths between the same points.
teaching_path.why_valid: Using identical endpoints isolates path choice from state choice, which is necessary to test state dependence.
teaching_path.output: same endpoints: A and B | path 1: upper route | path 2: lower route

teaching_path.action: Compare the geometric area under the two paths without moving A or B.
teaching_path.why_valid: Mechanical work in a pressure-volume process depends on the path traced, so different path shapes can produce different work while endpoints remain fixed.
teaching_path.output: A,B unchanged; area under path 1 != area under path 2 -> process work differs

teaching_path.action: Ask which quantity must remain the same for both processes solely because the initial and final states are identical.
teaching_path.why_valid: A state function is determined by the endpoint states, so its change cannot depend on which of the two process paths was taken.
teaching_path.output: endpoint states equal across paths -> internal-energy change equal | heat/work allocations may differ

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If two processes start and finish at the same states, they must transfer the same heat and do the same work.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two P-V paths connect the same initial and final states but enclose different areas under the curves. Must W and Q be equal for both?
misconceptions.repair: Keep delta U fixed by the endpoints; different path work is balanced by a different heat transfer through the first law.

exit_task.prompt: Two different pressure-volume paths connect the same initial state A to the same final state B. State which energy change must match between the paths and which transfers may differ, explaining the distinction without calculating areas.

answer.summary: The internal-energy change must be the same because the endpoints are the same, while heat and work may differ because they depend on the process path.
reasoning: The initial and final thermodynamic states are identical for both processes.
Internal energy is a state property, so its change is fixed by those endpoints.
The paths differ geometrically, so the transfer history can differ even though the state change does not.
answer.check: Change the final endpoint while keeping one path shape visually similar; the internal-energy change must be reconsidered because the endpoint state has changed.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer compares state dependence with path dependence and contains no computed work, heat, or internal-energy value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created state-function rung. It uses the pressure-volume plot qualitatively and does not author the blocked R2 energy-balance equation as a relation.

predict.prompt: Two processes start at A and finish at B but follow different paths on a pressure-volume plot. Must they do the same work?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Work can differ with path even though the internal-energy change is the same because the endpoints match.

attempt.produces: A two-path pressure-volume sketch annotated with 'same endpoint state change' and 'path-dependent transfers may differ'.

rubric.criterion: Both paths begin at the identical A point and end at the identical B point.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner is testing path dependence without changing the state change.

rubric.criterion: The response separates the common internal-energy change from potentially different transfers.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner distinguishes a state function from path quantities.

accepted: The diagram keeps A and B fixed, shows distinct path shapes, and labels internal-energy change as common while heat/work are allowed to differ.
rejected: The response concludes every energy quantity is identical because the endpoints match, erasing the path-dependent distinction.

route.ask: What is identical about the two processes before you compare any area?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the shared endpoints as the controlled feature.

route.ask: What visible feature differs between the paths?
route.why_this_ask: The learner identifies the process history represented by the plot.

route.ask: Which energy change is determined only by the endpoints?
route.why_this_ask: It elicits the state-function claim after the contrast is built.

route.ask: What does that leave free to differ between paths?
route.why_this_ask: The learner states the path-dependent consequence rather than memorizing a label.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative route draws two paths and points to their differing areas before stating the invariant; the elicitation first makes the learner identify what is common and what changes, then asks which quantity belongs to the endpoints.

boundary_test.prompt: If the two processes follow the same-looking path shape but end at different final states, must their internal-energy changes match?
boundary_test.answer: No. Endpoint state has changed, so the state-function change need not be the same.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner attributes invariance to matching states rather than to visual similarity of a plotted path.

microtopics.title: A complete cycle returns the state while its loop records net work
microtopics.badge_reason: The rung depends on reading a directed closed pressure-volume loop while keeping state return separate from nonzero energy transfer over the cycle.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish state-function change from path-dependent transfers.
Can interpret direction and enclosed area on a pressure-volume plot.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Over a complete thermodynamic cycle the system returns to its initial state, so net internal-energy change is zero and net heat balances net work; the directed pressure-volume loop records the sign of net work.

teaching_path.action: Trace a closed pressure-volume path until the system returns exactly to its starting state.
teaching_path.why_valid: A complete cycle has identical initial and final states by definition, so every state function returns to its initial value.
teaching_path.output: start state A -> path around loop -> final state A | state returned

teaching_path.action: Reverse the direction around the same geometric loop while leaving every plotted point unchanged.
teaching_path.why_valid: Reversing traversal changes the sign of process work while the enclosed geometric area keeps the same magnitude.
teaching_path.output: clockwise loop -> one work sign | same loop counter-clockwise -> opposite work sign | enclosed area magnitude = same

teaching_path.action: Use the returned state to check whether zero internal-energy change implies zero heat transfer for the full cycle.
teaching_path.why_valid: Returning the state only forces the net state-function change to vanish; if the cycle has nonzero net work, energy conservation requires a matching net heat transfer.
teaching_path.output: full cycle: internal-energy change = 0 | nonzero net work -> nonzero net heat with matching ledger balance

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A cyclic engine must have zero heat transfer because its internal energy returns to the starting value.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If delta U over one full cycle is zero but the loop encloses positive work area, what must be true of net heat?
misconceptions.repair: Apply the first law to the whole cycle: zero delta U requires net heat and net work to match under the chosen convention.

exit_task.prompt: A directed closed pressure-volume loop returns to its starting state and encloses a nonzero area. Explain the internal-energy change over the cycle and how reversing loop direction changes the net work sign.

answer.summary: The internal-energy change over the complete cycle is zero because the state returns to its start; reversing the loop reverses the net work sign while keeping the enclosed-area magnitude unchanged.
reasoning: The final state equals the initial state, so the net change of the state function is zero.
A directed pressure-volume loop can still represent nonzero net process work.
Reversing the path direction reverses the sign of that work, so the corresponding net heat balance must reverse consistently under the same convention.
answer.check: Collapse the loop to a path retraced exactly forward and backward; the enclosed area disappears, so the net work should also disappear.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer interprets signs and state return qualitatively and does not compute a loop area or energy value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created cyclic-process rung based on Cartesian pressure-volume reasoning. It states the qualitative cycle balance without introducing a new symbolic thermodynamic relation.

predict.prompt: A system completes a closed pressure-volume loop and returns to its starting state. Does that force every energy transfer over the cycle to be zero?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The internal-energy change is zero, but net heat and net work can both be nonzero and balance over the cycle.

attempt.produces: A directed closed-loop sketch with the returned state marked separately from the nonzero enclosed work area.

rubric.criterion: The start and finish are the same thermodynamic state.
rubric.evidence_of: The zero state-function change is justified by state return.

rubric.criterion: The loop direction is used to distinguish opposite net-work signs.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner reads the directed area as a process quantity rather than a state label.

accepted: The response marks A as both start and finish, gives zero internal-energy change, and shows that clockwise versus counter-clockwise traversal reverses the work sign.
rejected: The response says every transfer is zero merely because the system returns to A, ignoring the loop's nonzero directed area.

route.ask: What is true of the final thermodynamic state after one complete loop?
route.why_this_ask: It anchors the only conclusion that follows directly from cyclic return.

route.ask: What feature of the plot remains even though the state returns?
route.why_this_ask: It separates process history from endpoint state.

route.ask: What changes if the same loop is traversed in the opposite direction?
route.why_this_ask: It makes sign depend on directed traversal rather than on shape alone.

route.ask: Can zero state change coexist with nonzero transfer over the cycle?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must reject the central misconception explicitly.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path begins from a completed loop, reverses it, then checks the energy ledger; the elicitation begins with the false inference from state return and makes the learner identify which graphical feature still carries process information.

boundary_test.prompt: If the plotted process goes from A to B and then retraces exactly from B to A along the same curve, is there a nonzero enclosed loop area?
boundary_test.answer: No. Exact retracing encloses no area, so the net pressure-volume work over that out-and-back path is zero.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner ties net work to the directed enclosed loop rather than to the mere fact that a process returns to its start.

microtopics.title: Heat engines require heat rejection and obey a reservoir-temperature ceiling
microtopics.badge_reason: The distinction is conceptual: removing mechanical losses does not remove the second-law need for a cold-reservoir heat flow.
entry_assumptions: Can read a cyclic energy-flow diagram with heat entering, work leaving, and heat rejected.
Can compare hot- and cold-reservoir temperatures qualitatively.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A heat engine cannot convert all absorbed heat into work; even an ideal reversible engine between finite-temperature reservoirs has a maximum efficiency set by those reservoir temperatures.

teaching_path.action: Draw a cyclic engine between one hot reservoir and one colder reservoir, with absorbed heat entering, work leaving, and rejected heat leaving toward the cold reservoir.
teaching_path.why_valid: A cyclic heat engine returns its working substance to its starting state, so sustained work output requires an energy-flow ledger across the cycle rather than storage inside the engine.
teaching_path.output: hot reservoir -> heat in -> engine -> work out + heat out -> cold reservoir

teaching_path.action: Imagine removing friction and other mechanical losses while keeping the same two finite-temperature reservoirs.
teaching_path.why_valid: Removing dissipative losses can improve performance, but it does not remove the thermodynamic requirement that a cyclic engine reject some heat to the colder reservoir.
teaching_path.output: mechanical losses: present -> removed; rejected heat: remains required; efficiency: improves but stays below complete conversion

teaching_path.action: Lower the cold-reservoir temperature while holding the hot-reservoir temperature fixed, then compare the reversible performance ceiling.
teaching_path.why_valid: The maximum reversible efficiency depends on the separation of the reservoir temperatures, so changing the cold reservoir changes the ceiling without changing mechanical friction.
teaching_path.output: hot reservoir fixed; cold temperature -> lower; reversible efficiency ceiling -> higher, still below complete conversion for finite temperatures

misconceptions.wrong_idea: An ideal engine can reach 100% efficiency if friction and other mechanical losses are removed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: An engine absorbs heat from a hot reservoir and rejects none to a colder reservoir. Is that allowed merely because the engine is otherwise frictionless?
misconceptions.repair: The second-law limitation is not a mechanical-loss correction; some heat rejection is unavoidable for a cyclic heat engine between finite-temperature reservoirs.

exit_task.prompt: A frictionless cyclic heat engine operates between finite hot and cold reservoirs. Explain why frictionlessness does not permit complete conversion of absorbed heat into work and how making the cold reservoir colder changes the ideal ceiling.

answer.summary: Eliminating mechanical losses does not remove the need to reject some heat to the colder reservoir; lowering the cold-reservoir temperature raises the reversible efficiency ceiling but does not make a finite-temperature engine a complete heat-to-work converter.
reasoning: Mechanical friction is one source of loss, but the second-law restriction is not caused by friction.
A cyclic engine between finite reservoirs must reject heat to the colder reservoir.
Increasing the temperature separation can raise the reversible ceiling, yet the existence of the cold-reservoir heat flow remains part of the cycle.
answer.check: Compare two real engines between the same reservoirs; neither may be justified as exceeding the reversible benchmark simply by claiming better bearings or less friction.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The response compares qualitative efficiency limits and heat-flow requirements without calculating an efficiency percentage.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created second-law ceiling rung. It deliberately omits the quantitative reservoir-temperature efficiency formula because no engineering gate relation owns it for this bucket.

predict.prompt: Suppose every mechanical friction loss in a heat engine vanished. Could the engine then turn all absorbed heat into work during each cycle?
predict.defensible_answer: No. A cyclic engine between finite-temperature reservoirs still must reject some heat to the colder reservoir.

attempt.produces: An energy-flow diagram separating heat input, work output, and required heat rejection from mechanical-loss annotations.

rubric.criterion: Rejected heat remains on the diagram after friction is removed.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner separates the thermodynamic limit from mechanical dissipation.

rubric.criterion: Changing reservoir temperature changes the ideal ceiling without changing the definition of the energy flows.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner locates the bound in the reservoirs rather than in machine friction.

accepted: The frictionless diagram still contains heat rejection to the cold reservoir, and a colder cold reservoir is described as raising the reversible performance ceiling.
rejected: The response deletes the cold-reservoir heat flow as soon as friction is removed and claims complete conversion.

route.ask: Which energy flows must a cyclic engine exchange with its surroundings?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the ledger before efficiency claims are made.

route.ask: Which of those flows is directly caused by mechanical friction?
route.why_this_ask: It separates removable machine losses from the thermodynamic structure of the cycle.

route.ask: After friction is removed, what heat flow still cannot simply be deleted?
route.why_this_ask: The learner supplies the second-law distinction before seeing the completed claim.

route.ask: What qualitative change follows if the cold reservoir is made colder while the hot one stays fixed?
route.why_this_ask: It tests whether the learner connects the ideal ceiling to reservoir temperatures.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path draws the full engine ledger, removes friction, then varies reservoir temperature; the elicitation first asks which flow is actually attributable to friction and forces the learner to retain heat rejection before discussing the ceiling.

boundary_test.prompt: Two engines operate between identical reservoirs, but one has less mechanical friction. May the lower-friction engine exceed the reversible ceiling for those reservoirs?
boundary_test.answer: No. It may approach the reversible benchmark more closely, but reducing friction does not permit crossing that thermodynamic ceiling.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner distinguishes improved real-machine performance from the reservoir-set reversible limit.

teaching_routes.title: Declarative thermodynamics conceptual route
entry_needs: Keep R2 as an explicit quantitative gap; do not infer its sign equation from the later conceptual rungs.
learner_actions: Use system boundaries and pressure-volume plots to separate state from process.
Explain cycle and engine limits through scalar energy-flow reasoning.
help_plan: Keep transfer arrows at the system boundary.
Use paired pressure-volume paths before naming state dependence.
Keep reservoir heat flows distinct in the engine diagram.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: Completed conceptual constructions are visible without inserting a vector representation or the missing R2 equation.

source_preferences.reason: The record is self-contained and does not elevate the imported candidate packet.

when_not_suitable: Do not use this route as authority for the quantitative first-law sign convention.

entry_needs: The same scalar and pressure-volume conceptual scope as Core1A, with decisions elicited before model responses.
learner_actions: Classify, compare, and predict before reading the completed construction.
Use boundary cases to test everyday heat language, endpoint reasoning, loop interpretation, and engine-limit claims.
help_plan: Ask for the system boundary before energy labels.
Ask what endpoints are shared before comparing process paths.
Ask which engine flow is actually removed by reducing friction.
