subject: Physics
scope_summary: Conceptual rung records for buoyancy, steady incompressible continuity, and qualitative Bernoulli reasoning; the hydrostatic entry equation and quantitative efflux/Venturi rung remain un-authored.

resources.title: Track B authored fluids rung source
resources.selection_reason: Provides authored provenance for the conceptual fluid rungs while preserving the blocked quantitative entry and application rungs.

buckets.title: Fluid statics, buoyancy and Bernoulli flow
buckets.badge_reason: The ladder begins with a blocked quantitative static-pressure rung before moving into conceptual buoyancy and flow distinctions.

capabilities.action: Compare buoyant force from displaced-fluid volume.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify which fully submerged object has the larger buoyant force from its displaced volume.

capabilities.action: Infer flow-speed ordering from cross-sectional area in steady incompressible flow.
capabilities.success_criterion: Rank section speeds from the conserved volume flow.

capabilities.action: Reason across pressure, motion and height contributions along one ideal-flow path.
capabilities.success_criterion: State when speed alone is insufficient to rank static pressure.

microtopics.title: Buoyant force follows displaced fluid
microtopics.badge_reason: The key distinction is between the object's own mass and the volume of fluid removed by the submerged part.
entry_assumptions: Can reason that pressure forces on a submerged object come from the surrounding static fluid.
Can compare object volume with submerged volume qualitatively.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid, so submerged volume and fluid density—not the object's mass by itself—set the buoyant force.

teaching_path.action: Submerge two equal-mass objects of different volume in the same fluid and outline the volume occupied by each submerged object.
teaching_path.why_valid: For full submersion, the outlined object volume is exactly the volume of fluid displaced from that region.
teaching_path.output: same object mass | object A: smaller submerged volume | object B: larger submerged volume

teaching_path.action: Replace each object outline by an imagined parcel of the same fluid occupying the displaced region, then compare the parcel weights.
teaching_path.why_valid: The upward buoyant effect is set by the surrounding pressure imbalance and equals the weight of the fluid that would occupy the displaced volume.
teaching_path.output: smaller displaced volume -> lighter fluid parcel -> smaller buoyant force | larger displaced volume -> heavier fluid parcel -> larger buoyant force

teaching_path.action: Keep the object's mass label unchanged while changing only how much of it is submerged.
teaching_path.why_valid: If submerged volume decreases, the amount of displaced fluid decreases even though object mass has not changed, separating the controlling variables.
teaching_path.output: same object mass; submerged fraction: full -> partial; displaced volume -> smaller; buoyant force -> smaller

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Objects with equal mass experience equal buoyant force in the same fluid.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A 1 kg lead sphere and a 1 kg aluminium sphere are fully submerged in water. Must their buoyant forces be equal?
misconceptions.repair: Compare displaced volumes: buoyant force follows the weight of displaced fluid, not the object's mass label.

exit_task.prompt: Two equal-mass objects with different volumes are fully submerged in the same fluid. Predict which experiences the larger buoyant force and explain the deciding quantity.

answer.summary: The larger-volume object experiences the larger buoyant force because full submersion makes it displace a larger volume of the same fluid.
reasoning: Object mass is held equal, so it cannot explain a difference in buoyant force between the two cases.
Full submersion makes displaced volume match object volume.
In one fluid, the larger displaced volume corresponds to a larger weight of displaced fluid and therefore a larger buoyant force.
answer.check: Partly lift the larger object out of the fluid while leaving its mass unchanged; the buoyant force should decrease with its submerged volume.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer makes a qualitative comparison of buoyant force and displaced volume without asserting a computed force value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created buoyancy distinction from the matrix. The imported fluid packet remains source-only and no Archimedes equation is promoted as a gate-owned relation.

predict.prompt: A lead sphere and an aluminium sphere have the same mass and are fully submerged in the same water. Must the water push upward on them equally?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The object with the larger submerged volume displaces more water and therefore has the larger buoyant force.

attempt.produces: A paired drawing that highlights each displaced-fluid region separately from the equal object-mass labels.

rubric.criterion: The displaced region is larger for the larger-volume object.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner treats submerged volume as the fluid-side input.

rubric.criterion: Equal object mass is explicitly held fixed.
rubric.evidence_of: The conclusion cannot be attributed to a mass difference between the objects.

accepted: Both objects carry the same mass label, but the larger object has a visibly larger highlighted displaced-fluid region and is assigned the larger buoyant force.
rejected: The response says the forces are equal solely because the object masses are equal, without considering displaced volume.

route.ask: What quantity is guaranteed equal in this comparison?
route.why_this_ask: It makes object mass a controlled variable rather than an automatic explanation.

route.ask: Which object removes more fluid from the region it occupies?
route.why_this_ask: It redirects attention from object mass to displaced volume.

route.ask: What imagined fluid parcel corresponds to each displaced region?
route.why_this_ask: It constructs the fluid-weight interpretation before the force comparison.

route.ask: What happens if one object emerges partly while its mass stays the same?
route.why_this_ask: The boundary case tests whether submerged volume, not mass, controls the buoyant effect.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path replaces displaced regions with fluid parcels and then tests partial submersion; the elicitation first traps the equal-mass intuition and makes the learner identify the displaced region before any repair is shown.

boundary_test.prompt: An object is lowered farther into the same fluid without changing its mass, but it is not yet fully submerged. Should the buoyant force stay fixed?
boundary_test.answer: No. While the submerged volume is still increasing, the displaced-fluid volume and buoyant force increase too.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner ties buoyant force to displaced fluid rather than to the object's fixed mass.

microtopics.title: Steady incompressible flow speeds up in a narrower section
microtopics.badge_reason: The rung requires a conserved through-flow picture rather than the everyday intuition that less room means slower motion.
entry_assumptions: Can compare cross-sectional areas and interpret directional velocity arrows along one tube.
Can reason about equal volumes passing a section during equal time intervals.
microtopics.inferential_jump: For steady incompressible flow through one tube, the volume-flow rate is conserved, so smaller cross-sectional area requires larger flow speed.

teaching_path.action: Mark a wide section and a narrow section of one tube, then choose the same short time interval at both sections.
teaching_path.why_valid: Steady flow is compared over one common time interval, so the amount passing each section can be meaningfully matched.
teaching_path.output: one tube | wide section A | narrow section B | same time interval at A and B

teaching_path.action: Draw equal volumes of incompressible fluid crossing the wide and narrow sections during that common interval.
teaching_path.why_valid: In steady flow with no accumulation and no density change, the same fluid volume per time must pass every cross-section of the tube.
teaching_path.output: equal volume per equal time; wide section -> shorter travel distance | narrow section -> longer travel distance

teaching_path.action: Convert the travel-distance comparison into velocity-arrow lengths while leaving the section areas unchanged.
teaching_path.why_valid: Over the same time interval, the longer travel distance corresponds to the larger average speed.
teaching_path.output: wide section: shorter velocity arrow | narrow section: longer velocity arrow

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Water must slow down in a narrower pipe because there is less space available.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: In steady incompressible flow, if the pipe area halves, does the average speed halve or double?
misconceptions.repair: Conserve volume flow rate: the same volume per time must pass every section, so area and average speed vary inversely.

exit_task.prompt: A steady incompressible flow passes through three sections of one tube with different areas. Rank the flow speeds qualitatively and justify the ranking from equal volume crossing each section per equal time.

answer.summary: The narrowest section has the greatest average speed and the widest has the smallest because each section must pass the same fluid volume during the same time interval.
reasoning: Steady incompressible flow prevents fluid from accumulating between the sections.
Therefore each section passes the same volume during a chosen common time interval.
A smaller area must carry that volume through a longer distance in the same time, which means a larger average speed.
answer.check: Make two sections equal in area; the predicted average speeds at those sections should become equal in the same steady incompressible flow.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The response supplies a qualitative speed ranking from conserved volume flow and contains no computed speed.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created continuity concept. It teaches the invariant through equal-volume motion without authoring a symbolic continuity equation as subject truth.

predict.prompt: The same steady water flow enters a narrower part of a pipe. Before using a formula, should the water there move faster or slower on average?
predict.defensible_answer: Faster, because the same volume must pass through the smaller cross-section during the same time.

attempt.produces: A two-section flow sketch showing equal fluid volumes crossing a wide and a narrow section during one common time interval.

rubric.criterion: Equal crossing volumes are shown for the same time interval.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner represents the steady-flow invariant rather than comparing unrelated snapshots.

rubric.criterion: The narrow section has the longer travel distance or velocity arrow.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner links smaller area to greater speed through conserved volume flow.

accepted: The sketch uses one common time interval, equal crossing volumes, and a longer motion arrow through the narrow section.
rejected: The narrow section is assigned a shorter arrow because it has less room, while no conserved through-flow quantity is shown.

route.ask: If the flow is steady, can fluid keep piling up between the wide and narrow sections?
route.why_this_ask: It removes accumulation as an escape from the conservation decision.

route.ask: What must therefore be equal when you compare one common time interval?
route.why_this_ask: The learner identifies the conserved crossing volume.

route.ask: How can the narrower section pass that same volume in the same time?
route.why_this_ask: It elicits the required travel-distance change before naming speed.

route.ask: What should the velocity arrows look like after that comparison?
route.why_this_ask: It translates the constructed motion into the requested representation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path fixes sections and time, demonstrates equal crossing volumes, then maps distance to speed; the learner route begins by ruling out accumulation and must supply the conserved quantity before seeing the arrow comparison.

boundary_test.prompt: If the flow stops being steady and fluid temporarily accumulates between the sections, must the two section flow rates match at that instant?
boundary_test.answer: No. The equal-through-flow conclusion used here depends on the steady-flow condition.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner recognizes the conservation statement as conditional rather than as a rule about every pipe snapshot.

microtopics.title: Pressure, speed and height trade along an ideal-flow path
microtopics.badge_reason: The main failure is using a two-variable slogan when the energy ledger also contains height and model conditions.
entry_assumptions: Can relate section area to flow speed for steady incompressible flow.
Can compare heights and distinguish static pressure from flow speed.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Along a streamline in steady ideal flow, pressure, kinetic, and gravitational energy-per-volume contributions trade; a speed increase alone does not determine the pressure change unless the other contributions are controlled.

teaching_path.action: Choose two marked points on the same ideal-flow path and list three ledger columns at each point: static pressure, motion contribution, and height contribution.
teaching_path.why_valid: The comparison is only interpretable when both points belong to the same applicable flow path and all energy-per-volume contributions are kept visible.
teaching_path.output: point 1: pressure | motion | height ; point 2: pressure | motion | height

teaching_path.action: First narrow a horizontal section so speed rises while the two point heights remain equal.
teaching_path.why_valid: With height fixed in this controlled case, the increased motion contribution must be balanced by a decrease in the static-pressure contribution along the ideal-flow path.
teaching_path.output: horizontal narrowing: height = same; speed -> higher; static pressure -> lower

teaching_path.action: Now move the faster point to a lower height and ask whether speed alone still fixes the pressure ordering.
teaching_path.why_valid: Changing height adds another ledger change, so the earlier two-variable conclusion cannot be transferred without considering the full comparison.
teaching_path.output: speed at point 2: higher | height at point 2: lower | pressure ordering: not decidable from speed alone

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Wherever fluid speed is higher, static pressure must be lower, regardless of height or losses.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Point 2 has higher speed than point 1 but is also much lower. Can speed alone determine which point has higher pressure?
misconceptions.repair: Use all Bernoulli terms between points on the same streamline and state the ideal-flow assumptions before drawing a pressure conclusion.

exit_task.prompt: Two points lie on one steady ideal-flow path. Point 2 has higher speed and lower height than point 1. Explain why speed alone is insufficient to rank the static pressures and identify what must be considered.

answer.summary: The static-pressure ordering cannot be inferred from speed alone because both the motion contribution and the height contribution change between the points; the complete ideal-flow energy ledger must be compared.
reasoning: A higher speed increases the motion contribution at point 2.
A lower height decreases the gravitational contribution at point 2.
Those two changes act in different parts of the ledger, so static pressure must be determined from the whole balance rather than a slogan about speed.
answer.check: Return the two points to equal height while keeping the ideal-flow assumptions; only then does the controlled horizontal narrowing support the simpler higher-speed/lower-static-pressure comparison.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer identifies which qualitative energy contributions change and does not calculate a pressure value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created Bernoulli reasoning rung expressed as a qualitative ledger. No Bernoulli equation is authored as a library relation, preserving the engineering-gate authority boundary.

predict.prompt: Point 2 on an ideal-flow path has higher speed than point 1, but it is also lower. Can you conclude immediately that its static pressure is lower?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Height changed too, so the full energy-per-volume ledger must be considered before ranking the pressures.

attempt.produces: A two-point three-column ledger marking which of pressure, motion, and height contributions are known to rise, fall, or remain unknown.

rubric.criterion: The speed change is recorded in the motion column rather than turned directly into a pressure verdict.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner keeps separate contributions separate.

rubric.criterion: The height change is recorded before pressure is ranked.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner recognizes why the horizontal special case cannot be overgeneralized.

accepted: The ledger marks motion higher and height lower at point 2, leaving static pressure to be determined from the complete balance rather than from speed alone.
rejected: The response writes 'faster means lower pressure' immediately and ignores the changed height.

route.ask: Which three contributions must be kept visible at each comparison point?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents the learner from reducing the situation to a pressure-speed slogan.

route.ask: What does a horizontal narrowing show when height is deliberately held fixed?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the familiar special case under controlled conditions.

route.ask: What extra contribution changes when the faster point is also lower?
route.why_this_ask: It creates the reason the special-case inference can fail.

route.ask: Can speed alone still decide the pressure ordering?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must withdraw the overgeneralization explicitly.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path builds a full ledger, demonstrates the horizontal special case, then breaks one held condition; the elicitation starts from the tempting pressure slogan and makes the learner discover which missing column blocks it.

boundary_test.prompt: If the fluid has substantial dissipative loss between the two points, is this ideal-flow ledger sufficient by itself?
boundary_test.answer: No. The rung's comparison assumes the stated ideal-flow model; appreciable loss means the model choice must be reconsidered.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner treats the pressure-speed relation as conditional on both the full ledger and the model assumptions.

buckets.title: Vector direction and unit representation
buckets.badge_reason: The arithmetic is short, but learners commonly lose quadrant information, treat i/j notation as new physics, or try to normalize the zero vector.

conventions.statement: Declare +x/+y before interpreting component signs or reporting a direction.
Normalize only a nonzero vector; the zero vector has no unit direction.

scope.covers: Translate 2-D signed components into i-hat/j-hat notation, recover direction from component signs plus an acute inverse-trigonometric reference angle, and normalize a nonzero 2-D vector to unit direction.
excluded: General dot product and scalar projection.
Cross product and normal-to-plane reasoning.
Three-dimensional vector algebra.
Calculus or vector-function differentiation.

capabilities.action: Use an inverse tangent on a positive right-triangle ratio to recover an acute reference angle, leaving quadrant selection to the consuming subject.
capabilities.success_criterion: Given positive leg magnitudes a and b, evaluate or represent alpha = tan^-1(b/a) as an acute reference angle and state that this reference angle still requires the consuming subject to place it in the directed geometry. Draft bridge only; Mathematics-provider acceptance remains required.

capabilities.action: Translate a 2-D signed component pair into i-hat/j-hat notation and back without changing the vector.
capabilities.success_criterion: Given declared x/y axes, write (v_x,v_y) as v_x i-hat + v_y j-hat with signs preserved, and recover the same component pair from that notation.

capabilities.action: Recover the direction of a nonzero 2-D vector from its signed x/y components using quadrant information plus an acute inverse-trigonometric reference angle.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify the quadrant or axis from component signs, obtain an acute reference angle from |v_y/v_x| when both components are nonzero, and place that angle in the correct directed quadrant rather than reporting tan^-1(v_y/v_x) blindly.

capabilities.action: Normalize a nonzero 2-D vector to a dimensionless unit vector in the same direction.
capabilities.success_criterion: Compute or retain the vector magnitude |v|>0, divide every signed component by that same magnitude, express the result consistently, verify magnitude 1, and refuse normalization when v is the zero vector.

microtopics.title: Translate signed components to i-hat/j-hat notation
microtopics.badge_reason: The notation is compact but can tempt learners to drop a negative coefficient or treat basis labels as extra vector magnitudes.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed x/y components against declared positive axes.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The component pair and v_x i-hat + v_y j-hat are two notations for the same 2-D vector; coefficients carry the same signs and units as the original components.

teaching_path.action: Declare +x and +y and identify i-hat with the +x unit direction and j-hat with the +y unit direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The basis symbols are meaningless without the axes they name.
teaching_path.output: i-hat = +x unit direction; j-hat = +y unit direction

teaching_path.action: Replace the ordered pair (v_x,v_y) by v_x i-hat + v_y j-hat, carrying each coefficient sign unchanged.
teaching_path.why_valid: The coefficients are exactly the signed components along the two basis directions.
teaching_path.output: (v_x,v_y) <-> v_x i-hat + v_y j-hat

teaching_path.action: Read the two coefficients back from the i-hat/j-hat expression and compare with the original component pair.
teaching_path.why_valid: A notation translation is correct only if the original signed components are recovered.
teaching_path.output: recovered pair equals the starting pair

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A negative coefficient should be made positive because i-hat and j-hat already contain the direction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If v_x is negative while +x is declared to the right, what sign must multiply i-hat?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the coefficient sign. The hat symbol names the positive basis direction; a negative coefficient reverses that component.

exit_task.prompt: With declared +x/+y axes, a vector has components (a,-b), where a and b are positive. Write it in i-hat/j-hat notation and state how you would recover the component pair.

answer.summary: v = a i-hat - b j-hat, and the coefficients recover the pair (a,-b).
reasoning: i-hat names +x and j-hat names +y.
The x component is +a, so its coefficient is +a.
The y component is -b, so its coefficient is -b.
answer.check: Read the two signed coefficients back; they must be exactly (a,-b).

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer is a symbolic representation translation and asserts no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Owner-approved ExamSIDE Vector Algebra demand makes compact unit-basis notation a useful preparation action. The teaching is locally authored and does not import dot/cross-product content.

predict.prompt: If the y-component is negative, should the coefficient of j-hat be positive or negative?
predict.defensible_answer: Negative; j-hat names +y, so a negative coefficient is required for a component pointing against +y.

attempt.produces: A one-line translation from a signed component pair to i-hat/j-hat notation.
attempt.model_response: Preserve each component as the coefficient of its matching basis vector, including its sign.

route.ask: Which basis symbol names +x?
route.why_this_ask: It anchors the notation to the declared axis.

route.ask: What signed number multiplies that basis symbol?
route.why_this_ask: It forces the learner to carry the original component sign into the new notation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner route begins from the coefficient decision and reconstructs the notation from axis meaning rather than being shown the completed expression first.

boundary_test.prompt: If the x-component is zero, what happens to the i-hat term?
boundary_test.answer: Its coefficient is zero, so the term may be written as 0 i-hat or omitted without changing the vector.
boundary_test.confirms: The notation represents components rather than requiring both basis terms to appear visibly.

microtopics.title: Recover direction from signed components
microtopics.badge_reason: The ratio is simple, but a calculator's inverse tangent does not by itself preserve quadrant information.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed x/y components.
Can use an inverse tangent to obtain an acute reference angle through the declared Mathematics bridge.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Direction recovery is two-stage: component signs locate the quadrant or axis, while inverse tangent of the positive component-magnitude ratio supplies only an acute reference angle to place inside that quadrant.

teaching_path.action: Use the signs of v_x and v_y to identify the quadrant or an exact axis before taking any ratio.
teaching_path.why_valid: The signs retain directional information that a ratio can lose.
teaching_path.output: quadrant or axis fixed from signs

teaching_path.action: When both components are nonzero, form the positive ratio |v_y|/|v_x| and obtain the acute reference angle alpha = tan^-1(|v_y|/|v_x|).
teaching_path.why_valid: The absolute component magnitudes form the legs of the right triangle; inverse tangent returns the acute reference angle, not the full directed angle.
teaching_path.output: alpha = tan^-1(|v_y|/|v_x|), 0<alpha<90 degrees

teaching_path.action: Place alpha in the previously identified quadrant and report the requested directed angle or verbal direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: Quadrant placement restores the signs discarded by the positive ratio.
teaching_path.output: quadrant I: theta=alpha; quadrant II: theta=180°-alpha; quadrant III: theta=180°+alpha; quadrant IV: theta=360°-alpha for standard 0°<=theta<360° reporting

teaching_path.action: Check that the reported direction has the same x/y sign pattern as the original components.
teaching_path.why_valid: Any correct direction must point into the same quadrant or axis as the signed component pair.
teaching_path.output: direction sign pattern matches (v_x,v_y)

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The value tan^-1(v_y/v_x) is always the final direction angle.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If v_x<0 and v_y>0, can a negative raw ratio by itself tell you that the vector lies in quadrant II?
misconceptions.repair: Fix the quadrant from the component signs first. Use an acute reference angle from absolute component magnitudes, then place it in that quadrant.

exit_task.prompt: A nonzero vector has v_x<0, v_y>0 and |v_y|<|v_x|. State its quadrant, write the acute reference-angle expression, and show how the directed angle from +x is obtained symbolically.

answer.summary: It lies in quadrant II. Let alpha = tan^-1(|v_y|/|v_x|); the standard directed angle from +x is 180 degrees - alpha.
reasoning: Negative x and positive y place the vector in quadrant II.
The positive magnitude ratio gives only the acute reference angle alpha.
Quadrant II places that reference angle above the -x direction, giving 180 degrees - alpha from +x.
answer.check: The final angle must have cosine negative and sine positive, matching the original component signs.
acceptable_alternatives: State the direction as alpha above the -x axis instead of using a 0-360 degree angle.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer is symbolic and asserts no computed numerical angle.

microtopics.research_contribution: ExamSIDE Vector Algebra demand exposes direction/resultant-orientation questions that are not closed by magnitude or component decomposition alone. The route keeps inverse-trig readiness explicit as a Mathematics bridge.

predict.prompt: A vector has negative x-component and positive y-component. Before using a calculator, which quadrant must the answer lie in?
predict.defensible_answer: Quadrant II.

attempt.produces: A quadrant decision, an acute reference-angle expression, and a directed-angle placement.
attempt.model_response: Use signs first for quadrant, then alpha = tan^-1(|v_y|/|v_x|), then place alpha in that quadrant.

route.ask: What do the two component signs tell you before any trigonometry?
route.why_this_ask: It preserves the directional information a ratio can erase.

route.ask: Which positive leg ratio gives the acute angle to the x-axis?
route.why_this_ask: It separates reference-angle recovery from quadrant placement.

route.ask: How must that acute angle be placed in the quadrant you already fixed?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents the calculator output from becoming the direction by default.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner commits to a quadrant before seeing the inverse-trig construction, so the calculator cannot become the source of direction.

boundary_test.prompt: What if v_x=0 and v_y>0?
boundary_test.answer: The vector points exactly along +y; report that axis direction directly and do not divide by v_x.
boundary_test.confirms: Axis cases are handled directly rather than forced through an invalid ratio.

microtopics.title: Normalize a nonzero vector to unit direction
microtopics.badge_reason: The division is simple, but the same magnitude must divide every component and the zero vector is a hard domain boundary.
entry_assumptions: Can express the vector in signed components or i-hat/j-hat notation.
Can obtain the nonnegative magnitude from perpendicular components through the declared Mathematics bridge.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Dividing every component of the same nonzero vector by its positive magnitude removes units and scale while preserving the component ratio and therefore the direction.

teaching_path.action: Confirm that the vector is nonzero and identify its positive magnitude |v|.
teaching_path.why_valid: Normalization divides by |v|, so |v| must be greater than zero.

teaching_path.action: Divide every signed component by the same magnitude: v_hat = (v_x/|v|) i-hat + (v_y/|v|) j-hat.
teaching_path.why_valid: Multiplication by the same positive scalar reciprocal changes length but preserves direction and component signs.
teaching_path.output: v_hat = v/|v|

teaching_path.action: Recompute the magnitude of the normalized components and confirm it is 1.
teaching_path.why_valid: A unit vector is defined to have magnitude 1.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A unit vector keeps the original physical unit because it points in the same direction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If every component is divided by a magnitude carrying the same unit, what unit remains in the ratio?
misconceptions.repair: The units cancel. A unit vector carries direction and has magnitude 1; it is dimensionless in this representation.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The zero vector can be normalized by dividing each zero component by its magnitude.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What is the magnitude of the zero vector, and what denominator would normalization require?
misconceptions.repair: Its magnitude is zero, so normalization would divide by zero. The zero vector has no unit direction.

exit_task.prompt: A nonzero vector has symbolic components (a,b) and magnitude M>0. Write its unit-direction vector in component and i-hat/j-hat form, then give the magnitude check.

answer.summary: The unit direction is (a/M,b/M) = (a/M)i-hat + (b/M)j-hat, and its magnitude is 1.
reasoning: M is the positive magnitude of the original nonzero vector.
Dividing both components by the same positive M preserves direction.
answer.check: Confirm M>0 first; if M=0 the normalization is undefined.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer is symbolic; the magnitude-one check is algebraic and asserts no computed numerical measurement.

microtopics.research_contribution: The owner-approved Vector Algebra demand supports unit-direction preparation, but this microtopic keeps the operation bounded to 2-D normalization and explicitly rejects the zero-vector case.

predict.prompt: If every component of a nonzero vector is divided by its own magnitude, does its direction change?
predict.defensible_answer: No. A positive common scale factor changes length but not direction.

attempt.produces: A normalized symbolic vector plus a magnitude-one check.
attempt.model_response: Use v_hat=v/|v| only when |v|>0, divide every signed component by the same |v|, and verify the new magnitude is 1.

route.ask: What denominator must be shared by both components if only the scale is to change?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents component-wise rescaling that would rotate the vector.

route.ask: What must be true of that denominator before division?
route.why_this_ask: It exposes the zero-vector domain boundary.

route.ask: What magnitude should the result have?
route.why_this_ask: It gives the independent closure criterion.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner starts from the invariance requirement—same direction, new length 1—and reconstructs the shared scaling factor rather than receiving the formula first.

boundary_test.prompt: Can the zero vector be normalized?
boundary_test.answer: No. Its magnitude is zero, so v/|v| would divide by zero and the zero vector has no direction to preserve.
boundary_test.confirms: The normalization relation is domain-restricted to nonzero vectors.

relations.meaning: A two-dimensional vector expressed on declared perpendicular x/y axes can be written equivalently as the signed x coefficient times the +x unit basis vector plus the signed y coefficient times the +y unit basis vector.

symbols.meaning: The physical two-dimensional vector
Signed x-component of v
Signed y-component of v
Dimensionless unit basis vector along declared +x
Dimensionless unit basis vector along declared +y

conditions: The x and y axes are declared and perpendicular.
i_hat and j_hat name the positive unit directions of those axes.
The signed coefficients retain the physical units of the vector components.

derivation.action: Treat i-hat and j-hat as the +x and +y unit basis directions.
derivation.why_valid: A basis direction identifies where each component acts.

derivation.action: Attach the signed x/y components as coefficients of their matching basis vectors.
derivation.why_valid: The coefficients are precisely the vector's components on those axes.

limits: This notation does not define a dot product or cross product.
It does not by itself determine a direction angle.
checks: Reading the coefficients back must recover the original signed component pair.

relations.expression: alpha = arctan(|v_y|/|v_x|); component signs determine the quadrant
relations.meaning: For a nonzero vector with both perpendicular components nonzero, inverse tangent of the positive component-magnitude ratio gives an acute reference angle; the signed components independently determine the quadrant in which that reference angle must be placed.

symbols.meaning: Acute reference angle to the x-axis
Signed x-component
Signed y-component

conditions: The vector is nonzero.
When both components are nonzero, use positive component magnitudes for the acute ratio.
If either component is zero, report the exact axis direction directly rather than dividing by zero.
Quadrant selection comes from component signs, not from the inverse-tangent output alone.

derivation.action: Use component signs to identify the quadrant or axis.
derivation.why_valid: The signs are the directional information carried by the component pair.

derivation.action: For nonzero v_x and v_y, use tan(alpha)=|v_y|/|v_x| and invert the tangent.
derivation.why_valid: The absolute components form the legs of the right triangle for the acute reference angle.

derivation.action: Check that the placed direction has the original x/y sign pattern.
derivation.why_valid: A direction in the wrong quadrant cannot reproduce the signed components.

limits: The formula shown supplies an acute reference angle, not a quadrant-complete calculator shortcut.
The zero vector has no direction angle.
This relation does not introduce dot products, projections or cross products.
checks: Direction quadrant agrees with signs of v_x and v_y.
Axis cases are handled without a zero denominator.

relations.meaning: Dividing a nonzero vector and every signed component by the same positive magnitude produces a dimensionless vector of magnitude 1 in the same direction.

symbols.meaning: Unit vector in the direction of v
Original nonzero vector
Positive magnitude of v
Signed x-component of v
Signed y-component of v

conditions: Every component is divided by the same magnitude.
The component axes and basis notation refer to the same declared frame.

derivation.action: Require |v|>0 so division is defined.
derivation.why_valid: The zero vector has zero magnitude and no direction to normalize.

derivation.action: Multiply the vector by the positive scalar 1/|v|.
derivation.why_valid: A positive scalar changes length but preserves direction.

derivation.action: Apply the magnitude relation to the normalized components.
derivation.why_valid: The resulting magnitude must equal 1 by definition of normalization.

limits: Undefined for the zero vector.
This normalization does not create a new physical dimension or unit.
It does not require a direction angle to be computed first.
checks: The normalized magnitude is 1.
The signs and component ratio match the original vector.

subject: Physics
scope_summary: Grade-10 refraction and spherical-lens self-study spine: normal-based refraction, refractive index/Snell geometry, thin-lens principal-ray construction, signed lens equation, signed magnification and lens power. Human-eye correction, prism dispersion/scattering and later optics remain outside this bounded slice.

resources.title: Author-created Grade-10 refraction and spherical-lens constructions
resources.rights_status: Author-created local adaptation; current curriculum scope is audited separately and donor readiness/curriculum authority is not inherited.
resources.selection_reason: Provides self-contained Grade9V3 teaching for the bounded Grade-10 refraction/lens slice while keeping donor semantics local and current-scope authority separate.

buckets.title: Refraction and spherical lenses
buckets.badge_reason: The durable difficulty is keeping normal-referenced refraction, medium labels, thin-lens ray geometry, Cartesian signs and power units consistent across representations.

conventions.statement: Measure incidence and refraction angles from the local surface normal and name both media before applying Snell's law.
Use the optical centre as origin; declare the incident-light direction as positive longitudinal direction and upward from the principal axis as positive height before assigning signs.

scope.covers: Grade-10 refraction and spherical lenses: normal-based refraction, refractive index and Snell relation, glass-slab ray tracing, spherical-lens image formation, signed thin-lens formula, signed magnification, optical power and focal-length practical reasoning.
excluded: Human-eye accommodation, vision defects and corrective-lens selection.
Prism dispersion, atmospheric scattering and colourful-world explanations.
Total internal reflection and optical-fibre applications unless later current-source demand explicitly adds them.
Lens combinations, optical instruments, thick-lens principal planes and wave-optics calculations.

capabilities.action: Trace a refracted light path at a transparent boundary by using the surface normal and the direction of refractive-index change.
capabilities.success_criterion: Draws the normal, names the two media, and predicts toward-normal, away-from-normal, or undeviated propagation without measuring angles from the surface.

capabilities.action: Relate refractive index, light speed and normal-referenced incidence/refraction angles using the Grade-10 refraction relations.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses n = c/v and n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r) with the media and normal declared, and interprets higher refractive index as lower light speed.

capabilities.action: Construct and interpret a thin spherical-lens image using a consistent pair of principal rays.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses valid principal-ray rules for one thin lens, locates one common physical or backward-extension image point, and classifies image nature/orientation without mixing incompatible ray rules.

capabilities.action: Use the signed thin-lens equation within its paraxial model and cross-check the predicted image region with a ray construction.
capabilities.success_criterion: Declares the optical-centre Cartesian convention, uses 1/v - 1/u = 1/f for the same paraxial lens state, preserves signs while rearranging, and does not treat the relation as an exact thick-lens or arbitrary-ray law.

capabilities.action: Use signed lens magnification to connect image size and orientation with signed object/image distances.
capabilities.success_criterion: Relates m = v/u = h_i/h_o for one lens state and interprets |m| as relative size and the sign of m as erect/inverted orientation.

capabilities.action: Interpret and compare lens power from signed focal length expressed in metres.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses P = 1/f with f in metres, keeps the focal-length sign, states power in dioptres, and connects larger |P| with shorter |f|.

microtopics.title: Refraction begins with the normal and the two media
microtopics.badge_reason: The visible ray kink is easy to copy while using the wrong angular reference or forgetting that a slab contains two separate boundaries.
entry_assumptions: Can trace a directed straight path and identify where it crosses a surface.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The bend is a normal-referenced consequence of entering a medium with a different light speed/index; a parallel-sided slab applies the rule at two boundaries.

teaching_path.action: At the incidence point, draw the surface normal and label the incident and transmitted media before naming any angle.
teaching_path.why_valid: Incidence and refraction angles are defined from the normal and medium order determines the direction of the speed/index change.
teaching_path.output: boundary + normal + medium 1 -> medium 2

teaching_path.action: Predict toward-normal bending when entering the higher-index/slower medium, away-from-normal bending when leaving it, and no directional change at normal incidence.
teaching_path.why_valid: The direction change follows the relative wave speed while the normal fixes the angular reference.
teaching_path.output: index/speed comparison -> qualitative refracted direction

teaching_path.action: Trace a ray through both parallel faces of a rectangular glass slab and compare the incident and emergent directions.
teaching_path.why_valid: The second boundary reverses the sense of the first angular change for parallel faces, so the simple model yields a parallel emergent ray with possible lateral displacement.
teaching_path.output: two boundary events -> emergent direction check

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The angle of refraction is measured from the glass surface, so a ray along the normal has a 90-degree incidence angle.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A ray strikes a glass surface exactly along the normal. What are its incidence and refraction angles?
misconceptions.repair: Draw the normal first. A ray along it has zero incidence angle and continues without a directional bend even though its speed changes.

exit_task.prompt: A ray enters a parallel-sided glass slab obliquely from air. Without calculating an angle, state which reference line is used at each boundary, how the ray bends on entry and exit, and how the final emergent direction compares with the incident direction.

answer.summary: Use the normal at each face. The ray bends toward the normal on entering the higher-index glass, away from the normal on leaving it, and for parallel faces the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray in the simple slab model.
reasoning: Each angle is measured from the local normal.
The index change reverses at the second face.
Parallel faces give parallel normals, so the two directional changes restore the original direction while allowing lateral shift.
answer.check: If the answer measures from the surface or treats the slab as one boundary, the reasoning is incomplete.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit asks for qualitative ray direction and reference-line reasoning; it contains no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Local Grade-10 construction adapted from the donor's normal/refraction invariants and bounded to the current glass-slab/source demand.

predict.prompt: If a ray hits a glass surface exactly along the normal, must it bend simply because its speed changes?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Its speed changes, but with zero incidence angle there is no directional deflection.

attempt.produces: A two-boundary glass-slab ray trace with both normals and medium labels.

rubric.criterion: Both boundary normals are drawn and angles are referenced to them.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the physical angular reference rather than the surface.

rubric.criterion: Entry and exit bends respond to opposite index changes.
rubric.evidence_of: Understanding refraction as a medium transition rather than a memorized ray kink.

accepted: The ray bends toward the normal on entering glass, away on leaving, and emerges parallel for parallel slab faces.
rejected: The ray bends the same way at both faces because glass always bends light toward the normal.

route.ask: What line at the contact point can define both incidence and refraction angles?
route.why_this_ask: It elicits the normal before the rule is named.

route.ask: Which medium has the higher index and lower light speed?
route.why_this_ask: It connects medium order to bending direction.

route.ask: At the second parallel face, what changed relative to the first?
route.why_this_ask: It forces the learner to treat the slab as two inverse transitions.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path names the normal and index direction immediately; the elicitation route begins from the need for a common angular reference and a two-boundary explanation.

boundary_test.prompt: Can light change speed at a boundary without changing direction?
boundary_test.answer: Yes. At normal incidence the direction is unchanged even though the propagation speed changes.
boundary_test.confirms: Refraction is not synonymous with a visible bend; the normal-referenced geometry matters.

microtopics.title: Refractive index connects speed change to Snell geometry
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often remember a sine ratio but reverse the media or interpret higher refractive index as faster light.
entry_assumptions: Can draw the interface normal and distinguish incident from refracted medium.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The same material property that reduces light speed determines the normal-referenced angle relation across a boundary.

teaching_path.action: Interpret n = c/v as a dimensionless speed ratio and state that higher n means lower v in the ordinary transparent-medium model.
teaching_path.why_valid: c is fixed while the medium speed appears in the denominator.
teaching_path.output: higher n -> lower v

teaching_path.action: Write n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r) with n1 attached to the incident medium and n2 to the refracting medium.
teaching_path.why_valid: Snell's law binds the two material indices to angles measured from the same normal.
teaching_path.output: declared media + angles -> Snell relation

teaching_path.action: Check the qualitative direction implied by the equation against the medium comparison before accepting any algebra.
teaching_path.why_valid: For n2 > n1 and nonzero incidence below the model boundary, sin(r) must be smaller than sin(i), matching toward-normal bending.
teaching_path.output: equation result agrees with qualitative ray bend

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A medium with a larger refractive index lets light travel faster.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If material B has a larger refractive index than material A, which material has the lower light speed?
misconceptions.repair: Use n = c/v. With the same c, increasing n requires a smaller v.

exit_task.prompt: For light passing from medium 1 into a higher-index medium 2, write the Snell relation with the media labels attached and state whether the refraction angle should be larger or smaller than the incidence angle. Do not calculate an angle.

answer.summary: Use n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r). With n2 > n1, the refraction angle is smaller than the incidence angle, so the ray bends toward the normal.
reasoning: The indices are attached to their media before algebra.
A higher n2 requires a smaller sine of the refracted angle for the same incident state.
The qualitative result agrees with the toward-normal ray trace.
answer.check: Reversing n1 and n2 would predict the wrong bending direction.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit checks symbolic relation setup and qualitative angle ordering; it contains no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copies the durable donor Snell/index semantics into a smaller local learner capability without importing donor readiness or JEE metadata.

predict.prompt: If light enters a higher-index medium at an oblique angle, should the refracted angle from the normal grow or shrink?
predict.defensible_answer: It should shrink; the ray bends toward the normal.

attempt.produces: A labelled Snell-law setup plus a speed/index interpretation.

rubric.criterion: n1 and n2 are attached to the correct incident/refracting media.
rubric.evidence_of: Preserving medium ownership through the equation.

rubric.criterion: The predicted angle direction matches the index comparison.
rubric.evidence_of: Using Snell's law as a physical model rather than bare algebra.

accepted: Higher n means lower speed; n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r) predicts toward-normal bending when n2 > n1.
rejected: Higher n means faster light, so the ray bends away from the normal on entering glass.

route.ask: What ratio tells you whether light is slower or faster in the medium?
route.why_this_ask: It recovers the physical meaning of n.

route.ask: Which index belongs beside the incidence angle and which beside the refraction angle?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents media reversal.

route.ask: Does your equation predict the same bending direction as the sketch?
route.why_this_ask: It supplies an independent qualitative check.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path gives the two relations first; the elicitation route begins from the speed comparison and forces the learner to reconstruct the correct index-angle pairing.

boundary_test.prompt: If n1 = n2, what directional change should Snell's law predict at the boundary?
boundary_test.answer: None; the incidence and refraction angles are equal.
boundary_test.confirms: The bending comes from a refractive-index contrast, not merely from crossing a drawn boundary.

microtopics.title: A thin lens image must be supported by independent principal rays
microtopics.badge_reason: Memorized image tables can hide incompatible ray rules or the false idea that a ray through the optical centre must bend strongly.
entry_assumptions: Can trace refracted rays and identify real versus backward-extension intersections.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Several principal-ray rules are alternative constraints on one thin-lens ray bundle; any valid pair must locate the same image point.

teaching_path.action: Draw the principal axis, optical centre O, and focal points F1 and F2 before tracing a spherical-lens image.
teaching_path.why_valid: Every principal ray rule is defined relative to this shared geometry.
teaching_path.output: axis + O + two foci

teaching_path.action: For a convex or concave thin lens, apply two independent principal-ray rules consistently to the same object point.
teaching_path.why_valid: A valid image is a property of the whole refracted bundle; two independent constrained rays must agree on one image or backward-extension point.
teaching_path.output: object point -> two consistent principal rays -> image point

teaching_path.action: Use a distant-object convex-lens setup to connect nearly parallel incident rays with an image near the principal focus.
teaching_path.why_valid: A distant object supplies an approximate parallel bundle, which is the operational basis of the standard focal-length practical.
teaching_path.output: distant object -> near-parallel rays -> focal region check

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any ray through the optical centre of a thin lens must bend toward the focus.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: In the Grade-10 thin-lens ray model, what happens to a ray directed through the optical centre?
misconceptions.repair: Use the thin-lens principal-ray rule: a ray through the optical centre is treated as undeviated in the simple paraxial construction.

exit_task.prompt: For a convex thin lens with an object outside the focal point, describe two independent principal rays you would use to locate the image and state what their common intersection tells you. Do not use the lens formula.

answer.summary: Use any two valid principal rays, such as parallel-to-axis then through the far focus, and through the optical centre approximately undeviated. Their physical intersection locates the real image point.
reasoning: Both rays start from the same object point.
Each obeys a different thin-lens principal-ray rule.
Agreement at one physical intersection independently determines the image.
answer.check: If two valid rays predict different image points, the construction or labels are inconsistent.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit is a geometric construction/explanation and contains no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Adapts the donor's thin-lens ray invariant into a local image-construction capability and adds the current distant-object focal-length practical interpretation.

predict.prompt: Why should a second principal ray be drawn if the first ray already looks as though it points to an image?
predict.defensible_answer: Because the image point is constrained by the whole ray bundle; an independent ray must agree on the same intersection.

attempt.produces: A labelled thin-lens diagram using two independent valid principal rays.

rubric.criterion: Principal axis, optical centre and focal points are labelled.
rubric.evidence_of: Using one common lens geometry.

rubric.criterion: Two independent rays meet at one image or common backward-extension point.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating the image as a ray-bundle property rather than a memorized location.

accepted: Two valid principal rays agree on one physical or backward-extension image point.
rejected: One decorative ray is enough; the image is wherever that ray is drawn to go.

route.ask: Which geometric labels must every principal-ray rule share?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the common lens geometry.

route.ask: What does a second independent ray contribute?
route.why_this_ask: It makes the image location a constrained result.

route.ask: What special incident bundle does a very distant object approximately provide?
route.why_this_ask: It links the geometry to the focal-length practical.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative route lists the principal-ray rules; the elicitation route starts from why multiple independent rays must agree before the finished diagram is trusted.

boundary_test.prompt: For a concave lens with a real object, do the outgoing rays physically meet on the far side of the lens?
boundary_test.answer: No. They diverge; their backward extensions meet on the object side to define a virtual image.
boundary_test.confirms: Real versus virtual is determined by physical ray intersection versus backward-extension intersection.

microtopics.title: Use the signed thin-lens equation only after the ray model fixes the geometry
microtopics.badge_reason: The algebra is short, but mirror/lens sign confusion and loss of the paraxial model boundary produce plausible-looking wrong answers.
entry_assumptions: Can construct a thin-lens image with principal rays and identify the optical centre and incident-light direction.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The lens equation is a signed coordinate model for the same paraxial image already constrained by the ray diagram; it is not an isolated formula or a mirror relation with copied signs.

teaching_path.action: Use the optical centre as origin, take the incident-light direction as positive longitudinal direction, and declare upward height as positive before assigning u, v and f.
teaching_path.why_valid: The lens relation uses signed coordinates, so labels such as object/image alone cannot determine signs.
teaching_path.output: declared Cartesian lens coordinates

teaching_path.action: Use 1/v - 1/u = 1/f for the same thin, paraxial lens state; rearrange for the requested signed unknown without making formula derivation a learner requirement.
teaching_path.why_valid: The governed Grade-10 relation connects the signed coordinates already established by the ray model.

teaching_path.action: Compare the sign and region of the equation's image result with the principal-ray construction and reject an inconsistent setup.
teaching_path.why_valid: The ray construction is an independent representation of the same thin-lens model.
teaching_path.output: algebraic image region agrees with ray geometry

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The spherical-mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f can be copied unchanged for a lens.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Before substituting any numbers, which sign appears between the 1/v and 1/u terms in the governed thin-lens relation?
misconceptions.repair: Identify the optical model first. For the Grade-10 thin lens use 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with one declared Cartesian convention.

exit_task.prompt: For a real object in front of a convex thin lens that forms a real image on the far side, state the expected signs of u, f and v under the declared Cartesian convention, write the lens equation, and name the independent diagram check you would use. Do not calculate a distance.

answer.summary: With incident light chosen positive, the real object is on the negative side so u < 0, a convex lens has f > 0, and the real image is on the positive side so v > 0. Use 1/v - 1/u = 1/f and check the image region with a principal-ray construction.
reasoning: Declare the optical-centre coordinate convention first.
Assign signs from coordinate direction rather than object/image labels alone.
Use the governed lens equation and compare the predicted region with the ray diagram.
answer.check: Using the mirror plus-sign formula or assigning u positive for the usual real-object geometry signals a model/sign mismatch.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit checks signs, symbolic relation choice and independent verification; it contains no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Localizes the donor lens-formula invariant, adds explicit no-derivation/current-scope handling, and binds formula use to the already-authored ray model.

predict.prompt: Why should the ray diagram be considered before accepting a lens-equation result?
predict.defensible_answer: Because it independently predicts the image region/nature and can expose a wrong sign convention or wrong optical formula.

attempt.produces: A signed u/v/f setup plus a symbolic thin-lens equation and ray-diagram cross-check.

rubric.criterion: Origin and positive directions are declared before u, v and f are signed.
rubric.evidence_of: Coordinate-based rather than label-based signs.

rubric.criterion: The lens equation and ray construction predict compatible image regions.
rubric.evidence_of: One physical model across algebra and geometry.

accepted: The learner uses 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with declared lens signs and checks it against the ray diagram.
rejected: The learner uses the mirror plus-sign equation because both topics involve focal length.

route.ask: Where is the lens-coordinate origin and which longitudinal direction is positive?
route.why_this_ask: It fixes the sign system before formula choice.

route.ask: Is this reflection from a mirror or refraction through a lens?
route.why_this_ask: It forces model selection before recalling a relation.

route.ask: Where does the ray diagram say the image must lie?
route.why_this_ask: It creates an independent algebra check.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path states the coordinate convention then the relation; the elicitation route begins by forcing model selection and image-region prediction before formula acceptance.

boundary_test.prompt: If rays are strongly non-paraxial or the lens is thick, should this simple Grade-10 lens equation be treated as exact?
boundary_test.answer: No. It is the thin-lens, paraxial model and richer optics may require a different treatment.
boundary_test.confirms: Formula authority is conditional on the optical model rather than unlimited.

microtopics.title: Lens magnification sign carries image orientation
microtopics.badge_reason: Using only |m| preserves size while erasing the erect/inverted information that the signed optical state contains.
entry_assumptions: Can assign signed u and v for one thin-lens image.
microtopics.inferential_jump: One signed ratio links longitudinal image placement and transverse image orientation: magnitude gives relative size while sign distinguishes erect from inverted.

teaching_path.action: Use m = v/u = h_i/h_o for the same signed lens state.
teaching_path.why_valid: The governed relation ties signed image/object distances to signed heights for one image.
teaching_path.output: m = v/u = h_i/h_o

teaching_path.action: Interpret |m| as relative size and the sign of m as orientation under the declared height convention.
teaching_path.why_valid: Removing the sign loses physically meaningful image orientation.
teaching_path.output: |m| -> size; sign(m) -> erect/inverted

teaching_path.action: Compare the magnification sign and size class with the principal-ray diagram.
teaching_path.why_valid: The geometry supplies an independent orientation/size check.
teaching_path.output: signed magnification agrees with ray geometry

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Magnification is only a positive size factor, so its sign can be discarded.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can an unsigned magnification distinguish an erect image from an inverted image?
misconceptions.repair: Keep m signed. Use |m| for relative size and the sign of m for orientation.

exit_task.prompt: A thin-lens ray diagram shows an image that is inverted and larger than the object. Without calculating a numerical magnification, state what must be true about the sign of m and about |m|.

answer.summary: The magnification must be negative for an inverted image, and its magnitude must be greater than one because the image is enlarged.
reasoning: The sign of m carries orientation under the declared height convention.
The magnitude compares image size with object size.
The ray diagram independently supplies both qualitative checks.
answer.check: A positive or signless answer loses the inverted-image information.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit asks only for qualitative sign and size-class interpretation; it contains no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Adapts the donor lens-magnification semantics into a separate independently fail-able learner action rather than hiding orientation inside the lens-equation step.

predict.prompt: If two images have the same |m| but opposite signs, what physical feature differs?
predict.defensible_answer: Their relative size is the same but their orientation differs: one is erect and the other inverted.

attempt.produces: A signed magnification interpretation checked against a ray diagram.

rubric.criterion: Magnification sign is retained.
rubric.evidence_of: Encoding erect/inverted orientation.

rubric.criterion: |m| is interpreted separately from sign.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating size from orientation.

accepted: Negative m is used for inverted orientation and |m| determines enlarged/diminished/same size.
rejected: Only |m| matters because magnification is just a size ratio.

route.ask: What information survives if you keep only |m|?
route.why_this_ask: It isolates size from orientation.

route.ask: What information is lost when the sign is removed?
route.why_this_ask: It elicits the physical role of sign.

route.ask: Does the ray diagram agree with that sign interpretation?
route.why_this_ask: It supplies independent verification.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path presents the signed relation first; the elicitation route starts from what information an unsigned ratio cannot carry.

boundary_test.prompt: If m is positive and |m| is less than one, what qualitative image description follows?
boundary_test.answer: The image is erect and diminished under the declared sign convention.
boundary_test.confirms: Sign and magnitude encode different physical aspects of the image.

microtopics.title: Lens power is signed inverse focal length in metres
microtopics.badge_reason: A correct reciprocal can still be wrong by a factor of one hundred if centimetres are substituted directly, and dropping sign erases converging/diverging character.
entry_assumptions: Can identify the signed focal length of a convex or concave thin lens.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Power compresses focal-length strength into an inverse-metre quantity, so both the metre conversion and focal-length sign are essential.

teaching_path.action: Convert the signed focal length to metres before using the power relation.
teaching_path.why_valid: A dioptre is inverse metre, so unit conversion is part of the physical definition.
teaching_path.output: signed f in metres

teaching_path.action: Use P = 1/f and retain the sign of f.
teaching_path.why_valid: The reciprocal preserves converging positive and diverging negative character while mapping shorter |f| to larger |P|.
teaching_path.output: P = 1/f in D

teaching_path.action: Compare power magnitude and sign with the lens type and qualitative focal length.
teaching_path.why_valid: A stronger converging lens should have a larger positive |P| and shorter positive |f|; a diverging lens should carry negative power.
teaching_path.output: power agrees with focal behavior

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Focal length in centimetres can be inserted directly into P = 1/f to obtain dioptres.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What unit must focal length use before its reciprocal is reported in dioptres?
misconceptions.repair: Convert f to metres first, then take the reciprocal and keep the sign.

exit_task.prompt: Lens A has positive power with a larger magnitude than lens B, which also has positive power. Without calculating focal lengths, which lens has the shorter focal length, and what common lens behavior does the positive sign indicate?

answer.summary: Lens A has the shorter positive focal length because larger |P| means smaller |f|. The positive sign indicates converging/convex-lens power in this Grade-10 convention.
reasoning: Power magnitude is the reciprocal of focal-length magnitude in metres.
Increasing |P| therefore decreases |f|.
The positive sign follows the positive focal length of the converging lens.
answer.check: If larger power is said to mean longer focal length, the reciprocal relation has been reversed.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit uses qualitative reciprocal ordering and sign interpretation; it contains no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Adapts the donor power relation while making metre conversion and sign interpretation explicit enough for independent Grade-10 use.

predict.prompt: If two convex lenses have focal lengths of different magnitudes, which one has the larger power magnitude?
predict.defensible_answer: The one with the shorter focal length has the larger positive power magnitude.

attempt.produces: A signed power/focal-length comparison with explicit metre-unit reasoning.

rubric.criterion: Focal length is conceptually in metres for dioptres.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the correct inverse-length unit.

rubric.criterion: Power sign and magnitude are both interpreted.
rubric.evidence_of: Connecting lens type and optical strength.

accepted: Shorter positive focal length means larger positive power; negative focal length would give negative power.
rejected: A larger positive power means a longer focal length because the numerical power is larger.

route.ask: What unit is hidden inside one dioptre?
route.why_this_ask: It forces the metre conversion into the definition.

route.ask: What happens to a reciprocal when its positive denominator gets smaller?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs the strength ordering.

route.ask: What optical behavior does the sign of f carry?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents a signless strength-only interpretation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path starts from the metre-based definition; the elicitation route begins from comparing lens strength and reconstructs the inverse relationship and sign.

boundary_test.prompt: Can a concave lens and convex lens have the same power sign if their focal lengths have opposite signs?
boundary_test.answer: No. P = 1/f preserves the focal-length sign, so the powers have opposite signs.
boundary_test.confirms: Lens power is a signed optical quantity, not only a positive strength magnitude.

relations.meaning: At one interface between two transparent media, the normal-referenced incidence and refraction angles are related by the refractive indices of the two media.

symbols.meaning: Refractive index of the incident medium
Refractive index of the refracting medium
Angle of incidence measured from the normal
Angle of refraction measured from the normal

conditions: Angles i and r are measured from the same surface normal at the boundary.
The media and wavelength remain fixed while the angle relation is used.
The incident ray, normal and refracted ray are coplanar.

derivation.action: Use n_1 sin(i) = n_2 sin(r) with each index attached to its declared medium.
derivation.why_valid: The governed relation ties material index to normal-referenced ray geometry.

derivation.action: Check that the equation's angle ordering agrees with the higher-index/lower-speed medium comparison.
derivation.why_valid: The qualitative bend is an independent check on media/index reversal.

limits: This Grade-10 relation does not authorize total-internal-reflection or dispersion calculations that are outside the bounded slice.
checks: Both angles are measured from the normal.
Index labels remain attached to the same media throughout.
The predicted bending direction matches the refractive-index comparison.

relations.meaning: Absolute refractive index is the ratio of light speed in vacuum to light speed in the transparent medium.

symbols.meaning: Absolute refractive index of the medium
Speed of light in vacuum
Speed of light in the medium

conditions: c and v refer to the same light frequency/wavelength context for the stated medium.
v is positive and not greater than c in the ordinary transparent-media model used here.

derivation.action: Use n = c/v to interpret refractive index as a speed ratio.
derivation.why_valid: The current Grade-10 scope treats refractive index as physically connected to light speed in the medium.

limits: The relation does not by itself determine wavelength-dependent dispersion behavior.
checks: n is dimensionless because it is a ratio of speeds.
Higher n corresponds to lower v for fixed c.

relations.meaning: For one thin spherical lens in the paraxial model, signed image distance minus signed object-distance reciprocal equals reciprocal signed focal length.

symbols.meaning: Signed object distance used by the thin-lens equation
Signed image distance used by the thin-lens equation
Signed focal length of the thin lens

conditions: u, v and f use the same declared Cartesian sign convention and optical centre as origin.
The lens is treated as thin and the construction is paraxial/small-angle.
u, v and f describe the same lens and object-image state.

derivation.action: Take 1/v - 1/u = 1/f as the governed Grade-10 thin-lens relation; no formula derivation is required in this slice.
derivation.why_valid: The current Grade-10 scope requires use of the lens formula while not requiring its derivation.

derivation.action: Compare the signed image region with the principal-ray construction.
derivation.why_valid: The ray diagram is an independent representation of the same paraxial lens state.
derivation.output: signed equation agrees with ray geometry

limits: This is a thin-lens, paraxial/small-angle model rather than an exact thick-lens or arbitrary-wide-angle law.
The relation does not cover multi-element optical systems or human-eye correction by itself.
checks: u, v and f have the same length dimension.
The coordinate convention is declared before substitution.
The image region agrees with a valid principal-ray construction.

relations.meaning: For the same thin-lens image, transverse magnification is the signed image-to-object height ratio and equals signed image distance divided by signed object distance.

symbols.meaning: Signed transverse magnification
Signed object distance used in the lens magnification ratio
Signed image distance used in the lens magnification ratio
Signed image height relative to the principal axis
Signed object height relative to the principal axis

conditions: u, v, h_i and h_o use one declared Cartesian sign convention.
Object and image refer to the same thin-lens state.
h_o is nonzero when the height ratio is evaluated.

derivation.action: Use m = v/u = h_i/h_o for the same signed lens state.
derivation.why_valid: The governed relation connects longitudinal and transverse image ratios.

derivation.action: Interpret |m| as relative size and sign(m) as orientation, then compare with the ray diagram.
derivation.why_valid: Geometry independently exposes size class and erect/inverted orientation.
derivation.output: signed magnification agrees with ray geometry

limits: Magnification does not by itself establish image brightness or optical quality.
The relation does not authorize multi-element or thick-lens magnification models.
checks: m is dimensionless.
The sign of m agrees with erect/inverted orientation.
|m| agrees qualitatively with enlarged, same-size or diminished geometry.

relations.meaning: Optical power is reciprocal signed focal length when focal length is expressed in metres.

symbols.meaning: Signed optical power
Signed focal length of the lens

conditions: Focal length f is expressed in metres before taking the reciprocal.
The sign of f is retained, so converging and diverging lens powers have opposite signs.

derivation.action: Convert signed focal length to metres and use P = 1/f.
derivation.why_valid: The dioptre is inverse metre, so unit conversion and sign are part of the physical definition.

derivation.action: Check that shorter |f| gives larger |P| and that converging/diverging sign is preserved.
derivation.why_valid: The reciprocal ordering and sign provide independent sanity checks.
derivation.output: power magnitude/sign agrees with focal behavior

limits: Power alone does not describe image location for a particular object.
This relation does not authorize lens combinations or human-eye correction in the current bounded slice.
checks: P has inverse-length units.
The sign of P equals the sign of f.
Larger |P| corresponds to shorter |f|.

teaching_routes.title: Reveal Grade-10 refraction and spherical-lens spine
entry_needs: Learners can trace directed paths and read simple Cartesian directions.
learner_actions: Trace refraction from the normal through one or two boundaries.
Connect refractive index to speed and Snell geometry.
Construct a thin-lens image using independent principal rays.
Use the signed thin-lens equation inside its paraxial model.
Interpret signed lens magnification as size plus orientation.
Interpret signed lens power from focal length in metres.
help_plan: Draw the normal and name both media before angle language.
Check index ordering against light-speed ordering before Snell algebra.
Use a second independent principal ray before trusting an image location.
Declare optical-centre coordinates before assigning u, v and f.
Keep magnification sign separate from |m|.
Convert focal length to metres before using dioptres.
