Spherical-lens formulae, lens power and human-eye correction.
Dispersion/scattering and atmospheric-optics explanations.
Aberration calculations, thick-mirror models and advanced multi-element optics.

conventions.statement: Use the mirror pole as origin; declare the incident-light direction as positive longitudinal direction and upward from the principal axis as positive height before assigning signs.

capabilities.action: Construct a reflected path by measuring both ray directions from the surface normal.
capabilities.success_criterion: Draw the outgoing path with the same normal-referenced angle as the incoming path.

capabilities.action: Classify an image point from actual reflected-path intersection versus backward-extension intersection.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify real or virtual image geometry from where the light paths or their backward extensions meet.

capabilities.action: Assign signs to mirror distances and heights from a declared pole, incident-light direction and vertical convention.
capabilities.success_criterion: Give the sign of each optical coordinate by its measurement direction rather than by object or image labels.

capabilities.action: Construct and interpret a spherical-mirror image using a consistent pair of principal rays.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses valid principal-ray rules for one mirror state, locates one common physical or backward-extension intersection, and classifies the resulting image geometry without mixing incompatible ray rules.

capabilities.action: Use the signed spherical-mirror equation within its paraxial model and cross-check the predicted image with the ray construction.
capabilities.success_criterion: Declares the coordinate convention, uses 1/v + 1/u = 1/f for the same paraxial mirror state, preserves signs while rearranging, and rejects the equation as an exact arbitrary-wide-aperture law.

capabilities.action: Use signed mirror magnification to connect image size and orientation with signed object/image distances.
capabilities.success_criterion: Relates m = h_i/h_o = -v/u for one mirror state and interprets magnification magnitude as relative size and sign as erect/inverted orientation.

microtopics.title: Measure reflection from the normal, not the surface
microtopics.badge_reason: A familiar mirror picture becomes wrong immediately if the reference line for the angle is the surface instead of the normal.
entry_assumptions: Can trace a directed straight path and identify where it meets a surface.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Angles in specular reflection are measured from the surface normal, and the reflected ray leaves with the same angle to that normal as the incident ray.

teaching_path.action: At the point where the incoming light path meets the mirror, draw the line perpendicular to the surface before marking any angle.
teaching_path.why_valid: The reflection angle is defined relative to this perpendicular reference, so drawing it first fixes the reference instead of letting the page edge stand in for it.
teaching_path.output: mirror surface ⟂ normal at the contact point

teaching_path.action: Copy the incoming path's tilt from the normal to the opposite side of that normal to construct the outgoing path.
teaching_path.why_valid: Using the same reference line on both sides preserves the reflection rule while making the outgoing direction observable on the drawing.
teaching_path.output: incoming tilt from normal -> matching outgoing tilt on the other side

teaching_path.action: Rotate the entire drawing on the page and repeat the construction without changing the physical geometry.
teaching_path.why_valid: A page rotation changes how the paper is oriented but not perpendicularity or the pair of equal normal-referenced angles.
teaching_path.output: rotated page -> same normal-based construction

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The angle of incidence is measured from the mirror surface.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A ray makes 20 degrees with the mirror surface. Is its angle of incidence 20 degrees?
misconceptions.repair: Draw the normal first; incidence and reflection angles are defined from that line, not from the surface.

exit_task.prompt: Given an incoming light path and a plane mirror drawn at an arbitrary page angle, construct the normal and the reflected path, and state which line the two reflection angles are measured from.

answer.summary: Draw the perpendicular normal at the contact point, then place the outgoing path on the other side with the same tilt to that normal; both angles are measured from the normal.
reasoning: Locate the point where the incoming path meets the surface.
Draw the perpendicular reference there before reading or copying any angle.
Use the same reference on the opposite side to place the outgoing path.
answer.check: Rotate the page mentally. If the construction depends on the page edge rather than the normal, it will change; a correct construction will not.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit task is a geometric construction and reference-line explanation, not a numerical angle calculation.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created construction turns the normal-reference rule into a directed-path task suitable for review before any spherical-mirror equation is introduced.

predict.prompt: If you rotate the mirror drawing on the page but keep the physical incoming path fixed relative to it, should the reflection construction change?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The construction is tied to the surface normal at the contact point, not to the page orientation.

attempt.produces: A reflected-path construction on an oblique mirror with the normal drawn first and both angle arcs referenced to it.

rubric.criterion: The normal is perpendicular to the mirror at the contact point.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the correct reference line for both angles.

rubric.criterion: Incoming and outgoing angle marks are placed on opposite sides of the same normal.
rubric.evidence_of: Applying the reflection symmetry to a single local reference.

accepted: The drawing places one perpendicular normal at the contact point and shows matching angle marks between each path and that normal.
rejected: The angle arcs are drawn between each path and the mirror surface, so the construction uses the wrong reference even if the final path happens to look symmetric.

route.ask: At the exact contact point, which line could give both the incoming and outgoing path the same local reference?
route.why_this_ask: It elicits the missing perpendicular reference before the rule is named.

route.ask: Once that line is drawn, where would you place an outgoing path with the same tilt but on the other side?
route.why_this_ask: The learner performs the geometric transformation rather than receiving the finished ray.

route.ask: If the paper is rotated, which relationships in your construction must remain unchanged?
route.why_this_ask: The page-rotation check exposes surface-based memorization.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path names the normal immediately; the elicitation route begins from the need for a common local reference and makes the learner propose the perpendicular line.

boundary_test.prompt: What happens for an incoming path that lies exactly along the normal?
boundary_test.answer: The outgoing path retraces the same line in the opposite direction because its tilt from the normal is zero on both sides.
boundary_test.confirms: The normal, rather than the surface, is the defining angular reference.

microtopics.title: Real and virtual describe how light paths meet
microtopics.badge_reason: The everyday word virtual invites a false not-recordable interpretation unless image type is tied directly to ray geometry.
entry_assumptions: R1: reflection direction is fixed by equal angles measured from the normal.
microtopics.inferential_jump: An image location is determined by where reflected rays actually meet or where their backward extensions appear to meet; virtual describes ray geometry, not whether a camera can record it.

teaching_path.action: Trace at least two reflected light paths from the same object point and keep their physical forward portions solid.
teaching_path.why_valid: One path cannot locate an image point; two or more paths reveal whether the light itself converges.
teaching_path.output: two reflected paths -> enough geometry to test a meeting point

teaching_path.action: When the reflected paths diverge, extend them backward with a visibly different line style until the extensions meet.
teaching_path.why_valid: The extensions are a geometric inference about apparent origin, not additional light travelling behind the mirror, so changing the line style preserves that distinction.
teaching_path.output: solid paths diverge -> dashed backward extensions meet behind the mirror

teaching_path.action: Place an eye or camera where it can receive the reflected bundle and ask whether collecting those diverging paths changes where their backward extensions meet.
teaching_path.why_valid: A detector can refocus incoming light without converting the mirror's apparent-origin geometry into an actual meeting point at the mirror.
teaching_path.output: camera receives reflected bundle -> apparent mirror-image location remains virtual

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A virtual image is not a usable image and therefore cannot be photographed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A camera points at a plane mirror and records your reflection. Does that make the mirror image real?
misconceptions.repair: Separate image geometry from recording: the mirror sends diverging rays that a camera lens can collect and refocus.

exit_task.prompt: Given two reflected light paths from one object point, classify the image location from whether the physical paths meet or only their backward extensions meet, and explain why visibility or photography does not change that classification.

answer.summary: An actual meeting of reflected light paths gives a real image point; a meeting only of backward extensions gives a virtual image point, and either ray bundle can still enter an eye or camera.
reasoning: Use more than one reflected path so an intersection is a geometric fact rather than an assumption.
Distinguish physical forward paths from backward extensions by line style and direction.
Classify the image from which kind of intersection occurs, not from whether a detector can receive the light.
answer.check: Remove the observer or camera from the drawing. The path intersection or backward-extension intersection that defines the image should not move.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer classifies path geometry and detector independence; it asserts no computed distance or image size.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created two-path construction gives the virtual-image misconception a geometric diagnostic without invoking later principal-ray or mirror-equation machinery.

predict.prompt: If a camera successfully records a plane-mirror image, does that prove the reflected light actually met behind the mirror?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The camera can collect diverging reflected light even though only backward extensions meet behind the mirror.

attempt.produces: A two-path diagram with physical reflected paths and backward extensions drawn differently, plus a real-or-virtual classification justified from the intersection.

rubric.criterion: Physical reflected paths and backward extensions are visually distinguished.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping actual light travel separate from apparent origin.

rubric.criterion: The image type is tied to which lines intersect, not to whether the image can be seen.
rubric.evidence_of: Using ray geometry as the classification rule.

accepted: The reflected paths are solid, their behind-mirror extensions are dashed, and the answer calls the behind-mirror point virtual because only the extensions intersect there.
rejected: The answer calls the image real solely because a camera can photograph it, without checking whether the reflected paths themselves ever meet behind the mirror.

route.ask: How many reflected paths do you need before an image location can be fixed by intersection?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents one arbitrary path from being treated as an image locator.

route.ask: If those paths spread apart, what lines could you extend backward to ask where they appear to come from?
route.why_this_ask: The learner constructs apparent origin from observed directions.

route.ask: Would putting a camera in the bundle move that apparent origin?
route.why_this_ask: It directly tests the mistaken link between recordability and image type.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path distinguishes solid paths from extensions; the elicitation route starts with the successful camera observation and forces the learner to decide whether detection changes the mirror geometry.

boundary_test.prompt: If two reflected light paths actually cross in front of a mirror before entering a detector, which classification follows from that crossing?
boundary_test.answer: That crossing is a real image point because the physical reflected paths themselves meet there.
boundary_test.confirms: Real versus virtual is determined by path intersection, independent of whether an observer is present.

microtopics.title: Optical signs come from declared directions
microtopics.badge_reason: Memorized object-and-image sign tables fail as soon as the drawing is mirrored or a less familiar optical configuration is used.
entry_assumptions: R2: image nature is determined by actual versus backward-extended ray intersection.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The Cartesian sign convention turns a mirror diagram into signed distances and heights; the signs come from declared directions, not from memorized object/image labels.

teaching_path.action: Mark the pole as the distance origin, declare the direction of incident light as the positive horizontal direction, and declare upward from the principal axis as positive height.
teaching_path.why_valid: Signs can only be reproducible when the origin and positive directions are fixed before any object or image is classified.
teaching_path.output: pole = origin; incident-light direction = positive distance; upward = positive height

teaching_path.action: Take several marked points and assign each a distance sign from the pole and a height sign from the principal axis using only the declared directions.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same coordinate rule applies to every point, so the result cannot depend on whether a point is called object, image, center or another label.
teaching_path.output: with incident direction -> positive distance; against it -> negative distance; above axis -> positive height; below -> negative height

teaching_path.action: Redraw the same physical setup reversed left-to-right on the page, carrying the declared incident-light arrow with it, and assign the signs again.
teaching_path.why_valid: A correct convention follows the declared physical direction, so changing the page layout does not change the signs of the same physical quantities.
teaching_path.output: page reversed + direction declaration carried with setup -> physical sign assignments preserved

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Object distance is always negative and image distance is always positive.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Move the same object-and-mirror sketch so incident light travels the opposite page direction. Should the sign rule follow the page or the declared incident-light direction?
misconceptions.repair: Apply the coordinate convention from the pole every time; signs follow measurement direction and height orientation.

exit_task.prompt: A mirror diagram declares its pole, incident-light direction and upward direction. Assign signs to the object distance, image distance, focal-location distance and image height from those declarations, and explain why an object-or-image sign table was unnecessary.

answer.summary: Each sign follows the declared coordinate direction from the pole or principal axis; the labels object and image do not determine signs by themselves.
reasoning: Use the pole as the horizontal origin and compare every longitudinal position with the declared incident-light direction.
Use the principal axis as the vertical reference and compare each height with the declared upward direction.
Apply those two rules consistently to every named point instead of switching rules when the label changes.
answer.check: Mirror the whole drawing left-to-right while carrying the incident-light arrow with the physical setup; a convention-based answer should remain physically consistent.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer assigns qualitative signs from a declared coordinate convention and computes no numerical optical result.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created sign-assignment routine makes the coordinate convention explicit before any gated mirror equation or magnification relation is used.

predict.prompt: If the same mirror setup is drawn on the opposite side of the page, should an object's sign change merely because its ink moved left or right?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The sign follows the declared incident-light and vertical directions, which move with the physical setup rather than staying attached to page left or page right.

attempt.produces: A sign-labelled mirror sketch with origin and positive directions declared before any object, image or focal-location signs are assigned.

rubric.criterion: The pole and both positive directions are declared before signs are written.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating the coordinate convention as the source of the signs.

rubric.criterion: Every longitudinal and vertical sign is justified by direction from the declared reference.
rubric.evidence_of: Avoiding memorized sign rules tied to object or image labels.

accepted: The sketch marks the pole, incident-light arrow and upward direction first, then gives each position and height a sign by comparing it with those declarations.
rejected: The response writes object is negative and image is positive before declaring any direction, so the signs are attached to labels rather than coordinates.

route.ask: Before assigning any sign, where is the distance origin in this diagram?
route.why_this_ask: A sign without an origin is not a coordinate decision.

route.ask: Which physical direction has been declared positive for longitudinal distance, and which for height?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must state both coordinate directions before classifying points.

route.ask: Take one point without calling it object or image. Which sign follows from its direction from the pole?
route.why_this_ask: Removing the familiar label tests whether the coordinate rule can stand on its own.

route.ask: If the page drawing is reversed, what must move with the setup so your signs remain physically consistent?
route.why_this_ask: The reversal exposes page-left or page-right memorization.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path declares a full coordinate system first; the elicitation route removes object and image labels and makes the learner recover signs from an unlabeled point before testing a mirrored page layout.

boundary_test.prompt: What sign should a point exactly at the pole have for its longitudinal distance?
boundary_test.answer: Its distance is zero, so it is neither on the positive nor negative side of the origin.
boundary_test.confirms: The sign convention is a coordinate system with an origin, not a permanent label attached to a class of optical object.

microtopics.title: Principal rays are consistent shortcuts to one spherical-mirror image
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners can memorize individual ray rules yet combine them inconsistently or treat one ray as sufficient to locate an image.
entry_assumptions: Can classify real versus virtual intersections and assign optical signs from the declared pole/axis convention.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A small set of principal-ray rules are not independent tricks: any valid pair for the same object point and spherical mirror must locate the same image point within the model.

teaching_path.action: Label the mirror type, pole, principal axis, focus and centre of curvature, then identify whether each referenced focus/centre is physical or reached by backward extension for that mirror.
teaching_path.why_valid: Principal-ray rules depend on one declared spherical-mirror geometry; the same labels cannot be moved independently from the mirror.
teaching_path.output: one labelled spherical-mirror geometry with P, principal axis, F and C

teaching_path.action: From one object point, construct two valid principal rays: parallel-axis/focus, focus/parallel, or centre-of-curvature/retrace, using backward extensions where the convex-mirror rule requires them.
teaching_path.why_valid: Each construction is a constrained consequence of the same spherical-mirror geometry, so a valid pair determines one image point.
teaching_path.output: two consistent reflected paths or reflected paths plus backward extensions

teaching_path.action: Use a third valid principal ray as a consistency check and classify the image from actual versus backward-extension intersection, orientation and relative size.
teaching_path.why_valid: An independent third construction should agree with the image location if the first two ray rules were applied consistently.
teaching_path.output: one cross-checked image point with real/virtual and erect/inverted classification

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any two memorized principal-ray sketches can be combined even if they predict different image points.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two correctly labelled rays from the same object point and mirror predict different image locations. Can both constructions be valid?
misconceptions.repair: No. Recheck the mirror type, focus/centre side and before/after ray directions until all valid rays agree on one physical or backward-extension intersection.

exit_task.prompt: For a concave mirror with the object beyond the centre of curvature, describe two principal rays from the top of the object and use their meeting to state the image region and whether the image is real or virtual and erect or inverted.

answer.summary: A parallel ray reflects through the focus and a ray through the centre of curvature retraces its path; they meet in front of the mirror between F and C, giving a real inverted image.
reasoning: Both rays belong to the same concave-mirror geometry.
The physical reflected rays meet in front of the mirror, so the image is real.
Their intersection lies below the principal axis for an upright object, so the image is inverted.
answer.check: A third ray directed through the focus should reflect parallel to the axis and pass through the same image point.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit verifies qualitative ray geometry, image region and image nature; it asserts no computed distance or magnification.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copies/adapts durable spherical-mirror ray-construction invariants from prior internal Physics engineering while retaining the existing Grade9V3 coordinate/image foundations and current Grade-10 scope.

predict.prompt: If you use two different valid principal-ray pairs for the same object point and spherical mirror, may they legitimately locate two different images?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Within the model, every valid pair must locate the same image point or the same backward-extension point.

attempt.produces: A labelled spherical-mirror diagram with two independently chosen principal rays and an image classification justified from their intersection.

rubric.criterion: Both rays obey valid before/after directions for the declared mirror geometry.
rubric.evidence_of: Using geometry rather than decorative memorized lines.

rubric.criterion: The image classification follows physical versus backward-extension intersection and orientation.
rubric.evidence_of: Connecting the construction to image nature.

accepted: Two valid rays meet at one point and the answer classifies that point from the actual reflected paths or their backward extensions.
rejected: The two rays predict different image points but the response keeps both without resolving the inconsistency.

route.ask: What mirror points must be fixed before you choose a principal ray?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents ray rules from floating independently of the mirror geometry.

route.ask: If one ray is parallel to the principal axis, where must its reflected path go for this mirror?
route.why_this_ask: It forces one concrete principal-ray decision.

route.ask: Which second ray can independently locate the same image point?
route.why_this_ask: One ray gives a direction, not an image location.

route.ask: Do the physical rays meet, or only their backward extensions?
route.why_this_ask: That distinction determines image nature.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path presents the labelled geometry first; the learner route starts by needing a second independent locator and reconstructs why two rays, not a memorized finished diagram, define the image.

boundary_test.prompt: For a convex mirror, reflected rays diverge in front of the mirror. If their backward extensions meet behind it, is the image real or virtual?
boundary_test.answer: Virtual, because only backward extensions meet behind the mirror; the physical reflected rays do not converge there.
boundary_test.confirms: Image classification still comes from path geometry when the focus and image are virtual.

microtopics.title: The mirror equation is a signed paraxial model of the ray geometry
microtopics.badge_reason: Correct algebra can still represent the wrong physical mirror if signs are assigned from labels or if the paraxial model condition is forgotten.
entry_assumptions: Can construct a spherical-mirror image with principal rays and apply the declared Cartesian sign convention.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f does not replace the ray picture: signed u, v and f must refer to the same mirror geometry and the formula is used only within the paraxial/small-angle model.

teaching_path.action: Before substitution, mark the pole/origin and positive longitudinal direction, then assign signed u and f from the diagram.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MIRROR-EQUATION relates signed coordinates, so signs must come from the declared coordinate system rather than memorized object/image labels.
teaching_path.output: one mirror diagram with signed u and f

teaching_path.action: Use 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and rearrange it to the requested unknown without discarding signs.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MIRROR-EQUATION owns the algebraic relation for the same paraxial mirror state.
teaching_path.output: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u, or an equivalent signed rearrangement

teaching_path.action: Compare the sign/region predicted for v with the principal-ray construction and state the paraxial/small-angle condition behind the equation.
teaching_path.why_valid: A sign or region disagreement reveals a coordinate/construction error, while wide-aperture disagreement can reveal a model-limit issue.
teaching_path.output: equation prediction and ray construction agree within the stated model

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The mirror formula is an exact law for every ray on any part of a spherical mirror, so ray height and aperture never matter.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If rays strike far from the principal axis at large angles and fail to meet at one point, must the algebra be wrong?
misconceptions.repair: Not necessarily. State the paraxial/small-angle approximation before using the simple mirror equation; wide-aperture disagreement can be a model-limit effect.

exit_task.prompt: A concave-mirror diagram uses the declared Cartesian convention with a real object and real image in front of the mirror, so u < 0 and the ray construction says v < 0. Write the mirror equation rearranged for 1/v, state the sign you expect for v, and name the model condition that must be satisfied before trusting the equation.

answer.summary: Use 1/v = 1/f - 1/u; the physical ray construction requires v to be negative in this convention, and the spherical-mirror equation is used in the paraxial/small-angle regime.
reasoning: Keep the signs attached to u and f when rearranging.
Use the ray construction as an independent sign/region check on v.
State the paraxial model boundary rather than treating the formula as exact for arbitrary wide-aperture rays.
answer.check: If the algebra predicts an image region inconsistent with two valid principal rays, revisit signs/model use before accepting the result.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit checks symbolic rearrangement, sign consistency and model validity; no numerical image distance is asserted.

microtopics.research_contribution: Adapts the donor mirror-formula model condition and falsifier into the local Grade9V3 teaching/verification contract without importing donor readiness or requiring a formula derivation that current Grade-10 scope does not demand.

predict.prompt: If a correctly drawn concave-mirror image is real and lies in front of the mirror, can a positive v from your algebra be accepted without rechecking anything?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Under the declared convention a real image in front has negative v, so the sign disagreement is evidence to recheck the setup or algebra.

attempt.produces: A sign-declared mirror-equation setup, symbolic rearrangement for the unknown, ray-diagram cross-check and explicit model-condition statement.

rubric.criterion: Signs are assigned from the declared coordinate system before substitution.
rubric.evidence_of: Preventing label-based sign memorization.

rubric.criterion: The equation result is checked against ray geometry and the paraxial model boundary is stated.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating equation and construction as one bounded physical model.

accepted: The response preserves signed u/f, solves symbolically for v, checks v's region against the ray diagram and names the paraxial condition.
rejected: The response inserts unsigned distances into the formula and treats any numerical result as valid without a ray or model check.

route.ask: Before writing the formula, what fixes the signs of u and f?
route.why_this_ask: The coordinate system must precede the algebra.

route.ask: What relation links u, v and f for this spherical-mirror model?
route.why_this_ask: It selects the governing relation rather than a lens formula.

route.ask: What image region should the principal rays predict before you trust v?
route.why_this_ask: It creates an independent physical cross-check.

route.ask: What assumption about the rays lets the simple spherical-mirror equation represent the geometry?
route.why_this_ask: It exposes the model boundary.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path moves from declared signs to algebra; the learner route starts from an expected image region and uses that physical prediction to reconstruct which signs and model condition the algebra must respect.

boundary_test.prompt: If the mirror aperture is made very wide and the relevant rays strike far from the principal axis at large angles, is failure of one-point convergence automatically an arithmetic error?
boundary_test.answer: No. It can be failure of the paraxial approximation; the simple mirror equation is not being used inside its intended small-angle model.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner distinguishes algebraic failure from model-validity failure.

microtopics.title: Signed magnification carries image size and orientation
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often keep only the absolute size ratio and lose the orientation information carried by the sign.
entry_assumptions: Can obtain signed u and v for one spherical-mirror state and classify the image from its ray construction.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Mirror magnification is not merely 'times bigger': m = h_i/h_o = -v/u is signed, so |m| gives relative size while the sign records erect versus inverted orientation under the declared convention.

teaching_path.action: Keep signed u, v, object height h_o and image height h_i tied to the same declared mirror coordinates.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MIRROR-MAGNIFICATION compares quantities from one object-image state; mixing states or dropping height direction breaks its meaning.
teaching_path.output: one signed object-image state with u, v, h_o and h_i

teaching_path.action: Use m = -v/u = h_i/h_o and preserve the sign while comparing image and object size.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MIRROR-MAGNIFICATION binds the distance ratio and height ratio for the same spherical-mirror image.
teaching_path.output: m = -v/u = h_i/h_o; |m| gives the image/object size ratio while sign(m) is retained for orientation.

teaching_path.action: Predict erect/inverted and enlarged/same-size/diminished from m, then check those claims against the ray diagram.
teaching_path.why_valid: The ray geometry independently shows orientation and approximate relative size, so it can falsify a dropped or reversed sign.
teaching_path.output: magnification sign/size agrees with the ray construction

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Magnification is only a positive size factor, so taking |m| loses nothing important.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two images have the same absolute size ratio, but one is erect and one inverted. Can one unsigned magnification distinguish them?
misconceptions.repair: No. Preserve the sign: |m| describes relative size while the sign carries orientation under the declared convention.

exit_task.prompt: For a real object with u < 0, a principal-ray diagram shows a real inverted image in front of the mirror, so v < 0. Without using numbers, determine the sign of m = -v/u and state what that sign says about orientation.

answer.summary: m is negative, which is consistent with an inverted image.
reasoning: With u < 0 and v < 0, v/u is positive.
The leading minus sign makes m negative.
Negative signed magnification corresponds to inversion under this convention.
answer.check: The ray diagram should also show the image below the principal axis for an upright object.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit checks only the sign and physical interpretation of magnification; no computed magnitude is asserted.

microtopics.research_contribution: Adapts the donor magnification-sign invariant into the local Grade10 mirror spine and keeps orientation as part of the learner capability instead of reducing magnification to an unsigned arithmetic ratio.

predict.prompt: If two mirror images are equally large but one is erect and the other inverted, can they have the same signed magnification?
predict.defensible_answer: No. They can have the same magnitude |m| but opposite signs because the sign carries orientation.

attempt.produces: A signed magnification statement connecting -v/u with h_i/h_o and a ray-diagram prediction of size and orientation.

rubric.criterion: The response preserves the sign of m and interprets |m| separately.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping orientation and relative size as distinct information.

rubric.criterion: The predicted orientation agrees with the ray construction.
rubric.evidence_of: Cross-checking algebra against physical geometry.

accepted: The response reports negative m for an inverted image and separately interprets whether |m| is greater than, equal to or less than one.
rejected: The response replaces m with |m| immediately and cannot distinguish erect from inverted images.

route.ask: What does the ray diagram already tell you about the image orientation?
route.why_this_ask: It creates a physical target before the ratio is manipulated.

route.ask: Which signed distance ratio connects that image to the object?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs the -v/u form rather than an unsigned scale factor.

route.ask: What information is carried by the sign, and what is carried by |m|?
route.why_this_ask: It separates orientation from relative size.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path introduces the signed relation and then interprets it; the learner route starts from visible image orientation and reconstructs why an unsigned ratio is insufficient.

boundary_test.prompt: If m = -1 for a spherical-mirror image, what two separate claims follow about size and orientation?
boundary_test.answer: The image has the same size as the object because |m| = 1, and it is inverted because m is negative.
boundary_test.confirms: Magnitude and sign of magnification carry different physical information.

relations.meaning: For one spherical mirror in the paraxial model, signed image distance and object distance combine to the reciprocal signed focal length.

symbols.meaning: Signed object distance measured from the mirror pole
Signed image distance measured from the mirror pole
Signed focal length of the spherical mirror

conditions: u, v and f use the same declared Cartesian sign convention and mirror pole as origin.
The spherical-mirror construction is used in the paraxial/small-angle regime.
u, v and f describe the same mirror and object-image state.

derivation.action: Take 1/v + 1/u = 1/f as the governed Grade-10 mirror relation; no formula derivation is required in this teaching slice.
derivation.why_valid: The current Grade-10 scope requires use of the mirror formula while explicitly not requiring its derivation.

derivation.action: Rearrange algebraically for the requested signed unknown while preserving the declared signs.
derivation.why_valid: Algebraic isolation does not change the governed relation.

limits: This simple spherical-mirror relation is a paraxial/small-angle model rather than an exact arbitrary-wide-aperture ray law.
The relation does not cover spherical lenses, multi-element optics or thick optical systems.
checks: u, v and f have the same length dimension.
The sign/region predicted for v agrees with a valid principal-ray construction.
The coordinate convention is declared before numerical substitution.

relations.meaning: For the same spherical-mirror image, transverse magnification is the signed image-to-object height ratio and equals negative signed image distance divided by signed object distance.

symbols.meaning: Signed transverse magnification
Signed object distance from the mirror pole
Signed image distance from the mirror pole
Signed image height relative to the principal axis
Signed object height relative to the principal axis

conditions: u, v, h_i and h_o use one declared Cartesian sign convention.
Object and image refer to the same spherical-mirror state.
h_o is nonzero when the height ratio is evaluated.

derivation.action: Use m = -v/u = h_i/h_o for the same signed object-image state.
derivation.why_valid: The governed relation binds distance and transverse-height ratios for one spherical-mirror image.

derivation.action: Separate the interpretation of |m| from the interpretation of the sign of m.
derivation.why_valid: Magnitude gives relative size while sign carries orientation under the declared convention.

limits: Magnification describes the same object-image state and does not by itself establish brightness or image quality.
The relation does not authorize lens magnification or multi-element optical systems.
checks: m is dimensionless because both ratios compare like dimensions.
The sign of m agrees with erect/inverted orientation in the ray diagram.
The magnitude |m| agrees qualitatively with enlarged, same-size or diminished ray geometry.

subject: Physics

It supports the owner-supplied ExamSIDE machine-gun demand without importing a general collision, impulse-integral, rocket-equation or variable-mass curriculum.

buckets.title: Momentum-transfer force rate
buckets.badge_reason: The arithmetic is short, but the learner must distinguish momentum change of one ejected item, transfer rate, force direction on the ejecta, reaction on the launcher, and the external holding force.

conventions.statement: Declare one positive ejection direction before assigning signs to item momentum change, launcher recoil and holding force.
Use an ejection rate in items per second and a momentum change per item measured in one declared inertial frame.

scope.covers: Linear momentum p = m v for one fixed-mass item, external force as momentum-change rate, and the average force from a steady discrete stream R Delta p_item including opposite launcher reaction and balancing holding-force direction.
excluded: General collision taxonomy or coefficient of restitution.
Momentum-conservation derivations unrelated to the approved ejection-stream demand.
Impulse integrals or force-time curve integration.
Rocket equation, continuously varying-mass dynamics or exhaust-relative-velocity derivations.
Center-of-mass collision methods.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns average external force from repeated discrete fixed-mass item momentum changes in one inertial frame, including recoil and balancing holding-force roles. It does not own the instantaneous force-time pulse, collision conservation, impulse integration, rocket dynamics, or continuously varying-mass equations.

capabilities.action: Relate an external average force to momentum transferred per unit time and, for repeated identical fixed-mass ejecta, compute the signed force from ejection rate times momentum change per item before inferring the opposite launcher reaction and any balancing holding force.
capabilities.success_criterion: Declares a positive direction and one inertial frame, forms Delta p_item = m(v_out - v_in), uses F_avg,on_ejecta = R Delta p_item for a steady repeated stream, gives the launcher interaction force the opposite sign, gives the external holding force the sign required to balance recoil when the launcher is held fixed, and verifies (1/s)(kg m/s) = N without invoking collision conservation, impulse integration or rocket dynamics.

microtopics.title: Force from a steady stream of discrete momentum changes
microtopics.badge_reason: The key decisions are the system/direction choice and distinguishing force on the ejecta from equal-and-opposite launcher recoil and the external support force that balances it.
entry_assumptions: Can assign forces to the body they act on.
Can use Newton II as a force-motion relation for a chosen body.
Can keep Newton-third-law interaction partners on different bodies.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A repeated stream converts a momentum change per item into a momentum change per unit time: if each fixed-mass item receives signed Delta p_item and R such items are ejected per second, the average force on the ejecta is R Delta p_item; the launcher receives the opposite interaction force, so a stationary launcher requires an external holding force that balances that recoil.

teaching_path.action: Choose one inertial frame and declare the positive ejection direction before writing any momentum or force sign.
teaching_path.why_valid: Momentum and force are directed quantities; the recoil/holding-force signs are only meaningful relative to a declared frame and axis.
teaching_path.output: + direction = ejection direction; v_in and v_out are signed in the same inertial frame

teaching_path.action: For one fixed-mass ejected item, compute its signed momentum change from Delta p_item = m(v_out - v_in).
teaching_path.why_valid: Linear momentum of that item is p = m v, so its change is final momentum minus initial momentum in the same frame.
teaching_path.output: p_in = m v_in; p_out = m v_out; Delta p_item = m(v_out - v_in)

teaching_path.action: If R identical items are ejected per second with the same represented momentum change, multiply the per-item change by the ejection rate.
teaching_path.why_valid: Over a time Delta t containing n = R Delta t items, the ejecta gain total momentum n Delta p_item; dividing by Delta t gives the average momentum-change rate and therefore the average external force on the ejecta.
teaching_path.output: F_avg,on_ejecta = Delta p_total/Delta t = (n/Delta t) Delta p_item = R Delta p_item

teaching_path.action: Use the interaction-pair direction to assign the launcher's average recoil force opposite the force on the ejecta; if the launcher is held stationary, assign the external holding force opposite the recoil.
teaching_path.why_valid: The launcher-on-ejecta and ejecta-on-launcher forces are interaction partners on different bodies; a stationary launcher needs zero net average force.
teaching_path.output: F_avg,on_launcher_by_ejecta = -R Delta p_item; held stationary -> F_avg,holding_on_launcher = +R Delta p_item

teaching_path.action: Check units and signs before reporting the force.
teaching_path.why_valid: The rate-times-momentum product must reduce to force units and the launcher/holding directions must be consistent with the chosen positive ejection direction.
teaching_path.output: R Delta p_item units = (1/s)(kg m/s) = kg m/s^2 = N; recoil sign is opposite ejecta momentum gain

teaching_path.action: State the time meaning of the computed stream force: R Delta p_item is an average over the repeated events, not a claim that the force on the launcher or on each item is constant at every instant.
teaching_path.why_valid: A rate of repeated discrete momentum changes fixes the average momentum transferred per unit time. The detailed force pulse during one launch requires additional force-versus-time or interaction-time information that this bounded model does not provide.
teaching_path.output: known repeated-event data -> F_avg = R Delta p_item; instantaneous force waveform remains undetermined without extra time-profile information

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The force magnitude is firing rate times m v_out even when the item already had nonzero velocity in the chosen frame.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If an item enters the launch process with v_in not equal to zero, which momentum determines the transferred amount: final momentum alone or final minus initial?
misconceptions.repair: Use the momentum change per item: Delta p_item = m(v_out - v_in). Final momentum alone works only when the chosen-frame initial momentum is zero.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The force that accelerates the ejecta and the recoil force on the launcher point in the same direction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: With ejection defined positive, which body receives the positive interaction force and which receives its partner?
misconceptions.repair: The ejecta gain positive momentum and receive a positive force. The launcher receives the equal-and-opposite interaction force. A holding force that keeps the launcher fixed points opposite the recoil.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Once a momentum-rate formula appears, the problem should be treated as rocket or continuously varying-mass dynamics.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does this task require solving how a launcher's mass and velocity evolve continuously, or only the average momentum transferred by repeated fixed-mass items?
misconceptions.repair: Stay with the discrete stream: momentum change per item times items per second. Do not import a rocket equation or variable-mass differential model.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The value R Delta p_item is the instantaneous force at every moment during firing.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If each launch produces a short force pulse followed by a gap, can the event rate and momentum change alone determine the peak force inside the pulse?
misconceptions.repair: No. R Delta p_item gives the average force over the repeated stream. Peak or instantaneous force needs additional interaction-time or force-time information.

exit_task.prompt: A launcher is held fixed. Identical items of mass m enter the launch process with signed velocity v_in and leave with signed velocity v_out in the same inertial frame. The steady ejection rate is R items per second, and positive is the exit direction. Give the average force on the ejecta, the interaction force on the launcher, the external holding force required to keep the launcher fixed, and the unit check.

answer.summary: Delta p_item = m(v_out-v_in). The average force on the ejecta is F_ejecta = R Delta p_item. The ejecta exert -R Delta p_item on the launcher, so the holding force required for a fixed launcher is +R Delta p_item. The units are N.
reasoning: Use one declared inertial frame and the same positive direction for both item velocities.
One item's momentum change is final minus initial: m(v_out-v_in).
R items each second multiply the per-item momentum change into an average momentum-transfer rate R Delta p_item.
The launcher receives the opposite interaction force; a stationary launcher requires an external holding force that balances that recoil.
answer.check: (1/s)(kg m/s) = kg m/s^2 = N. If v_out = v_in, Delta p_item and this transfer force are zero; reversing the ejection direction reverses all signed force directions.
acceptable_alternatives: State only magnitudes after explicitly naming the corresponding directions.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit derives symbolic momentum-transfer and force relations and checks dimensions; it asserts no computed numerical force.

microtopics.research_contribution: The owner-supplied ExamSIDE machine-gun demand requires momentum transferred per unit time and cannot be represented honestly by the existing constant-mass F_net = m a learner action alone. This microtopic adds only the discrete ejection-stream extension needed by that demand.

predict.prompt: A held launcher sends identical items forward at a steady rate. Before calculating, should the interaction force on the launcher point with the ejection direction or opposite it?
predict.defensible_answer: Opposite the ejection direction. The ejecta gain forward momentum, while the launcher receives the interaction partner force backward.

attempt.produces: A declared sign convention, one-item momentum change, rate-to-force calculation, recoil direction, holding-force direction and unit check.
attempt.model_response: Choose + along ejection; compute Delta p_item=m(v_out-v_in); use F_on_ejecta=R Delta p_item; launcher recoil is the negative of that interaction force; a holding force for a fixed launcher balances the recoil; verify newtons.

route.ask: What is the signed momentum change of one item in the declared frame?
route.why_this_ask: The force depends on momentum transferred, so the per-item change must be correct before any rate is used.

route.ask: How much total item momentum changes during a time interval containing n identical ejections?
route.why_this_ask: It makes the rate relation a count of repeated changes rather than a memorized formula.

route.ask: After dividing by the interval, what force acts on the ejecta and what is the interaction-partner force on the launcher?
route.why_this_ask: It separates the force on the stream from the recoil force on a different body.

route.ask: If the launcher remains fixed, what external force must balance the recoil?
route.why_this_ask: The requested holding force is not the recoil itself; it is the external force that cancels it.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner reconstructs the rate relation from a finite count of repeated item momentum changes before seeing the compact R Delta p_item expression.

boundary_test.prompt: If the ejected item leaves with exactly the same signed velocity it had on entry in the chosen frame, what momentum-transfer force does this bounded model predict?
boundary_test.answer: Zero, because Delta p_item = m(v_out-v_in) = 0, so R Delta p_item = 0.
boundary_test.confirms: The relation responds to momentum change per item, not merely to the fact that items are being emitted.

relations.meaning: The signed one-dimensional linear momentum of one fixed-mass item equals its mass times its signed velocity in the declared inertial frame.

symbols.meaning: Signed linear momentum of one item
Positive fixed mass of that item
Signed velocity of the item in the declared inertial frame

conditions: The item mass is positive and fixed during the compared states.
Velocity and momentum use the same declared one-dimensional positive direction.
Initial and final velocities are measured in the same inertial frame.

derivation.action: Use p=m v for the same fixed-mass item in its initial and final states.
derivation.why_valid: The relation defines the bounded linear-momentum quantity used by this extension.

derivation.action: Subtract the initial value from the final value.
derivation.why_valid: A change is final minus initial in the same sign convention.

limits: This relation alone is not a momentum-conservation law.
This extension does not introduce relativistic momentum.
checks: Momentum units are kg m/s.
Reversing the velocity sign reverses the momentum sign.

relations.meaning: The net external force on a chosen system equals its directed rate of change of linear momentum; this bounded Grade-9 extension evaluates that rate through a steady discrete transfer rather than calculus.

symbols.meaning: Signed net external force on the chosen system
Signed linear momentum of the chosen system or stream
Time

conditions: System boundary, inertial frame and positive direction are declared.
The momentum and force refer to the same chosen system and frame.
For the learner route here, the rate is evaluated from repeated finite momentum transfers; no derivative calculation is required.

derivation.action: Over a finite interval Delta t, total the directed momentum change of the chosen ejecta stream.
derivation.why_valid: A force rate must be tied to the momentum of the same chosen system over the same interval.

derivation.action: Use the momentum change per unit time as the average force over that interval.
derivation.why_valid: The discrete average is the finite-interval evaluation of the force-momentum-rate principle used in this extension.

limits: No impulse integral is required.
No continuously varying-mass differential equation is introduced.
This relation is not itself a collision-conservation rule.
checks: (kg m/s)/s = kg m/s^2 = N.
The force sign follows the sign of the momentum-change rate for the chosen system.

relations.meaning: If identical fixed-mass items undergo the same signed momentum change and are ejected at steady rate R items per second, the ejecta stream's average momentum-change rate and average force equal R times the momentum change per item.

symbols.meaning: Signed average force on the ejecta stream
Steady number of identical items ejected per unit time
Signed momentum change of one ejected item

conditions: The represented items are identical for the calculation or share the same Delta p_item.
R is the number ejected per unit time over the averaging interval.
Delta p_item uses the same inertial frame and positive direction for every item.
The reported force is an average over the repeated discrete ejections.

derivation.action: For n identical items in interval Delta t, add their equal signed momentum changes.
derivation.why_valid: Momentum change of the represented ejecta stream is the sum of the item momentum changes.

derivation.action: Divide by Delta t and use R=n/Delta t.
derivation.why_valid: Items per unit time converts the per-item transfer into a momentum-transfer rate.
derivation.output: F_avg,on_ejecta = (n/Delta t) Delta p_item = R Delta p_item

limits: Do not apply one common Delta p_item when the ejected items have materially different momentum changes without averaging them appropriately.
This is not a rocket equation or a continuously varying-mass solution.
checks: R Delta p_item has newton units.
Doubling R while holding Delta p_item fixed doubles the average force.
If Delta p_item=0, the transfer force is zero.

question_families.title: Discrete momentum-transfer force practice
solution_structure: Declare one inertial frame and positive ejection direction.
Compute one item's final-minus-initial momentum change.
Convert repeated item changes into momentum transferred per unit time.
Separate force on ejecta, launcher recoil, and any external holding force.
Check force units and a zero-transfer/sign-reversal boundary.

demand_dimensions.model_choice: Recognize repeated discrete momentum transfer without being told to use a momentum-rate relation.
demand_dimensions.representation_translation: Convert item counts over an interval into an ejection rate or vice versa before applying the same momentum-transfer structure.
demand_dimensions.reasoning_steps: Keep per-item momentum change, stream force, launcher recoil and holding-force balance distinct.
demand_dimensions.novelty: Map a new discrete-ejection story onto the same fixed-mass-per-item rate structure without importing collision or rocket methods.

safe_variations: Change item mass, entry velocity, exit velocity or ejection rate while preserving one inertial frame and repeated fixed-mass items.
Change the physical story from pellets to another discrete stream while preserving the same per-item momentum change and rate structure.
Reverse the declared coordinate direction while preserving the same physical ejection so every signed momentum and force result must transform consistently.
Give a count over a finite time interval instead of an already-computed items-per-second rate.
Ask whether a computed stream force is an average or an instantaneous pulse quantity without supplying pulse-time information.
transfer_boundaries: Do not replace Delta p_item with final momentum unless initial momentum is zero in the chosen frame.
Do not import collision-conservation, impulse-integral or rocket/continuously varying-mass methods unless explicitly demanded.
Do not report R Delta p_item as an instantaneous or peak force; it is the average force determined by the repeated-event data.
A nonzero ejection rate does not imply a nonzero transfer force when each item's signed momentum change is zero.
common_wrong_routes: Use m v_out instead of m(v_out-v_in).
Give launcher recoil and holding force the same role or body.
Treat the derivative notation as a requirement to perform calculus.
Treat items per minute or a finite item count as though it were already items per second.
Treat the average stream force as a continuous instantaneous force trace.

questions.stem: A fixed launcher processes identical pellets of mass m. In the laboratory frame each pellet enters moving in the positive direction with speed u and leaves in the same direction with speed v, where v > u. The steady processing rate is R pellets per second. Find the average force on the pellets, the interaction force on the launcher, and the external holding force required to keep the launcher fixed.
conditions: Use one laboratory inertial frame.
Take the pellet exit direction as positive.
Treat the stream as repeated identical fixed-mass pellets with steady rate R.

answer.summary: Each pellet gains Delta p = m(v-u), so the average force on the pellets is +Rm(v-u). The pellets exert -Rm(v-u) on the launcher. To keep the launcher fixed, the external holding force is +Rm(v-u).
reasoning: Use final minus initial momentum for one pellet: Delta p_item = m(v-u).
R pellets per second multiply that per-item change into the momentum-change rate Rm(v-u).
That rate is the average force on the pellet stream in the positive direction.
The launcher receives the equal-and-opposite interaction force.
A fixed launcher requires an external holding force that balances the recoil.
answer.check: If v=u, the force from this momentum transfer must become zero even though the pellets still carry nonzero momentum.

hints.text: Do not start with the pellet's final momentum. What is the change in momentum of one pellet in the chosen frame?
Multiply the per-pellet momentum change by pellets per second, then keep the force on the pellets separate from the reaction on the launcher.

questions.stem: A launcher is held fixed and ejects 0.020 kg projectiles from rest at 8 projectiles per second. Each leaves at 300 m/s in the positive direction. Find the average force on the projectile stream, the average recoil force on the launcher, and the external holding force.
conditions: Use the laboratory frame.
Positive is the ejection direction.
The repeated stream is steady.

answer.summary: Each projectile gains 6 kg m/s of momentum, so the average force on the stream is +48 N. The stream exerts -48 N on the launcher, and the holding force on the fixed launcher is +48 N.
reasoning: One projectile changes momentum by Delta p=0.020(300-0)=6 kg m/s.
Eight identical changes each second give an average stream force 8(6)=48 N in the positive direction.
The projectile stream exerts the interaction-partner force -48 N on the launcher.
Because the launcher is held fixed, the external support must supply +48 N to balance the recoil.
answer.check: The rate-times-momentum units are (1/s)(kg m/s)=N, and the launcher recoil has the opposite sign from the projectile momentum gain.

hints.text: First find the momentum change of one projectile in the declared laboratory frame.
Convert the repeated identical changes into momentum gained each second, then assign the interaction-partner and holding-force directions to the correct bodies.

questions.stem: During a 6.0 s interval, a fixed launcher processes 90 identical 0.010 kg pellets. In the laboratory frame each pellet enters at +20 m/s and leaves at +140 m/s. Find the average force on the pellet stream over the interval.
conditions: Positive is the common entry/exit direction.
The same momentum change applies to each of the 90 pellets.

answer.summary: The rate is 90/6=15 pellets/s. Each pellet gains 0.010(140-20)=1.2 kg m/s, so the average force on the stream is +18 N.
reasoning: Convert the finite count into the event rate R=90/6=15 s^-1.
One pellet changes momentum by Delta p=0.010(120)=1.2 kg m/s.
The average momentum-transfer rate is R Delta p=15(1.2)=18 kg m/s^2.
The positive sign follows from the pellet momentum increase in the declared positive direction.
answer.check: Using 90 as though it were pellets per second would overstate the force by a factor of six.

hints.text: The question gives a number of pellets over a time interval, not yet a rate in pellets per second.
Compute R=n/Delta t, then multiply by the final-minus-initial momentum change of one pellet.

questions.stem: A fixed launcher ejects 0.050 kg projectiles to the left from rest at 5 projectiles per second. The coordinate axis is chosen positive to the right, and each projectile leaves with velocity -40 m/s. Give the signed average force on the projectile stream, the signed recoil force on the launcher, and the signed external holding force.
conditions: Use the laboratory frame.
Rightward is positive.
The launcher remains fixed.

answer.summary: Each projectile has Delta p=0.050(-40-0)=-2 kg m/s. The average stream force is -10 N, the recoil force on the launcher is +10 N, and the external holding force on the launcher is -10 N.
reasoning: Keep the declared right-positive coordinate even though the physical ejection is leftward.
One projectile's signed momentum change is -2 kg m/s.
Five such changes per second give -10 N on the projectile stream.
The launcher receives the opposite interaction force +10 N, so the support must apply -10 N to hold it fixed.
answer.check: Changing the coordinate convention would reverse all three signs but not the physical directions or force magnitudes.

hints.text: Use the declared right-positive axis; do not silently replace the signed exit velocity by its speed.
After finding the signed stream force, use body ownership to reverse the sign for launcher recoil and reverse it again for the holding force.

questions.stem: A held launcher ejects 120 identical 0.010 kg pellets from rest to +100 m/s during a 4.0 s interval. Compute the average force on the pellet stream. Then state whether this calculation proves that the instantaneous force is equal to that value at every moment of the 4.0 s interval.
conditions: Positive is the ejection direction.
Only the item count, interval and per-item velocity change are known; no force-time pulse shape or interaction time is supplied.

answer.summary: The rate is 30 pellets/s and each pellet gains 1 kg m/s, so the average stream force is +30 N. This does not determine the instantaneous force at every moment; the detailed pulses require additional time-profile information.
reasoning: The event rate over the interval is R=120/4=30 s^-1.
One pellet gains Delta p=0.010(100)=1 kg m/s.
The repeated-event momentum-transfer rate gives F_avg=30(1)=30 N.
That result is an average over the interval. The same impulse per event could arise from different short force pulses.
answer.check: A force trace containing brief peaks and zero-force gaps can still have a 30 N time average, so the average alone cannot specify the peak value.

hints.text: Separate the quantity determined by total momentum change divided by the full interval from the detailed force during one individual launch.
Compute n/Delta t and the per-item Delta p for the average; do not invent a peak force without pulse-time data.

questions.stem: A held launcher fires 0.004 kg projectiles from rest at 20 per second, each leaving at 500 m/s. No acceleration time or barrel length is supplied. A learner says the average holding force cannot be found because F=ma needs the projectile acceleration. Determine whether the requested average force is nevertheless fixed by the given information, and find it if it is.
conditions: Use the laboratory frame.
Positive is the ejection direction.
The question asks for the long-time average holding force, not the force pulse on one projectile.

answer.summary: Yes. Each projectile gains 2 kg m/s of momentum and 20 are fired each second, so the projectile stream gains momentum at +40 N. The launcher recoil is -40 N and the required average holding force is +40 N.
reasoning: The missing acceleration time prevents finding the detailed acceleration or instantaneous launch force on one projectile.
It does not prevent finding the momentum change of one projectile: 0.004(500)=2 kg m/s.
Twenty identical momentum changes each second give an average momentum-transfer rate of 40 N.
The support must balance the opposite launcher recoil.
answer.check: Any barrel-time profile consistent with the same projectile momentum change and firing rate gives the same long-time average momentum-transfer force.

rubric.criterion: Recognizes that the requested average force is determined even though projectile acceleration time is absent.
rubric.evidence_of: Selects the rate-of-momentum route instead of declaring the problem unsolvable from missing ma data.

rubric.criterion: Computes 2 kg m/s per projectile and 40 N for the stream.
rubric.evidence_of: Connects the available per-item momentum change to the event rate.

rubric.criterion: Assigns +40 N to the external holding force on the fixed launcher.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeps stream force, recoil and holding force on their correct bodies.

adaptation.reason: Withholds projectile acceleration time and asks whether the average force remains determined, forcing selection of the momentum-transfer representation rather than a direct ma calculation.

hints.text: Which change for one projectile can be computed from its mass and initial/final velocities without knowing the duration of the launch?
The question asks for a long-time average over many identical events, not the detailed force during one event.

transfer.statement: The learner must choose a momentum-change-rate representation when the requested average force is determined but the acceleration-time information needed for a direct per-projectile ma route is absent.

questions.stem: A test log records 600 identical projectiles during a 30 s run. Each has mass 5.0 g, enters the launcher at +50 m/s and leaves at +250 m/s. Convert the log into the quantities needed to determine the average holding force on a fixed launcher, and give that force.
conditions: Positive is the exit direction.
Use SI units before multiplying the rate by the per-item momentum change.

answer.summary: The log gives R=600/30=20 s^-1 and m=0.0050 kg. Each item gains 0.0050(250-50)=1.0 kg m/s, so the stream force is +20 N, the recoil is -20 N and the required holding force is +20 N.
reasoning: Translate the event log into an ejection rate of 20 items per second.
Translate 5.0 g into 0.0050 kg.
Use final-minus-initial momentum to obtain 1.0 kg m/s per item.
The average stream force is 20 N; the fixed launcher needs the opposite-of-recoil holding force +20 N.
answer.check: The count and time must first become s^-1; treating 600 as the rate would give a dimensionally misleading result.

rubric.criterion: Converts the finite log into 20 items/s and 5.0 g into 0.0050 kg.
rubric.evidence_of: Translates the supplied representation into the capability's SI rate and per-item quantities.

rubric.criterion: Uses the 200 m/s velocity change rather than the final 250 m/s alone.
rubric.evidence_of: Preserves the final-minus-initial momentum meaning after representation conversion.

rubric.criterion: Reports +20 N as the holding force on the fixed launcher.
rubric.evidence_of: Carries the translated quantities through the force-role sequence.

adaptation.reason: Changes a direct SI finite-count problem into a test-log representation with mass-unit conversion, requiring the learner to reconstruct the event rate and per-item momentum change before using the same physics.

hints.text: The log does not yet give the two quantities in the form used by the momentum-transfer relation: convert the count/time and the mass first.
After the representation is in SI form, compute one item's final-minus-initial momentum and then the repeated-event average.

transfer.statement: The learner must translate a finite event log and non-SI mass into the rate/per-item representation before applying the already-taught momentum-transfer relation.

questions.stem: A launcher ejects projectiles to the left while the laboratory x-axis is positive to the right. From the repeated stream calculation, the launcher experiences an average recoil force of +12 N. The launcher is held fixed by a support. State (i) the force of the support on the launcher and (ii) the force of the launcher on the support, with signs, and explain why these two forces must not be confused.
conditions: Rightward is positive.
The launcher remains fixed.
Only horizontal forces are being discussed.

answer.summary: The support must exert -12 N on the launcher so the launcher's average net force is zero. By Newton III, the launcher exerts +12 N on the support. These are an interaction pair on different bodies; the +12 N launcher recoil from the projectile stream is a different force acting on the launcher.
reasoning: The given projectile-stream recoil on the launcher is +12 N.
A fixed launcher requires zero average horizontal net force, so support-on-launcher must be -12 N.
The Newton-third-law partner of support-on-launcher is launcher-on-support, +12 N.
The projectile-stream recoil and the support interaction both act on the launcher and therefore are not a third-law pair with each other; they balance in the launcher's force sum.
answer.check: If support-on-launcher were also +12 N, the fixed launcher would have a nonzero +24 N average net force, contradicting the held condition.

rubric.criterion: Assigns -12 N to support-on-launcher.
rubric.evidence_of: Uses the fixed-launcher force balance on the correct body.

rubric.criterion: Assigns +12 N to launcher-on-support.
rubric.evidence_of: Forms the actual Newton-third-law pair across support and launcher.

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes the projectile recoil from the support reaction pair.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeps forces that balance on one body separate from interaction partners on different bodies.

adaptation.reason: Changes the target from computing recoil/holding magnitudes to identifying the additional support interaction pair, requiring a body-by-body force account after the signed recoil is known.

hints.text: For the held launcher, which force must cancel the stated +12 N recoil in the launcher's own force sum?
After identifying support-on-launcher, find its Newton-third-law partner by changing the body on which the force acts.

transfer.statement: The learner must extend the stream/recoil result into a support-body force account and distinguish a balancing force on one body from a Newton-third-law partner on another.

questions.stem: A device passes identical pellets through at a steady nonzero rate. In the chosen laboratory frame each pellet enters at +120 m/s and leaves at +120 m/s. A proposed shortcut says that because pellets emerge carrying momentum, the device must experience a nonzero average recoil equal to rate times m times 120 m/s. Decide whether that conclusion follows from the bounded momentum-transfer model.
conditions: The pellet mass is unchanged.
The stated entry and exit velocities are equal in the same inertial frame.
Consider only the momentum transfer associated with this through-stream.

answer.summary: No. Each pellet has Delta p=m(120-120)=0, so the average momentum-transfer force from this through-stream is zero despite the nonzero momentum carried by the pellets.
reasoning: The force is tied to momentum change of each item, not to final momentum carried away by itself.
Here final and initial signed velocities are identical, so Delta p_item=0.
Multiplying the nonzero event rate by zero momentum change still gives zero average transfer force.
Using Rmv_out would count momentum the pellets already possessed before entering the device.
answer.check: If the device changes the exit speed while the entry speed stays +120 m/s, the transfer force becomes nonzero again in proportion to that change.

rubric.criterion: Rejects the nonzero-force shortcut despite the nonzero stream momentum.
rubric.evidence_of: Uses momentum change rather than momentum presence as the causal quantity.

rubric.criterion: Sets Delta p_item to zero from equal signed entry and exit velocities.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeps both states in the same inertial frame.

rubric.criterion: Concludes zero average transfer force for the bounded stream contribution.
rubric.evidence_of: Applies the rate relation without inventing momentum change.

adaptation.reason: Changes the familiar speed-up case into a nonzero-throughput but zero-momentum-change case so the learner must decide whether the force depends on final momentum or on transferred momentum.

hints.text: Compare the pellet's signed momentum before and after the device rather than looking only at what leaves.

transfer.statement: The learner must refuse a final-momentum shortcut when a nonzero item stream carries momentum but the device produces no per-item momentum change.

questions.stem: A repeated-launch calculation gives F_avg=30 N for a held launcher. A high-speed force sensor, however, shows short force pulses separated by intervals close to zero force. A learner says the sensor disproves the 30 N result because the force is not constantly 30 N. Decide whether the two observations are compatible and state what additional information would be needed to determine a peak force.
conditions: The 30 N value was obtained from total transferred momentum divided by the full observation time.
No individual pulse duration or force-time shape is supplied.

answer.summary: They are compatible. The 30 N result is the time-average momentum-transfer force over many events, not an assertion of a constant instantaneous force. Determining a peak force requires additional pulse-duration or force-time-profile information.
reasoning: The repeated-event relation fixes total momentum change divided by the observation time.
A pulsed signal can have the same time average while taking values much larger than 30 N during a short event and near zero between events.
Therefore the sensor trace does not contradict the average result.
Peak force cannot be recovered from event rate and momentum change alone.
answer.check: Different pulse shapes can have the same impulse per event and the same event rate, so they can share the same average force while having different peaks.

rubric.criterion: Keeps the 30 N value as a time average rather than a constant-force claim.
rubric.evidence_of: Interprets the output of the repeated-event relation at the correct temporal scale.

rubric.criterion: Accepts a pulsed force trace as compatible with the same average.
rubric.evidence_of: Does not confuse average force with instantaneous waveform.

rubric.criterion: Names pulse duration or force-time profile as missing information for a peak value.
rubric.evidence_of: Respects the boundary of what the available data determine.

adaptation.reason: Changes a calculation-and-interpretation exercise into a conflict between an average-force result and a pulsed sensor representation, requiring the learner to decide which temporal claim the model actually makes.

hints.text: Ask whether total momentum change divided by a long observation time specifies every value of the force inside that interval.

transfer.statement: The learner must decide whether a pulsed instantaneous-force trace invalidates a correctly computed average momentum-transfer force and identify the missing information needed for a peak value.

teaching_routes.title: Completed discrete momentum-transfer force construction
entry_needs: Body-specific force ownership, Newton-II force reasoning and Newton-third-law interaction-pair direction remain explicit prerequisites from the ordinary NLM spine.
This route is entered only when a real question or owner request explicitly demands momentum-transfer force.
learner_actions: Declare frame and positive direction.
Compute one item's signed momentum change.
Convert repeated item changes into momentum transferred per unit time.
Separate force on ejecta, launcher recoil and external holding force.
Verify force units and boundary cases.
help_plan: Ask for final-minus-initial momentum of one item before giving the rate relation.
Ask how many identical transfers occur during a finite time interval before revealing R Delta p_item.
Ask which body each interaction force acts on before asking for the holding-force direction.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: The completed symbolic construction is shown only after the sign convention, item momentum change and system/body distinction are explicit.

source_preferences.reason: Justifies why this non-default extension exists without turning the external item into canonical curriculum or question custody.
Supplies the exact teaching route while preserving the issue's non-goals.

when_not_suitable: Do not use this route for general collisions, coefficient of restitution or center-of-mass methods.
Do not infer a rocket equation or continuously varying-mass model.
Do not use it in the ordinary default NLM path when no momentum-transfer demand exists.

teaching_routes.title: Reconstruct discrete momentum-transfer force from repeated item changes
entry_needs: Same NLM prerequisites as Core1A; no rough percentage or generic NLM request may silently activate this extension.
learner_actions: Predict recoil direction before calculation.
Build Delta p_item from signed initial and final item velocities.
Reconstruct force as repeated momentum change per unit time.
Infer the holding force only after identifying the launcher reaction.
help_plan: Keep the per-item momentum change separate from the ejection rate.
If signs are confused, return to the declared positive ejection direction and body ownership.
If the learner invokes collisions or rockets, ask which requested quantity actually requires those models.
